Open your ears; for which of you will stop / The vent of hearing when loud Rumour speaks? / I, from the orient to the drooping west, / Making the wind my post-horse, still unfold / The acts commenced on this ball of earth: / Upon my tongues continual slanders ride, / The which in every language I pronounce, / Stuffing the ears of men with false reports. / I speak of peace, while covert enmity / Under the smile of safety wounds the world: / And who but Rumour, who but only I, / Make fearful musters and prepared defence, / Whiles the big year, swoln with some other grief, / Is thought with child by the stern tyrant war, / And no such matter? Rumour is a pipe / Blown by surmises, jealousies, conjectures, / And of so easy and so plain a stop / That the blunt monster with uncounted heads, / The still-discordant wavering multitude, / Can play upon it. But what need I thus / My well-known body to anatomize / Among my household? Why is Rumour here? / I run before King Harry's victory; / Who in a bloody field by Shrewsbury / Hath beaten down young Hotspur and his troops, / Quenching the flame of bold rebellion / Even with the rebels' blood. But what mean I / To speak so true at first? my office is / To noise abroad that Harry Monmouth fell / Under the wrath of noble Hotspur's sword, / And that the king before the Douglas' rage / Stoop'd his anointed head as low as death. / This have I rumour'd through the peasant towns / Between that royal field of Shrewsbury / And this worm-eaten hold of ragged stone, / Where Hotspur's father, old Northumberland, / Lies crafty-sick: the posts come tiring on, / And not a man of them brings other news / Than they have learn'd of me: from Rumour's tongues / They bring smooth comforts false, worse than true wrongs.

Listen closely, for which of you would block your ears when loud Rumour is speaking? Riding the wind like a post-horse, I carry news from east to west of everything that starts on this earth. Slanders ride constantly on my tongues; I speak them in every language and stuff men's ears with false reports. I talk of peace while hidden hatred, smiling behind a mask of safety, wounds the world. And who but Rumour, who but I alone, causes frightened gathering of troops and defences, while the swollen year, pregnant with some other trouble, is thought to be carrying a child fathered by that tyrant, war, when it is nothing of the kind? Rumour is a pipe blown by guesses, suspicions and assumptions, and its finger-holes are so simple that even the dull many-headed monster, the ever-quarrelling, wavering crowd, can play on it. But why should I dissect my famous body for you, my own household? Why is Rumour here? I run ahead of King Henry's victory: at the bloody battle of Shrewsbury he has beaten young Hotspur and his troops and put out the fire of rebellion with the rebels' own blood. But why am I telling the truth at the start? My job is to spread the story that Prince Harry fell to noble Hotspur's sword, and that the King bowed his anointed head as low as death before the furious Douglas. I have spread this rumour through the country towns between that royal battlefield at Shrewsbury and this worm-eaten fortress of rough stone, where Hotspur's father, old Northumberland, is pretending to be ill. The messengers come riding in exhausted, and not one of them brings any news but what they learned from me. From Rumour's tongues they bring false comfort, which is worse than true bad news.
Who keeps the gate here, ho?
Who's keeping the gate here? Hello!
What shall I say you are?
Who shall I say you are?
Tell thou the earl / That the Lord Bardolph doth attend him here.
Tell the Earl that Lord Bardolph is waiting for him here.
His lordship is walk'd forth into the orchard: / Please it your honour, knock but at the gate, / And he himself will answer.
His lordship has gone for a walk in the orchard. If your honour will just knock at the gate, he'll answer it himself.

What news, Lord Bardolph? every minute now / Should be the father of some stratagem: / The times are wild; contention, like a horse / Full of high feeding, madly hath broke loose / And bears down all before him.
What news, Lord Bardolph? Every minute now should give birth to some new scheme. These are wild times: conflict, like an overfed horse, has broken loose and is trampling everything in its way.
Noble earl, / I bring you certain news from Shrewsbury.
Noble Earl, I bring you sure news from Shrewsbury.

As good as heart can wish: / The king is almost wounded to the death; / And, in the fortune of my lord your son, / Prince Harry slain outright; and both the Blunts / Kill'd by the hand of Douglas; young Prince John, / And Westmoreland and Stafford fled the field: / And Harry Monmouth's brawn, the hulk Sir John, / Is prisoner to your son: O, such a day, / So fought, so follow'd and so fairly won, / Came not till now to dignify the times, / Since Caesar's fortunes!

As good as anyone could wish. The King is wounded almost to death. Thanks to your son's success, Prince Harry has been killed outright, and both the Blunts killed by Douglas. Young Prince John, Westmoreland and Stafford ran from the field, and Prince Harry's lump of meat, that hulk Sir John, is your son's prisoner. Oh, such a day, so well fought, so well followed up and so honourably won, has not graced the times since Caesar's victories!
How is this derived? / Saw you the field? came you from Shrewsbury?
Where did you get this? Did you see the battle? Have you come from Shrewsbury?
I spake with one, my lord, that came from thence, / A gentleman well bred and of good name, / That freely render'd me these news for true.
I talked to a man who came from there, my lord, a well-bred gentleman of good reputation, who freely told me this news as true.
Here comes my servant Travers, whom I sent / On Tuesday last to listen after news.
Here comes my servant Travers, whom I sent out last Tuesday to listen for news.
My lord, I over-rode him on the way; / And he is furnish'd with no certainties / More than he haply may retail from me.
My lord, I overtook him on the road, and he has no sure facts beyond what he may have picked up from me.
Now, Travers, what good tidings comes with you?
Well, Travers, what good news do you bring?

My lord, Sir John Umfrevile turn'd me back / With joyful tidings; and, being better horsed, / Out-rode me. After him came spurring hard / A gentleman, almost forspent with speed, / That stopp'd by me to breathe his bloodied horse. / He ask'd the way to Chester; and of him / I did demand what news from Shrewsbury: / He told me that rebellion had bad luck / And that young Harry Percy's spur was cold. / With that, he gave his able horse the head, / And bending forward struck his armed heels / Against the panting sides of his poor jade / Up to the rowel-head, and starting so / He seem'd in running to devour the way, / Staying no longer question.

My lord, Sir John Umfrevile turned me back with happy news and, having a better horse, rode on ahead of me. After him came a gentleman spurring hard, almost worn out with speed, who stopped beside me to rest his bleeding horse. He asked the way to Chester, and I asked him what news there was from Shrewsbury. He told me the rebellion had had bad luck and that young Harry Percy's spur was cold. With that he gave his horse its head, leaned forward and drove his armoured heels into the panting sides of his poor nag right up to the spur-wheel, and set off so fast he seemed to swallow the road, without waiting for more questions.
Ha! Again: / Said he young Harry Percy's spur was cold? / Of Hotspur Coldspur? that rebellion / Had met ill luck?
What? Say that again: did he say young Harry Percy's spur was cold? That Hotspur was Coldspur? That the rebellion had bad luck?
My lord, I'll tell you what; / If my young lord your son have not the day, / Upon mine honour, for a silken point / I'll give my barony: never talk of it.
My lord, I'll tell you this: if your son hasn't won the day, I'll give my whole barony for a silk lace. Don't even talk about it.
Why should that gentleman that rode by Travers / Give then such instances of loss?
Then why should the gentleman who rode past Travers give such details of a defeat?
Who, he? / He was some hilding fellow that had stolen / The horse he rode on, and, upon my life, / Spoke at a venture. Look, here comes more news.
Who, him? He was some worthless fellow who'd stolen the horse he was riding and, I swear, said whatever came into his head. Look, here comes more news.

Yea, this man's brow, like to a title-leaf, / Foretells the nature of a tragic volume: / So looks the strand whereon the imperious flood / Hath left a witness'd usurpation. / Say, Morton, didst thou come from Shrewsbury?

Yes, this man's face, like the title page of a book, announces that a tragedy follows. He looks like a beach where the overpowering tide has left the marks of its invasion. Tell me, Morton, have you come from Shrewsbury?
I ran from Shrewsbury, my noble lord; / Where hateful death put on his ugliest mask / To fright our party.
I ran from Shrewsbury, my noble lord, where hateful death put on its ugliest mask to frighten our side.

How doth my son and brother? / Thou tremblest; and the whiteness in thy cheek / Is apter than thy tongue to tell thy errand. / Even such a man, so faint, so spiritless, / So dull, so dread in look, so woe-begone, / Drew Priam's curtain in the dead of night, / And would have told him half his Troy was burnt; / But Priam found the fire ere he his tongue, / And I my Percy's death ere thou report'st it. / This thou wouldst say: "Your son did thus and thus; / Your brother thus: so fought the noble Douglas:" / Stopping my greedy ear with their bold deeds: / But in the end, to stop my ear indeed, / Thou hast a sigh to blow away this praise, / Ending with "Brother, son, and all are dead."

How are my son and my brother? You're trembling, and the paleness of your cheek tells your message better than your tongue. A man just like you, as faint, as lifeless, as dull, as dreadful in his look and as miserable, opened King Priam's bed-curtains in the dead of night to tell him that half his Troy was burnt. But Priam saw the fire before the man could speak, and I see my Percy's death before you report it. This is what you'd say: "Your son did this and this; your brother this; this is how the noble Douglas fought," filling my greedy ears with their brave deeds. But in the end, to stop my ears for good, you have a sigh to blow all this praise away, and you finish with "Brother, son, and all are dead."
Douglas is living, and your brother, yet: / But, for my lord your son,—
Douglas is alive, and so is your brother, so far. But as for my lord your son —

Why, he is dead. / See what a ready tongue suspicion hath! / He that but fears the thing he would not know / Hath by instinct knowledge from others' eyes / That what he fear'd is chanced. Yet speak, Morton; / Tell thou an earl his divination lies, / And I will take it as a sweet disgrace / And make thee rich for doing me such wrong.

Why, he's dead. See how quickly suspicion speaks! A man who only fears the thing he doesn't want to know can read in other people's eyes, by instinct, that what he feared has happened. But speak, Morton. Tell an earl that his guess is wrong, and I'll take it as a sweet insult and make you rich for doing me such a wrong.
You are too great to be by me gainsaid: / Your spirit is too true, your fears too certain.
You are too great for me to contradict. Your instinct is too true, your fears too certain.

Yet, for all this, say not that Percy's dead. / I see a strange confession in thine eye; / Thou shakest thy head and hold'st it fear or sin / To speak a truth. If he be slain, say so; / The tongue offends not that reports his death: / And he doth sin that doth belie the dead, / Not he which says the dead is not alive / Yet the first bringer of unwelcome news / Hath but a losing office, and his tongue / Sounds ever after as a sullen bell, / Remember'd tolling a departing friend.

Even so, don't say that Percy's dead. I see a strange confession in your eye: you shake your head as if it were frightening or sinful to speak the truth. If he's been killed, say so. The tongue that reports his death does no wrong. It's a sin to lie about the dead, not to say that the dead are no longer alive. And yet the first person to bring bad news has a thankless job, and his voice sounds for ever after like a gloomy bell, remembered for tolling a friend's death.
I cannot think, my lord, your son is dead.
I can't believe, my lord, that your son is dead.

I am sorry I should force you to believe / That which I would to God I had not seen; / But these mine eyes saw him in bloody state, / Rendering faint quittance, wearied and outbreathed, / To Harry Monmouth; whose swift wrath beat down / The never-daunted Percy to the earth, / From whence with life he never more sprung up. / In few, his death, whose spirit lent a fire / Even to the dullest peasant in his camp, / Being bruited once, took fire and heat away / From the best-temper'd courage in his troops; / For from his metal was his party steel'd; / Which once in him abated, all the rest / Turn'd on themselves, like dull and heavy lead: / And as the thing that's heavy in itself, / Upon enforcement flies with greatest speed, / So did our men, heavy in Hotspur's loss, / Lend to this weight such lightness with their fear / That arrows fled not swifter toward their aim / Than did our soldiers, aiming at their safety, / Fly from the field. Then was that noble Worcester / Too soon ta'en prisoner; and that furious Scot, / The bloody Douglas, whose well-labouring sword / Had three times slain the appearance of the king, / 'Gan vail his stomach and did grace the shame / Of those that turn'd their backs, and in his flight, / Stumbling in fear, was took. The sum of all / Is that the king hath won, and hath sent out / A speedy power to encounter you, my lord, / Under the conduct of young Lancaster / And Westmoreland. This is the news at full.

I'm sorry I have to make you believe what I wish to God I had never seen. But these eyes of mine saw him covered in blood, fighting back feebly, exhausted and out of breath, against Prince Harry, whose swift fury beat the never-frightened Percy to the ground, and he never rose from it alive. In short, his death, whose spirit set fire even to the dullest peasant in his camp, once it was known, took the fire and heat from the bravest in his troops. His men took their steel from his metal, and once that was blunted all the rest turned in on themselves like dull, heavy lead. And just as something heavy flies fastest once it's thrown, so our men, made heavy by losing Hotspur, gave their weight such lightness with their fear that arrows never flew faster at their target than our soldiers, aiming at their own safety, fled from the field. Then that noble Worcester was taken prisoner too soon, and that furious Scot, the bloody Douglas, whose hard-working sword had three times killed men disguised as the King, began to lose heart and joined the shame of those who ran, and as he fled he stumbled in his fear and was captured. The sum of it is that the King has won and has quickly sent an army to meet you, my lord, under the command of young Lancaster and Westmoreland. That's the full news.

For this I shall have time enough to mourn. / In poison there is physic; and these news, / Having been well, that would have made me sick, / Being sick, have in some measure made me well: / And as the wretch, whose fever-weaken'd joints, / Like strengthless hinges, buckle under life, / Impatient of his fit, breaks like a fire / Out of his keeper's arms, even so my limbs, / Weaken'd with grief, being now enraged with grief, / Are thrice themselves. Hence, therefore, thou nice crutch! / A scaly gauntlet now with joints of steel / Must glove this hand: and hence, thou sickly quoif! / Thou art a guard too wanton for the head / Which princes, flesh'd with conquest, aim to hit. / Now bind my brows with iron; and approach / The ragged'st hour that time and spite dare bring / To frown upon the enraged Northumberland! / Let heaven kiss earth! now let not Nature's hand / Keep the wild flood confined! let order die! / And let this world no longer be a stage / To feed contention in a lingering act; / But let one spirit of the first-born Cain / Reign in all bosoms, that, each heart being set / On bloody courses, the rude scene may end, / And darkness be the burier of the dead!

I'll have plenty of time to mourn this. There's medicine in poison, and this news, which would have made me sick if I'd been well, has, now that I'm sick, made me almost well. And just as a sick wretch, whose fever-weakened joints buckle like feeble hinges under the weight of life, can't bear his fit and breaks out of his nurse's arms like a fire, so my limbs, weakened by grief and now enraged by grief, are three times their strength. Away with you, then, you dainty crutch! A scaly steel gauntlet must cover this hand now. And away, you sickly nightcap! You're too soft a protection for a head that princes, flushed with victory, are aiming at. Now bind my forehead with iron, and let the roughest hour that time and malice dare bring come and frown at the enraged Northumberland! Let heaven and earth collide! Let Nature's hand no longer hold back the wild sea! Let order die! And let this world no longer be a stage where conflict drags on through a slow act; instead let the spirit of Cain, the first murderer, rule in every heart, so that, with every heart set on bloodshed, the brutal play may end and darkness bury the dead!
This strained passion doth you wrong, my lord.
This violent passion is harming you, my lord.
Sweet earl, divorce not wisdom from your honour.
Dear Earl, don't divorce your wisdom from your honour.

The lives of all your loving complices / Lean on your health; the which, if you give o'er / To stormy passion, must perforce decay. / You cast the event of war, my noble lord, / And summ'd the account of chance, before you said / "Let us make head." It was your presurmise, / That, in the dole of blows, your son might drop: / You knew he walk'd o'er perils, on an edge, / More likely to fall in than to get o'er; / You were advised his flesh was capable / Of wounds and scars and that his forward spirit / Would lift him where most trade of danger ranged: / Yet did you say "Go forth;" and none of this, / Though strongly apprehended, could restrain / The stiff-borne action: what hath then befallen, / Or what hath this bold enterprise brought forth, / More than that being which was like to be?

The lives of all your loyal allies depend on your health, and if you give yourself up to stormy passion it must fail. You weighed the outcome of the war, my noble lord, and counted up the chances, before you said, "Let's raise an army." You foresaw that, in the sharing out of blows, your son might fall. You knew he was walking on a knife-edge over danger, more likely to fall in than to get across. You were told his body could be wounded and scarred and that his bold spirit would carry him wherever the danger was thickest. And yet you said "Go," and none of this, though you understood it well, could hold back the stubborn enterprise. So what has happened, what has this bold venture produced, except what was likely to happen?

We all that are engaged to this loss / Knew that we ventured on such dangerous seas / That if we wrought out life 'twas ten to one; / And yet we ventured, for the gain proposed / Choked the respect of likely peril fear'd; / And since we are o'erset, venture again. / Come, we will put forth, body and goods.

All of us involved in this loss knew we were sailing such dangerous seas that it was ten to one against coming out alive. And yet we took the risk, because the prize we hoped for smothered our fear of the danger. And since we've been overturned, let's take the risk again. Come, we'll stake everything, our lives and our goods.

'Tis more than time: and, my most noble lord, / I hear for certain, and dare speak the truth: / The gentle Archbishop of York is up / With well-appointed powers: he is a man / Who with a double surety binds his followers. / My lord your son had only but the corpse, / But shadows and the shows of men, to fight; / For that same word, rebellion, did divide / The action of their bodies from their souls; / And they did fight with queasiness, constrain'd, / As men drink potions, that their weapons only / Seem'd on our side; but, for their spirits and souls, / This word, rebellion, it had froze them up, / As fish are in a pond. But now the bishop / Turns insurrection to religion: / Supposed sincere and holy in his thoughts, / He's follow'd both with body and with mind; / And doth enlarge his rising with the blood / Of fair King Richard, scraped from Pomfret stones; / Derives from heaven his quarrel and his cause; / Tells them he doth bestride a bleeding land, / Gasping for life under great Bolingbroke; / And more and less do flock to follow him.

It's high time. And, my most noble lord, I hear for certain, and I dare say it's true, that the noble Archbishop of York has risen with well-equipped forces. He is a man who binds his followers with a double bond. My lord your son had only the bodies, the mere shadows and shapes of men, to fight with, because that word "rebellion" divided their bodies' actions from their souls. They fought queasily and under pressure, like men taking medicine, so that only their weapons seemed to be on our side; their spirits and souls were frozen by that word "rebellion", like fish in a frozen pond. But now the Bishop turns rebellion into religion. Since people believe he is sincere and holy in his thoughts, they follow him in body and mind. He adds weight to his rising with the blood of good King Richard, scraped from the stones of Pomfret Castle; he claims his quarrel and cause come from heaven; he tells them he is standing over a bleeding country that is gasping for life under the tyrant Bolingbroke; and high and low flock to follow him.

I knew of this before; but, to speak truth, / This present grief had wiped it from my mind. / Go in with me; and counsel every man / The aptest way for safety and revenge: / Get posts and letters, and make friends with speed: / Never so few, and never yet more need.

I knew this before, but to tell the truth, this grief had wiped it from my mind. Come inside with me, and let everyone advise the best way to safety and revenge. Get messengers and letters, and make allies quickly. We've never been so few, and never needed more.
Sirrah, you giant, what says the doctor to my water?
Now then, you giant, what does the doctor say about my urine?
He said, sir, the water itself was a good healthy water; but, / for the party that owed it, he might have moe diseases than he / knew for.
He said, sir, the urine itself was good healthy urine, but the person it belonged to might have more diseases than he knew about.

Men of all sorts take a pride to gird at me: the brain of / this foolish-compounded clay, man, is not able to invent any thing / that tends to laughter, more than I invent or is invented on me: / I am not only witty in myself, but the cause that wit is in other men. / I do here walk before thee like a sow that hath overwhelmed all her / litter but one. / If the prince put thee into my service for any other reason than to / set me off, why then I have no judgement. Thou whoreson mandrake, thou / art fitter to be worn in my cap than to wait at my heels. I was never / manned with an agate till now: but I will inset you neither in gold nor / silver, but in vile apparel, and send you back again to your master, for / a jewel,—the juvenal, the prince your master, whose chin is not yet / fledged. I will sooner have a beard grow in the palm of my hand than he / shall get one on his cheek; and yet he will not stick to say his face is / a face-royal: God may finish it when he will, 'tis not a hair amiss yet: / he may keep it still at a face-royal, for a barber shall never earn / sixpence out of it; and yet he'll be crowing as if he had writ man ever / since his father was a bachelor. He may keep his own grace, but he's / almost out of mine, I can assure him. What said Master Dombledon about / the satin for my short cloak and my slops?

People of every kind take pride in mocking me. The brain of this stupidly made lump of clay, mankind, can't come up with anything funny that isn't invented by me or about me. I'm not only witty myself, I'm the cause of wit in other men. Here I am walking in front of you like a sow that has crushed all her litter except one. If the Prince put you in my service for any reason except to show me off by contrast, then I have no judgment. You son-of-a-whore mandrake root, you'd be better worn as a badge in my cap than following at my heels. I've never had a dwarf for an attendant till now, but I won't set you in gold or silver; I'll dress you in rags and send you back to your master as a jewel — that juvenile, the Prince your master, whose chin hasn't sprouted any feathers yet. I'll grow a beard on the palm of my hand before he gets one on his cheek. And yet he'll happily say his face is a royal face. God can finish it whenever He likes; there isn't a hair out of place yet. He can keep it a royal face, because a barber will never earn sixpence from it. And yet he crows as if he'd been a grown man since his father was a bachelor. He can keep his own grace, but he's almost out of mine, I can tell him. What did Master Dombledon say about the satin for my short cloak and my breeches?
He said, sir, you should procure him better assurance than Bardolph: / he would not take his band and yours; he liked not the security.
He said, sir, you should get him a better guarantee than Bardolph. He wouldn't accept his bond together with yours; he didn't like the security.

Let him be damned, like the glutton! pray God his tongue be hotter! / A whoreson Achitophel! a rascally yea-forsooth knave! to bear a / gentleman in hand, and then stand upon security! The whoreson / smooth-pates do now wear nothing but high shoes, and bunches of keys / at their girdles; and if a man is through with them in honest taking / up, then they must stand upon security. I had as lief they would / put ratsbane in my mouth as offer to stop it with security. / I looked 'a should have sent me two and twenty yards of satin, as I / am a true knight, and he sends me security. Well, he may sleep in / security; for he hath the horn of abundance, and the lightness of / his wife shines through it: and yet cannot he see, though he have his / own lanthorn to light him. Where's Bardolph?

Let him be damned like the rich glutton in the Bible! I hope his tongue burns hotter! A son-of-a-whore traitor! A rascally yes-sir knave, to lead a gentleman on and then insist on security! These smooth-headed tradesmen now wear nothing but high shoes and bunches of keys at their belts, and when a man wants to buy honestly on credit, they insist on security. I'd sooner they put rat poison in my mouth than shut it with "security". I expected him to send me twenty-two yards of satin, as I'm a true knight, and he sends me "security". Well, he can sleep in security, because he has the horn of plenty, and his wife's loose behaviour shines through it; and yet he can't see, though he has his own lantern to light him. Where's Bardolph?
He's gone into Smithfield to buy your worship a horse.
He's gone to Smithfield to buy your worship a horse.
I bought him in Paul's, and he'll buy me a horse in Smithfield: / an I could get me but a wife in the stews, I were manned, horsed, / and wived.
I bought him in St Paul's, and he'll buy me a horse in Smithfield. If I could just get myself a wife in the brothels, I'd be served, horsed and wived.
Sir, here comes the nobleman that committed the Prince for / striking him about Bardolph.
Sir, here comes the nobleman who sent the Prince to prison for hitting him over Bardolph.
Wait close; I will not see him.
Stay close. I won't see him.
Falstaff, if it please your lordship.
He that was in question for the robbery?
The one who was under investigation for the robbery?
He, my lord; but he hath since done good service at / Shrewsbury; and, as I hear, is now going with some charge to the / Lord John of Lancaster.
That's him, my lord. But he has since done good service at Shrewsbury and, I hear, is now going with some command to Lord John of Lancaster.
What, to York? Call him back again.
What, to York? Call him back.
Boy, tell him I am deaf.
You must speak louder; my master is deaf.
You'll have to speak louder; my master is deaf.
I am sure he is, to the hearing of anything good. / Go, pluck him by the elbow; I must speak with him.
I'm sure he is, to hearing anything good. Go and pull him by the elbow; I must speak to him.

What! a young knave, and begging! Is there not wars? is / there not employment? doth not the king lack subjects? do not the / rebels need soldiers? Though it be a shame to be on any side but / one, it is worse shame to beg than to be on the worst side, were / it worse than the name of rebellion can tell how to make it.

What! A young rascal, and begging! Isn't there a war on? Isn't there work? Doesn't the King need subjects? Don't the rebels need soldiers? Though it's a shame to be on any side but one, it's a worse shame to beg than to be on the worst side, even if it were worse than the word "rebellion" can make it.
Why, sir, did I say you were an honest man? setting my knighthood / and my soldiership aside, I had lied in my throat, if I had said so.
Why, sir, did I say you were an honest man? Setting my knighthood and soldiering aside, I'd have lied through my teeth if I'd said so.
I pray you, sir, then set your knighthood and your soldiership aside; / and give me leave to tell you, you lie in your throat, if you say I / am any other than an honest man.
Then I beg you, sir, set your knighthood and soldiering aside, and allow me to tell you that you lie through your teeth if you say I'm anything other than an honest man.
I give thee leave to tell me so! I lay aside that which grows to me! / If thou gettest any leave of me, hang me; if thou takest leave, / thou wert better be hanged. You hunt counter: hence! avaunt!

I allow you to tell me so! I set aside something that's part of me! If you get any "allowing" from me, hang me; if you take that liberty, you'd be better off hanged. You're on the wrong scent: away! Get lost!
Sir, my lord would speak with you.
Sir, my lord wants to speak with you.
Sir John Falstaff, a word with you.
Sir John Falstaff, a word with you.

My good lord! God give your lordship good time of day. I am glad to / see your lordship abroad: I heard say your lordship was sick: / I hope your lordship goes abroad by advice. Your lordship, though / not clean past your youth, hath yet some smack of age in you, some / relish of the saltness of time; and I most humbly beseech your lordship / to have a reverend care of your health.

My good lord! God give your lordship good day. I'm glad to see your lordship out and about. I heard your lordship was ill; I hope your lordship goes out on doctor's advice. Your lordship, though not quite past your youth, still has some taste of age in you, some flavour of the saltiness of time, and I most humbly beg your lordship to take respectful care of your health.
Sir John, I sent for you before your expedition to Shrewsbury.
Sir John, I sent for you before your expedition to Shrewsbury.
An 't please your lordship, I hear his majesty is returned / with some discomfort from Wales.
If it please your lordship, I hear his Majesty has come back from Wales somewhat unwell.
I talk not of his majesty: you would not come when I / sent for you.
I'm not talking about his Majesty. You wouldn't come when I sent for you.
And I hear, moreover, his highness is fall'n into this same / whoreson apoplexy.
And I hear, too, that his Highness has fallen into this damned apoplexy.
Well God mend him! I pray you, let me speak with you.
Well, God heal him! Please, let me speak to you.
This apoplexy is, as I take it, a kind of lethargy, an 't please / your lordship; a kind of sleeping in the blood, a whoreson tingling.
This apoplexy, as I understand it, is a kind of lethargy, if it please your lordship, a kind of sleeping in the blood, a damned tingling.
What tell you me of it? be it as it is.
Why are you telling me about it? Let it be what it is.
It hath it original from much grief, from study and perturbation / of the brain: I have read the cause of his effects in Galen: / it is a kind of deafness.
It has its origin in much grief, in study and disturbance of the brain. I have read about its causes in Galen. It's a kind of deafness.
I think you are fallen into the disease, for you hear not / what I say to you.
I think you've caught the disease, because you don't hear what I'm saying to you.
Very well, my lord, very well: rather, an 't please you, it / is the disease of not listening, the malady of not marking, that / I am troubled withal.
Very true, my lord, very true. Or rather, if it please you, it's the disease of not listening, the illness of not paying attention, that I suffer from.
To punish you by the heels would amend the attention / of your ears; and I care not if I do become your physician.
Putting you in the stocks would cure the inattention of your ears, and I wouldn't mind being your doctor.

I am as poor as Job, my lord, but not so patient: your lordship / may minister the potion of imprisonment to me in respect of poverty; / but how I should be your patient to follow your prescriptions, / the wise may make some dram of a scruple, or indeed a scruple itself.

I'm as poor as Job, my lord, but not as patient. Your lordship may give me the medicine of prison for my poverty, but as for whether I'd be patient enough to follow your prescriptions, a wise man might have a scruple or two of doubt — or a whole scruple.
I sent for you, when there were matters against you / for your life, to come speak with me.
I sent for you to come and speak to me when there were charges against you that could have cost you your life.
As I was then advised by my learned counsel in the laws / of this land-service, I did not come.
I was advised by my learned lawyer in the laws of military service at the time not to come.
Well, the truth is, Sir John, you live in great infamy.
Well, the truth is, Sir John, you live in great disgrace.
He that buckles himself in my belt cannot live in less.
Anyone who wears a belt my size can't live in less.
Your means are very slender, and your waste is great.
Your income is very small, and your waste is great.
I would it were otherwise; I would my means were greater, / and my waist slenderer.
I wish it were the other way round: I wish my income were greater and my waist smaller.
You have misled the youthful prince.
You have led the young Prince astray.
The young prince hath misled me: I am the fellow with the / great belly, and he my dog.
The young Prince has led me astray. I'm the blind man with the big belly, and he's my guide dog.

Well, I am loath to gall a new-healed wound: your day's service / at Shrewsbury hath a little gilded over your night's exploit / on Gad's-hill: you may thank the unquiet time for your quiet / o'er-posting that action.

Well, I don't want to rub a newly healed wound. Your day's service at Shrewsbury has slightly gilded over your night's work at Gad's Hill. You can thank these troubled times that your action passed over quietly.
But since all is well, keep it so: wake not a sleeping wolf.
But since all is well, keep it that way. Don't wake a sleeping wolf.
To wake a wolf is as bad as smell a fox.
Waking a wolf is as bad as smelling a fox.
What! you are as a candle, the better part burnt out.
What! You're like a candle with the better part burnt away.
A wassail candle, my lord, all tallow: if I did say of wax, my / growth would approve the truth.
A cheap party candle, my lord, all tallow. If I said wax, my size would prove it true.
There is not a white hair in your face but should have his / effect of gravity.
There isn't a white hair on your face that shouldn't have the effect of making you grave.
His effect of gravy, gravy, gravy.
The effect of gravy, gravy, gravy.
You follow the young prince up and down, like his ill angel.
You follow the young Prince around like his bad angel.

Not so, my lord; your ill angel is light; but I hope he that looks / upon me will take me without weighing: and yet, in some respects, / I grant, I cannot go: I cannot tell. Virtue is of so little regard / in these costermonger times that true valour is turned bear-herd; / pregnancy is made a tapster, and hath his quick wit wasted in giving / reckonings: all the other gifts appertinent to man, as the malice of / this age shapes them, are not worth a gooseberry. You that are old / consider not the capacities of us that are young; you do measure the / heat of our livers with the bitterness of your galls: and we that / are in the vaward of our youth, I must confess, are wags too.

Not so, my lord. A bad angel is a light coin, but I hope anyone who looks at me will take me without weighing me. And yet in some ways, I admit, I won't pass as currency; I can't say. Virtue is so little valued in these shopkeeping times that true courage has become a bear-keeper; quick wits have become a barman, wasted on adding up bills. All the other gifts that belong to a man, as this spiteful age shapes them, aren't worth a gooseberry. You old men don't consider what we young men are capable of. You measure the heat of our passions by the bitterness of your bile, and we who are in the front line of our youth, I must admit, are rascals too.

Do you set down your name in the scroll of youth, that are written / down old with all the characters of age? Have you not a moist eye? / a dry hand? a yellow cheek? a white beard? a decreasing leg? an / increasing belly? is not your voice broken? your wind short? your / chin double? your wit single? and every part about you blasted / with antiquity? and will you yet call yourself young? Fie, fie, / fie, Sir John!

Do you put your name on the list of the young, when you're marked down as old with every sign of age? Don't you have a watery eye? A dry hand? A yellow cheek? A white beard? A shrinking leg? A growing belly? Isn't your voice broken, your breath short, your chin double, your wit single, and every part of you withered with old age? And you still call yourself young? Shame, shame, shame, Sir John!

My lord, I was born about three of the clock in the afternoon, / with a white head and something a round belly. For my voice, I / have lost it with halloing and singing of anthems. To approve my / youth further, I will not: the truth is, I am only old in judgement / and understanding; and he that will caper with me for a thousand / marks, let him lend me the money, and have at him! / For the box of the ear that the prince gave you, he gave it like a / rude prince, and you took it like a sensible lord. I have checked / him for it, and the young lion repents; marry, not in ashes and / sackcloth, but in new silk and old sack.

My lord, I was born at about three in the afternoon with a white head and a roundish belly. As for my voice, I lost it shouting and singing hymns. I won't try to prove my youth any further. The truth is, I'm only old in judgement and understanding, and anyone who wants to bet me a thousand marks at dancing, let him lend me the money and I'll take him on! As for the box on the ear the Prince gave you, he gave it like a rough prince and you took it like a sensible lord. I've told him off for it, and the young lion is sorry — not in sackcloth and ashes, but in new silk and old sack.
Well, God send the prince a better companion!
Well, God send the Prince a better companion!
God send the companion a better prince! I cannot rid my hands of him.
God send the companion a better prince! I can't get rid of him.
Well, the king hath severed you and Prince Harry: / I hear you are going with Lord John of Lancaster against the / Archbishop and the Earl of Northumberland.
Well, the King has separated you and Prince Harry. I hear you're going with Lord John of Lancaster against the Archbishop and the Earl of Northumberland.

Yea; I thank your pretty sweet wit for it. But look you pray, all / you that kiss my lady Peace at home, that our armies join not in a / hot day; for, by the Lord, I take but two shirts out with me, and I / mean not to sweat extraordinarily: if it be a hot day, and I brandish / any thing but a bottle, I would I might never spit white again. / There is not a dangerous action can peep out his head but I am thrust / upon it: well, I cannot last ever: but it was alway yet the trick of / our English nation, if they have a good thing, to make it too common. / If ye will needs say I am an old man, you should give me rest. I / would to God my name were not so terrible to the enemy as it is: / I were better to be eaten to death with a rust than to be scoured to / nothing with perpetual motion.

Yes, and I have your pretty sweet wit to thank for it. But look, all of you who stay home kissing my lady Peace, pray that our armies don't meet on a hot day, because, by God, I'm only taking two shirts with me and I don't intend to sweat more than usual. If it's a hot day and I brandish anything but a bottle, may I never spit white again. No dangerous action can poke its head out without my being pushed into it. Well, I can't last for ever. But it's always been a habit of our English nation that when they have a good thing they overuse it. If you insist on saying I'm an old man, you should let me rest. I wish to God my name weren't so terrifying to the enemy. I'd rather rust to death than be scrubbed to nothing by constant motion.
Well, be honest, be honest; and God bless your expedition!
Well, be honest, be honest, and God bless your expedition!
Will your lordship lend me a thousand pound to furnish me forth?
Will your lordship lend me a thousand pounds to equip myself?
Not a penny, not a penny; you are too impatient to bear crosses. / Fare you well: commend me to my cousin Westmoreland.
Not a penny, not a penny. You're too impatient to bear crosses — or coins stamped with them. Goodbye. Give my regards to my cousin Westmoreland.

If I do, fillip me with a three-man beetle. A man can no more separate / age and covetousness than 'a can part young limbs and lechery: but / the gout galls the one, and the pox pinches the other; and so both the / degrees prevent my curses. Boy!

If I do, you can flick me with a sledgehammer that takes three men to lift. You can no more separate old age from greed than you can separate young bodies from lust. But gout torments the one and the pox pinches the other, so both conditions make my curses unnecessary. Boy!
What money is in my purse?
How much money is in my purse?

I can get no remedy against this consumption of the purse: / borrowing only lingers and lingers it out, but the disease is / incurable. Go bear this letter to my Lord of Lancaster; this to the / prince; this to the Earl of Westmoreland; and this to old Mistress / Ursula, whom I have weekly sworn to marry since I perceived the / first white hair of my chin. About it: you know where to find me.

I can't find any cure for this wasting disease of the purse. Borrowing only drags it out; the illness is incurable. Go and take this letter to my Lord of Lancaster, this one to the Prince, this to the Earl of Westmoreland, and this to old Mistress Ursula, whom I've sworn every week to marry since I saw the first white hair on my chin. Off you go. You know where to find me.

A pox of this gout! or, a gout of this pox! for the one or the other / plays the rogue with my great toe. 'Tis no matter if I do halt; I / have the wars for my colour, and my pension shall seem the more / reasonable. A good wit will make use of any thing: I will turn / diseases to commodity.

A pox on this gout! Or a gout on this pox! One or the other is playing havoc with my big toe. Never mind if I limp: I can blame the war, and my pension will seem all the more justified. A good wit makes use of anything. I'll turn my diseases into profit.
Thus have you heard our cause and known our means; / And, my most noble friends, I pray you all, / Speak plainly your opinions of our hopes: / And first, lord marshal, what say you to it?
So you've heard our cause and know our resources. And, my noble friends, I ask you all to speak plainly about our hopes. First, Lord Marshal, what do you say?

I well allow the occasion of our arms; / But gladly would be better satisfied / How in our means we should advance ourselves / To look with forehead bold and big enough / Upon the power and puissance of the king.
I fully accept the reasons for taking up arms, but I'd like to be better convinced about how, with our resources, we can face the King's army and power boldly and strongly enough.

Our present musters grow upon the file / To five and twenty thousand men of choice; / And our supplies live largely in the hope / Of great Northumberland, whose bosom burns / With an incensed fire of injuries.

Our current roll is growing towards twenty-five thousand picked men, and our reinforcements rest largely on the hope of great Northumberland, whose heart is burning with an angry fire over the wrongs done to him.
The question then, Lord Hastings, standeth thus: / Whether our present five and twenty thousand / May hold up head without Northumberland?
Then the question, Lord Hastings, is this: can our present twenty-five thousand hold their own without Northumberland?

Yea, marry, there's the point: / But if without him we be thought too feeble, / My judgement is, we should not step too far / Till we had his assistance by the hand; / For in a theme so bloody-faced as this / Conjecture, expectation, and surmise / Of aids incertain should not be admitted.

Yes, indeed, that's the point. But if we're thought too weak without him, my judgment is that we shouldn't go too far until we have his help in hand. In a bloody business like this, guesses, expectations and hopes of uncertain help shouldn't be counted on.
'Tis very true, Lord Bardolph; for indeed / It was young Hotspur's case at Shrewsbury.
That's very true, Lord Bardolph, for that was exactly young Hotspur's situation at Shrewsbury.

It was, my lord; who lined himself with hope, / Eating the air on promise of supply, / Flattering himself in project of a power / Much smaller than the smallest of his thoughts: / And so, with great imagination / Proper to madmen, led his powers to death / And winking leap'd into destruction.

It was, my lord. He fed himself on hope, eating air on the promise of reinforcements, flattering himself with the prospect of an army that turned out smaller than the smallest of his expectations. And so, with the kind of wild imagination that belongs to madmen, he led his forces to their deaths and leapt into destruction with his eyes shut.
But, by your leave, it never yet did hurt / To lay down likelihoods and forms of hope.
But, with respect, it has never done any harm to set out likely outcomes and grounds for hope.

Yes, if this present quality of war, / Indeed the instant action: a cause on foot / Lives so in hope as in an early spring / We see the appearing buds; which to prove fruit, / Hope gives not so much warrant as despair / That frosts will bite them. When we mean to build, / We first survey the plot, then draw the model; / And when we see the figure of the house, / Then we must rate the cost of the erection; / Which if we find outweighs ability, / What do we then but draw anew the model / In fewer offices, or at least desist / To build at all? Much more, in this great work, / Which is almost to pluck a kingdom down / And set another up, should we survey / The plot of situation and the model, / Consent upon a sure foundation, / Question surveyors, know our own estate, / How able such a work to undergo, / To weigh against his opposite; or else / We fortify in paper and in figures, / Using the names of men instead of men; / Like one that draws the model of a house / Beyond his power to build it; who, half through, / Gives o'er and leaves his part-created cost / A naked subject to the weeping clouds / And waste for churlish winter's tyranny.

Yes, it does, in this kind of war, in this immediate action. A cause that's under way lives on hope the way we see buds appear in early spring: hope gives less guarantee that they'll become fruit than despair gives that the frost will nip them. When we plan to build, we first survey the site, then draw the plan, and when we see the shape of the house, we have to estimate the cost of building it. If we find it's more than we can afford, what do we do but draw the plan again with fewer rooms, or give up building altogether? All the more, in this great work, which is almost to pull a kingdom down and set another up, we should survey the site and the plan, agree on a firm foundation, consult the surveyors, know our own resources and how able we are to take on such a work, and weigh them against the opposition. Otherwise we build our defences on paper and in numbers, using the names of men instead of men, like someone who draws the plan of a house beyond his means to build, who gives up halfway and leaves his half-built expense standing bare under the weeping clouds, a ruin for harsh winter to batter.

Grant that our hopes, yet likely of fair birth, / Should be still-born, and that we now possess'd / The utmost man of expectation, / I think we are a body strong enough, / Even as we are, to equal with the king.

Suppose our hopes, which still look likely to be born healthy, turned out to be stillborn, and that we already had every man we could expect. I still think we're a force strong enough, just as we are, to match the King.
What, is the king but five and twenty thousand?
What, does the King only have twenty-five thousand?

To us no more; nay, not so much, Lord Bardolph. / For his divisions, as the times do brawl, / Are in three heads: one power against the French, / And one against Glendower; perforce a third / Must take up us: so is the unfirm king / In three divided; and his coffers sound / With hollow poverty and emptiness.

Against us, no more; in fact not even that, Lord Bardolph. With the times so full of conflict, his forces are split three ways: one army against the French, one against Glendower, and a third must deal with us. So the unsteady King is divided in three, and his treasure chests ring hollow with poverty and emptiness.
That he should draw his several strengths together / And come against us in full puissance, / Need not be dreaded.
There's no need to fear that he'll gather his separate forces together and come against us at full strength.
If he should do so, / He leaves his back unarm'd, the French and Welsh / Baying him at the heels: never fear that.
If he did, he'd leave his back unprotected, with the French and Welsh barking at his heels. Don't worry about that.
Who is it like should lead his forces hither?
Who is likely to lead his forces here?
The Duke of Lancaster and Westmoreland; / Against the Welsh, himself and Harry Monmouth: / But who is substituted 'gainst the French, / I have no certain notice.
The Duke of Lancaster and Westmoreland. The King himself and Prince Harry are going against the Welsh. But who has been appointed against the French I don't know for certain.

Let us on, / And publish the occasion of our arms. / The commonwealth is sick of their own choice; / Their over-greedy love hath surfeited: / An habitation giddy and unsure / Hath he that buildeth on the vulgar heart. / O thou fond many, with what loud applause / Didst thou beat heaven with blessing Bolingbroke, / Before he was what thou wouldst have him be! / And being now trimm'd in thine own desires, / Thou, beastly feeder, art so full of him, / That thou provokest thyself to cast him up. / So, so, thou common dog, didst thou disgorge / Thy glutton bosom of the royal Richard; / And now thou wouldst eat thy dead vomit up, / And howl'st to find it. What trust is in these times? / They that, when Richard lived, would have him die, / Are now become enamour'd on his grave: / Thou that threw'st dust upon his goodly head / When through proud London he came sighing on / After the admired heels of Bolingbroke, / Criest now "O earth, yield us that king again, / And take thou this!" O thoughts of men accursed! / Past and to come seems best; things present worst.

Let's go on and announce the reasons for our taking up arms. The people are sick of their own choice; their over-greedy love has made them overfull. Anyone who builds on the hearts of the common people has a dizzy, unsafe house. Oh, you foolish crowd, how you beat heaven with loud applause, blessing Bolingbroke before he was what you wanted him to be! And now that he's dressed up in your own desires, you greedy beast, you're so full of him that you're making yourself sick to throw him up. That's how you, common dog, vomited royal Richard out of your gluttonous stomach, and now you'd like to eat your dead vomit up again, and you howl to find it. What loyalty is there in these times? Those who wanted Richard dead when he was alive have now fallen in love with his grave. You who threw dust on his noble head when he came sighing through proud London behind the admired heels of Bolingbroke now cry, "Oh earth, give us that king back, and take this one!" Oh, the cursed thoughts of men! The past and future seem best; the present always worst.
Shall we go draw our numbers, and set on?
Shall we go and gather our troops and set off?
We are time's subjects, and time bids be gone.
We're time's subjects, and time tells us to go.
Master Fang, have you entered the action?
Master Fang, have you filed the lawsuit?
Where's your yeoman? Is 't a lusty yeoman? will 'a stand to 't?
Where's your assistant? Is he a strong assistant? Will he stand his ground?
O Lord, ay! good Master Snare.
Oh Lord, yes! Good Master Snare.
Snare, we must arrest Sir John Falstaff.
Snare, we have to arrest Sir John Falstaff.
Yea, good Master Snare; I have entered him and all.
Yes, good Master Snare, I've filed a case against him and everything.
It may chance cost some of our lives, for he will stab.
It might cost some of us our lives, because he'll stab.

Alas the day! take heed of him; he stabbed me in mine own house, / and that most beastly: in good faith, he cares not what / mischief he does, if his weapon be out: he will foin like any / devil; he will spare neither man, woman, nor child.

Oh dear! Watch out for him. He stabbed me in my own house, and most beastly too. Honestly, he doesn't care what damage he does once his weapon's out. He'll thrust like a devil; he won't spare man, woman or child.
If I can close with him, I care not for his thrust.
If I can get to grips with him, I don't care about his thrusting.
No, nor I neither: I'll be at your elbow.
No, nor do I. I'll be right beside you.
An I but fist him once; an 'a come but within my vice,—
If I can just get my fist on him once, if he just comes within my grip —

I am undone by his going; I warrant you, he's an / infinitive thing upon my score. Good Master Fang, hold him sure: / good Master Snare, let him not 'scape. A' comes continuantly to / Pie-corner—saving your manhoods—to buy a saddle; and he is / indited to dinner to the Lubber's-head in Lumbert Street, to / Master Smooth's the silkman: I pray ye, since my exion is / entered and my case so openly known to the world, let him be / brought in to his answer. A hundred mark is a long one for a poor / lone woman to bear: and I have borne, and borne, and borne; and / have been fubbed off, and fubbed off, and fubbed off, from this / day to that day, that it is a shame to be thought on. There is no / honesty in such dealing; unless a woman should be made an ass and / a beast, to bear every knave's wrong. Yonder he comes; and that / arrant malmsey-nose knave, Bardolph, with him. Do your offices, / do your offices, Master Fang and Master Snare, do me, do me, do me / your offices.

I'm ruined if he goes. I promise you, he owes me an infinite amount. Good Master Fang, hold him tight; good Master Snare, don't let him escape. He's always going to Pie Corner — excuse me, gentlemen — to buy a saddle, and he's invited to dinner at the Lubber's Head in Lombard Street, at Master Smooth's the silk merchant's. Please, since my case has been filed and is so publicly known, let him be brought to answer for it. A hundred marks is a long score for a poor lonely woman to carry, and I've carried it and carried it, and been fobbed off and fobbed off from one day to the next, so it's shameful to think about. There's no honesty in dealing like that, unless a woman is supposed to be a donkey and a beast of burden for every rogue's wrongs. There he comes, and that out-and-out red-nosed rogue Bardolph with him. Do your duty, do your duty, Master Fang and Master Snare. Do me, do me, do me your duty.
How now! whose mare's dead? what's the matter?
What's going on? Who's dead? What's the matter?
Sir John, I arrest you at the suit of Mistress Quickly.
Sir John, I arrest you on the complaint of Mistress Quickly.
Away, varlets! Draw, Bardolph: cut me off the villain's / head: throw the quean in the channel.
Get away, you rascals! Draw, Bardolph. Cut off the villain's head, and throw the slut in the gutter.

Throw me in the channel! I'll throw thee in the channel. / Wilt thou? wilt thou? thou bastardly rogue! Murder, murder! Ah, / thou honey-suckle villain! wilt thou kill God's officers and the / king's? / Ah, thou honey-seed rogue! thou art a honey-seed, a man-queller, / and a woman-queller.

Throw me in the gutter! I'll throw you in the gutter. Will you? Will you? You bastard rogue! Murder, murder! Oh, you honeysuckle villain! Will you kill God's officers and the King's? Oh, you honey-seed rogue! You're a honey-seed, a man-killer and a woman-killer.
Good people, bring a rescue or two. Thou wo't, wo't thou? / thou wo't, wo't ta? do, do, thou rogue! do, thou hemp-seed!
Good people, bring help. You will, will you? You will, will you? Go on, you rogue! Go on, you gallows-bird!
Away, you scullion! you rampallian! you fustilarian! I'll tickle / your catastrophe.
Get away, you kitchen slut! You scruffy wench! You frump! I'll tickle your backside.
What is the matter? keep the peace here, ho!
What's the matter? Keep the peace here!
Good my lord, be good to me. I beseech you, stand to me.
My good lord, be good to me. I beg you, stand by me.

How now, Sir John! what are you brawling here? / Doth this become your place, your time and business? / You should have been well on your way to York. / Stand from him, fellow: wherefore hang'st thou upon him?

What now, Sir John! Are you brawling here? Is this fitting for your position, your age and your business? You should be well on your way to York by now. Get away from him, fellow. Why are you hanging on him?
O my most worshipful lord, an't please your grace, I am a / poor widow of Eastcheap, and he is arrested at my suit.
Oh, my most worshipful lord, if it please your grace, I'm a poor widow from Eastcheap, and he's arrested on my complaint.

It is more than for some, my lord; it is for all, all I have. / He hath eaten me out of house and home; he hath put all my substance / into that fat belly of his: but I will have some of it out again, / or I will ride thee o' nights like the mare.

It's more than for some, my lord; it's for all, all I have. He's eaten me out of house and home; he's put everything I own into that fat belly of his. But I'll have some of it out again, or I'll ride you at night like a nightmare.
I think I am as like to ride the mare, if I have any / vantage of ground to get up.
I think I'm as likely to ride the mare, if I have any high ground to climb up from.
How comes this, Sir John? Fie! what man of good temper would / endure this tempest of exclamation? Are you not ashamed to enforce / a poor widow to so rough a course to come by her own?
What's this, Sir John? Shame! What man of good character would put up with this storm of shouting? Aren't you ashamed to force a poor widow to such rough measures to get back what's hers?
What is the gross sum that I owe thee?
What's the total I owe you?

Marry, if thou wert an honest man, thyself and the money too. / Thou didst swear to me upon a parcel-gilt goblet, sitting in / my Dolphin-chamber, at the round table, by a sea-coal fire, upon / Wednesday in Wheeson week, when the prince broke thy head for / liking his father to a singing-man of Windsor, thou didst swear to / me then, as I was washing thy wound, to marry me and make me my / lady thy wife. Canst thou deny it? Did not goodwife Keech, the / butcher's wife, come in then and call me gossip Quickly? Coming / in to borrow a mess of vinegar; telling us she had a good dish of / prawns, whereby thou didst desire to eat some, whereby I told / thee they were ill for green wound? And didst thou not, when she / was gone down stairs, desire me to be no more so familiarity with / such poor people; saying that ere long they should call me madam? / And didst thou not kiss me, and bid me fetch thee thirty shillings? / I put thee now to thy book-oath: deny it, if thou canst.

Indeed, if you were an honest man, yourself and the money too. You swore to me on a partly gilded goblet, sitting in my Dolphin room at the round table by a coal fire, on the Wednesday of Whitsun week, when the Prince cracked your head for comparing his father to a singer from Windsor — you swore to me then, while I was washing your wound, that you'd marry me and make me my lady your wife. Can you deny it? Didn't goodwife Keech, the butcher's wife, come in then and call me friend Quickly? She came in to borrow a dish of vinegar and told us she had a good dish of prawns, and you wanted to eat some, and I told you they were bad for a fresh wound. And didn't you, when she'd gone downstairs, tell me not to be so familiar with such poor people, saying that before long they'd be calling me madam? And didn't you kiss me and tell me to fetch you thirty shillings? I put you on your oath now: deny it if you can.

My lord, this is a poor mad soul; and she says up and down the / town that her eldest son is like you: she hath been in good case, / and the truth is, poverty hath distracted her. But for these / foolish officers, I beseech you I may have redress against them.

My lord, this is a poor mad soul, and she goes all over town saying her eldest son looks like you. She used to be well off, and the truth is poverty has driven her out of her mind. But as for these foolish officers, I ask for compensation against them.

Sir John, Sir John, I am well acquainted with your / manner of wrenching the true cause the false way. It is not a / confident brow, nor the throng of words that come with such more / than impudent sauciness from you, can thrust me from a level / consideration: you have, as it appears to me, practised upon the / easy-yielding spirit of this woman, and made her serve your uses / both in purse and in person.

Sir John, Sir John, I know very well your way of twisting a true case into a false one. It isn't a confident face, nor the flood of words that pours out of you with more than shameless cheek, that can push me off a fair judgement. It seems to me you've worked on this woman's easily persuaded nature and used her both for her money and her body.
Pray thee, peace. Pay her the debt you owe her, and unpay the / villany you have done her: the one you may do with sterling / money, and the other with current repentance.
Please, be quiet. Pay her the debt you owe her, and undo the wrong you've done her. The first you can do with good money, the second with sincere repentance.

My lord, I will not undergo this sneap without reply. / You call honourable boldness impudent sauciness: if a man will make / courtesy and say nothing, he is virtuous: no, my lord, my humble / duty remembered, I will not be your suitor. I say to you, I do desire / deliverance from these officers, being upon hasty employment in the / king's affairs.

My lord, I won't take this telling-off without replying. You call honourable boldness shameless cheek. If a man bows and says nothing, he's virtuous! No, my lord, with all due respect, I won't come begging to you. I tell you, I want to be freed from these officers, as I'm on urgent business for the King.
You speak as having power to do wrong: but answer / in the effect of your reputation, and satisfy the poor woman.
You speak as if you had a licence to do wrong. But act as your reputation demands, and pay the poor woman.
The king, my lord, and Harry Prince of Wales / Are near at hand: the rest the paper tells.
The King, my lord, and Harry Prince of Wales are close by. The letter tells the rest.
As I am a gentleman. Come, no more words of it.
As I am a gentleman. Come, not another word about it.
By this heavenly ground I tread on, I must be fain to pawn / both my plate and the tapestry of my dining-chambers.
By this holy ground I walk on, I'll have to pawn my silver plate and the tapestries in my dining rooms.

Glasses, glasses, is the only drinking: and for thy walls, a pretty / slight drollery, or the story of the Prodigal, or the German hunting / in water-work, is worth a thousand of these bed-hangings and / these fly-bitten tapestries. Let it be ten pound, if thou canst. / Come, an 'twere not for thy humours, there's not a better wench in / England. Go, wash thy face, and draw the action. Come, thou must not be / in this humour with me; dost not know me? come, come, I know thou wast / set on to this.

Glasses, glasses are the only thing to drink from. And for your walls, a pretty little comic picture, or the story of the Prodigal Son, or the German hunt painted in watercolour is worth a thousand of these bed-curtains and fly-spotted tapestries. Make it ten pounds if you can. Come on, if it weren't for your moods, there wouldn't be a better girl in England. Go and wash your face, and withdraw the lawsuit. Come, you mustn't be in this mood with me. Don't you know me? Come, come, I know someone put you up to this.
Pray thee, Sir John, let it be but twenty nobles: i' faith, / I am loath to pawn my plate, so God save me, la!
Please, Sir John, make it just twenty nobles. Honestly, I hate to pawn my plate, God help me!
Let it alone; I'll make other shift: you'll be a fool still.
Forget it; I'll find another way. You'll always be a fool.
Well, you shall have it, though I pawn my gown. I hope / you'll come to supper. You'll pay me all together?
Well, you'll have it, even if I have to pawn my gown. I hope you'll come to supper. You'll pay me back all at once?
Will I live? [To Bardolph] Go, with her, with her; / hook on, hook on.
As sure as I live. (To Bardolph) Go with her, go with her. Hook her, hook her.
Will you have Doll Tearsheet meet you at supper?
Do you want Doll Tearsheet to meet you at supper?
No more words; let's have her.
No more talk; let's have her.
Where lay the king last night?
Where did the King stay last night?
I hope, my lord, all's well: what is the news, my lord?
I hope all's well, my lord. What's the news, my lord?
Are all his forces coming back?
No; fifteen hundred foot, five hundred horse, / Are march'd up to my Lord of Lancaster, / Against Northumberland and the Archbishop.
No. Fifteen hundred foot soldiers and five hundred horsemen have marched to join my Lord of Lancaster against Northumberland and the Archbishop.
Comes the king back from Wales, my noble lord?
Is the King coming back from Wales, my noble lord?
You shall have letters of me presently: / Come, go along with me, good Master Gower.
You'll have letters from me shortly. Come with me, good Master Gower.
Master Gower, shall I entreat you with me to dinner?
Master Gower, may I invite you to dinner with me?
I must wait upon my good lord here; I thank you, good Sir John.
I have to attend my good lord here. Thank you, good Sir John.
Sir John, you loiter here too long, being you are to / take soldiers up in counties as you go.
Sir John, you're hanging about here too long, since you're supposed to be recruiting soldiers in the counties on your way.
Will you sup with me, Master Gower?
Will you have supper with me, Master Gower?
What foolish master taught you these manners, Sir John?
What foolish teacher taught you these manners, Sir John?
Master Gower, if they become me not, he was a fool that / taught them me. This is the right fencing grace, my lord; tap for / tap, and so part fair.
Master Gower, if they don't suit me, the man who taught them to me was a fool. This is proper fencing style, my lord: tit for tat, and part on equal terms.
Now the Lord lighten thee! thou art a great fool.
May the Lord enlighten you! You're a great fool.
Before God, I am exceeding weary.
Is 't come to that? I had thought weariness durst not have / attach'd one of so high blood.
Has it come to that? I'd have thought tiredness wouldn't dare to seize anyone of such high blood.
Faith, it does me; though it discolours the complexion of / my greatness to acknowledge it. Doth it not show vilely in me to / desire small beer?
Well, it seizes me, though it spoils the colour of my greatness to admit it. Doesn't it look shameful in me to want weak beer?
Why, a prince should not be so loosely studied as to / remember so weak a composition.
Well, a prince shouldn't be so badly educated as to remember such a feeble drink.

Belike then my appetite was not princely got; for, by my troth, / I do now remember the poor creature, small beer. But, indeed, / these humble considerations make me out of love with my greatness. / What a disgrace is it to me to remember thy name! or to know thy / face to-morrow! or to take note how many pair of silk stockings thou / hast, viz. these, and those that were thy peach-coloured ones! or to / bear the inventory of thy shirts, as, one for superfluity, and another / for use! / But that the tennis-court-keeper knows better than I; for it is a low / ebb of linen with thee when thou keepest not racket there; as thou hast / not done a great while, because the rest of thy low countries have made / a shift to eat up thy holland: and God knows, whether those that bawl / out of the ruins of thy linen shall inherit his kingdom: but the / midwives say the children are not in the fault; whereupon the world / increases, and kindreds are mightily strengthened.

Then I suppose my appetite wasn't born royal, because, honestly, I do now remember that poor creature, weak beer. But really, these humble thoughts make me fall out of love with my greatness. What a disgrace it is for me to remember your name! Or to recognise your face tomorrow! Or to keep count of how many pairs of silk stockings you have — these, and the ones that used to be your peach-coloured ones! Or to keep a list of your shirts: one spare and one for wearing! But the tennis-court keeper knows that better than I do, because your linen is at a low ebb when you don't play there, as you haven't for a long time, because your lowlands have managed to eat up your fine Dutch linen. And God knows whether the babies who bawl out of the remains of your shirts will inherit His kingdom; but the midwives say the children aren't to blame, and so the world grows and families are mightily increased.
How ill it follows, after you have laboured so hard, you / should talk so idly! Tell me, how many good young princes would / do so, their fathers being so sick as yours at this time is?
How badly it follows, after you've worked so hard, that you should talk such nonsense! Tell me, how many good young princes would carry on like this when their fathers were as ill as yours is now?
Shall I tell thee one thing, Poins?
Shall I tell you one thing, Poins?
Yes, faith; and let it be an excellent good thing.
Yes, indeed, and make it an excellent thing.
It shall serve among wits of no higher breeding than thine.
It will do for wits no better bred than yours.
Go to; I stand the push of your one thing that you will tell.
Go on. I'm ready to take the blow of this one thing you're going to tell me.

Marry, I tell thee it is not meet that I should be sad, now my father / is sick: albeit I could tell to thee, as to one it pleases me, for / fault of a better, to call my friend, I could be sad, and sad indeed too.

Well, I tell you it isn't proper for me to be sad now that my father is ill — although I could tell you, as one I'm pleased to call my friend for lack of anyone better, that I could be sad, and truly sad too.
Very hardly upon such a subject.

By this hand, thou thinkest me as far in the devil's book as thou / and Falstaff for obduracy and persistency: let the end try the man. / But I tell thee, my heart bleeds inwardly that my father is so sick: / and keeping such vile company as thou art hath in reason taken from / me all ostentation of sorrow.

By this hand, you think I'm as deep in the devil's book as you and Falstaff for stubbornness and persistence. Let the outcome test the man. But I tell you, my heart bleeds inside that my father is so ill, and keeping such low company as you has rightly robbed me of any outward show of grief.
What wouldst thou think of me, if I should weep?
What would you think of me if I cried?
I would think thee a most princely hypocrite.
I'd think you a most princely hypocrite.

It would be every man's thought; and thou art a blessed fellow to / think as every man thinks: never a man's thought in the world keeps / the road-way better than thine: every man would think me an / hypocrite indeed. And what accites your most worshipful thought to / think so?

That's what everyone would think, and you're a blessed fellow to think what everyone thinks. No man's thinking in the world keeps to the main road better than yours. Everyone would think me a hypocrite indeed. And what prompts your most worshipful mind to think so?
Why, because you have been so lewd and so much engraffed / to Falstaff.
Why, because you've been so wild and so attached to Falstaff.

By this light, I am well spoke on; I can hear it with mine own / ears: the worst that they can say of me is that I am a second / brother and that I am a proper fellow of my hands; and those two / things, I confess, I cannot help. By the mass, here comes Bardolph.

By this light, people speak well of me; I can hear it with my own ears. The worst they can say of me is that I'm a younger son and that I'm handy with my fists, and those two things, I admit, I can't help. By the mass, here comes Bardolph.
And the boy that I gave Falstaff: 'a had him from me Christian; / and look, if the fat villain have not transformed him ape.
And the boy I gave Falstaff. He got him from me a Christian, and look if the fat villain hasn't turned him into an ape.
Come, you virtuous ass, you bashful fool, must you be blushing? / wherefore blush you now? What a maidenly man-at-arms are you become! / Is 't such a matter to get a pottle-pot's maidenhead?
Come on, you virtuous ass, you bashful fool, must you be blushing? Why are you blushing now? What a maidenly soldier you've become! Is it such a big deal to take the virginity of a two-quart tankard?

'A calls me e'en now, my lord, through a red lattice, and I could / discern no part of his face from the window: at last I spied his / eyes, and methought he had made two holes in the ale-wife's new / petticoat and so peep'd through.

He called me just now, my lord, through a red window lattice, and I couldn't make out any part of his face from the window. In the end I spotted his eyes, and I thought he'd made two holes in the ale-woman's new petticoat and was peeping through.
Away, you whoreson upright rabbit, away!
Get away, you son-of-a-whore upright rabbit, get away!
Away, you rascally Althaea's dream, away!
Get away, you rascally Althaea's dream, get away!
Instruct us, boy; what dream, boy?
Teach us, boy. What dream, boy?
Marry, my lord, Althaea dreamt she was delivered of a / fire-brand; and therefore I call him her dream.
Well, my lord, Althaea dreamt she gave birth to a burning torch, so I call him her dream.
A crown's worth of good interpretation: there 'tis, boy.
That's a crown's worth of good interpretation. There it is, boy.
O, that this blossom could be kept from cankers! Well, / there is sixpence to preserve thee.
Oh, if only this blossom could be kept from the worms! Well, here's sixpence to protect you.
An you do not make him hanged among you, the gallows / shall have wrong.
If you lot don't get him hanged between you, the gallows will be cheated.
And how doth thy master, Bardolph?
Well, my lord. He heard of your grace's coming to town: / there's a letter for you.
Well, my lord. He heard your grace was coming to town. Here's a letter for you.
Deliver'd with good respect. And how doth the martlemas, / your master?
Delivered with proper ceremony. And how is your master, that fat Martinmas ox?
Marry, the immortal part needs a physician; but that moves / not him: though that be sick, it dies not.
Well, his immortal part needs a doctor, but that doesn't bother him. Though that's sick, it doesn't die.
I do allow this wen to be as familiar with me as my dog; / and he holds his place; for look you how he writes.
I allow this growth to be as familiar with me as my dog, and he keeps his place. Look how he writes.

[Reads] "John Falstaff, knight,"—every man must know that, as oft / as he has occasion to name himself: even like those that are kin / to the king; for they never prick their finger but they say, / "There's some of the king's blood spilt." / "How comes that?" says he, that takes upon him not to conceive. / The answer is as ready as a borrower's cap, / "I am the king's poor cousin, sir."

(Reads) "John Falstaff, knight" — everyone has to know that, every time he has the chance to name himself. He's just like those distant relatives of the King: they never prick their finger without saying, "There's some of the King's blood spilt." "How's that?" says someone who pretends not to understand. And the answer comes as quickly as a borrower doffs his cap: "I'm the King's poor cousin, sir."
Nay, they will be kin to us, or they will fetch it from Japhet. / But to the letter:
Yes, they'll be related to us even if they have to trace it back to Noah's son Japhet. But to the letter.
[Reads] "Sir John Falstaff, knight, to the son of the king, / nearest his father, Harry Prince of Wales, greeting." Why, this / is a certificate.
(Reads) "Sir John Falstaff, knight, to the son of the King nearest his father, Harry Prince of Wales, greeting." Why, this is a legal certificate.

[Reads] "I will imitate the honourable Romans in brevity:" he sure / means brevity in breath, short-winded. "I commend me to thee, I commend / thee, and I leave thee. Be not too familiar with Poins; for he misuses / thy favours so much, that he swears thou art to marry his sister Nell. / Repent at idle times as thou mayest; and so, farewell. / "Thine, by yea and no, which is as much as to say, as thou / usest him, / JACK FALSTAFF with my familiars, JOHN with my brothers and / sisters, and SIR JOHN with all Europe." / My lord, I'll steep this letter in sack and make him eat it.

(Reads) "I will imitate the honourable Romans in brevity." He must mean shortness of breath, being short-winded. "I commend myself to you, I commend you, and I leave you. Don't be too familiar with Poins, because he abuses your favours so much that he swears you're going to marry his sister Nell. Repent in your spare time as you can, and so farewell.
