Yours, yes and no (which is as much as to say, depending on how you treat him), Jack Falstaff to my friends, John to my brothers and sisters, and Sir John to all Europe." My lord, I'll soak this letter in sack and make him eat it.
That's to make him eat twenty of his words. But do you use / me thus, Ned? must I marry your sister?
That would make him eat twenty of his words. But do you treat me like this, Ned? Must I marry your sister?
God send the wench no worse fortune! But I never said so.
God send the girl no worse luck! But I never said so.
Well, thus we play the fools with the time, and the spirits of the / wise sit in the clouds and mock us. Is your master here in London?
Well, this is how we play the fool with our time, while the spirits of the wise sit in the clouds and laugh at us. Is your master here in London?
Where sups he? doth the old boar feed in the old frank?
Where does he eat? Does the old boar feed in the old pigsty?
At the old place, my lord, in Eastcheap.
At the old place, my lord, in Eastcheap.
Ephesians, my lord, of the old church.
Drinking companions, my lord, of the old congregation.
Are any women eating with him?
None, my lord, but old Mistress Quickly and Mistress Doll Tearsheet.
None, my lord, but old Mistress Quickly and Mistress Doll Tearsheet.
A proper gentlewoman, sir, and a kinswoman of my master's.
A decent gentlewoman, sir, and a relative of my master's.
Even such kin as the parish heifers are to the town bull. Shall / we steal upon them, Ned, at supper?
About as related as the parish cows are to the town bull. Shall we creep up on them at supper, Ned?
I am your shadow, my lord; I'll follow you.
I'm your shadow, my lord. I'll follow you.
Sirrah, you boy, and Bardolph, no word to your master that / I am yet come to town: there's for your silence.
You there, boy, and Bardolph, not a word to your master that I've arrived in town yet. Here's something for your silence.
And for mine, sir, I will govern it.
And as for mine, sir, I'll keep it under control.
This Doll Tearsheet should be some road.
This Doll Tearsheet must be a common road.
I warrant you, as common as the way between Saint Alban's and London.
I promise you, as common as the road between St Albans and London.
How might we see Falstaff bestow himself to-night in his true / colours, and not ourselves be seen?
How could we see Falstaff behave tonight in his true colours without being seen ourselves?
Put on two leathern jerkins and aprons, and wait upon him at / his table as drawers.
Put on two leather jackets and aprons and serve him at his table as waiters.

From a God to a bull? a heavy descension! it was Jove's case. / From a prince to a prentice? a low transformation! that shall be / mine; for in everything the purpose must weigh with the folly. / Follow me, Ned.

From a god to a bull? A heavy comedown! That's what happened to Jove. From a prince to an apprentice? A low transformation! That shall be mine, because in everything the purpose has to balance the foolishness. Follow me, Ned.
I pray thee, loving wife, and gentle daughter, / Give even way unto my rough affairs; / Put not you on the visage of the times / And be like them to Percy troublesome.
Please, loving wife and gentle daughter, let my rough business go smoothly. Don't put on the face of the times and be as troublesome to Percy as they are.
I have given over, I will speak no more: / Do what you will; your wisdom be your guide.
I've given up; I won't say any more. Do what you like; let your wisdom guide you.
Alas, sweet wife, my honour is at pawn; / And, but my going, nothing can redeem it.
Alas, dear wife, my honour is pledged, and nothing but my going can redeem it.

O yet, for God's sake, go not to these wars! / The time was, father, that you broke your word, / When you were more endear'd to it than now! / When your own Percy, when my heart's dear Harry, / Threw many a northward look to see his father / Bring up his powers; but he did long in vain. / Who then persuaded you to stay at home? / There were two honours lost, yours and your son's. / For yours, the God of heaven brighten it! / For his, it stuck upon him as the sun / In the grey vault of heaven; and by his light / Did all the chivalry of England move / To do brave acts: he was indeed the glass / Wherein the noble youth did dress themselves: / He had no legs that practis'd not his gait; / And speaking thick, which nature made his blemish, / Became the accents of the valiant; / For those who could speak low and tardily / Would turn their own perfection to abuse, / To seem like him: so that in speech, in gait, / In diet, in affections of delight, / In military rules, humours of blood, / He was the mark and glass, copy and book, / That fashion'd others. And him, O wondrous him! / O miracle of men! him did you leave, / Second to none, unseconded by you, / To look upon the hideous god of war / In disadvantage; to abide a field / Where nothing but the sound of Hotspur's name / Did seem defensible: so you left him. / Never, O never, do his ghost the wrong / To hold your honour more precise and nice / With others than with him! let them alone: / The marshal and the archbishop are strong: / Had my sweet Harry had but half their numbers, / To-day might I, hanging on Hotspur's neck, / Have talk'd of Monmouth's grave.

Oh, even so, for God's sake, don't go to these wars! There was a time, father, when you broke your word when you were more bound to keep it than now — when your own Percy, my heart's dear Harry, kept looking north to see his father bring up his army, and waited in vain. Who persuaded you to stay at home then? Two honours were lost there, yours and your son's. As for yours, may God in heaven polish it bright! As for his, it was fixed on him like the sun in the grey sky, and by its light all the knights of England were moved to brave deeds. He was truly the mirror in which the noble young men dressed themselves. Every young man copied his walk, and his quick, thick speech, a flaw nature gave him, became the way the brave talked, so that those who could speak slowly and quietly spoiled their own perfection to seem like him. In speech, in walk, in diet, in pleasures, in military discipline and in temperament, he was the target and the mirror, the copy and the book, that shaped everyone else. And him — oh, wonderful him! oh, miracle of men! — you left him, second to none, without your support, to face the hideous god of war at a disadvantage, to hold a battlefield where only the sound of Hotspur's name seemed to give any defence. That's how you left him. Never, oh never, do his ghost the wrong of keeping your honour more strictly and carefully with others than you did with him! Leave them alone. The Marshal and the Archbishop are strong. If my sweet Harry had had even half their numbers, I might today be hanging on Hotspur's neck and talking about Prince Harry's grave.

Beshrew your heart, / Fair daughter, you do draw my spirits from me / With new lamenting ancient oversights. / But I must go and meet with danger there, / Or it will seek me in another place, / And find me worse provided.

Curse you, fair daughter, you drain my spirit from me by lamenting old mistakes all over again. But I must go and meet the danger there, or it will come looking for me somewhere else and find me less prepared.
O, fly to Scotland, / Till that the nobles and the armed commons / Have of their puissance made a little taste.
Oh, escape to Scotland until the nobles and the armed common people have had a little taste of their strength.

If they get ground and vantage of the king, / Then join you with them, like a rib of steel, / To make strength stronger; but, for all our loves, / First let them try themselves. So did your son; / He was so suffer'd: so came I a widow; / And never shall have length of life enough / To rain upon remembrance with mine eyes, / That it may grow and sprout as high as heaven, / For recordation to my noble husband.

If they gain ground and an advantage over the King, then join them like a steel rib to make their strength stronger. But, for the love of all of us, let them test themselves first. That's what your son was allowed to do; that's how I became a widow. And I'll never live long enough to water his memory with my tears so that it grows and sprouts as high as heaven as a memorial to my noble husband.

Come, come, go in with me. 'Tis with my mind / As with the tide swell'd up unto his height, / That makes a still-stand, running neither way: / Fain would I go to meet the archbishop, / But many thousand reasons hold me back. / I will resolve for Scotland: there am I, / Till time and vantage crave my company.

Come, come, go in with me. My mind is like the tide when it has swelled to its height and stands still, flowing neither way. I'd like to go and meet the Archbishop, but many thousand reasons hold me back. I'll decide on Scotland. I'll stay there until the right time and advantage call for me.
What the devil hast thou brought there? apple-johns? / thou knowest Sir John cannot endure an apple-john.
What the devil have you brought there? Dried-up apples? You know Sir John can't stand old wrinkled apples.

Mass, thou sayest true. The prince once set a dish of apple-johns / before him, and told him there were five more Sir Johns, and, putting / off his hat, said "I will now take my leave of these six dry, round, / old, withered knights." It angered him to the heart: but he hath / forgot that.

By the mass, that's true. The Prince once put a dish of them in front of him, told him there were five more Sir Johns, and, taking off his hat, said, "I'll now take my leave of these six dry, round, old, withered knights." It made him furious, but he's forgotten that now.

Why, then, cover, and set them down: and see if thou canst find out / Sneak's noise; Mistress Tearsheet would fain hear some music. / Dispatch: The room where they supped is too hot; they'll come in / straight.

Well then, lay the cloth and put them down, and see if you can find Sneak's band; Mistress Tearsheet would like to hear some music. Hurry. The room where they had supper is too hot; they'll come in here in a moment.
Sirrah, here will be the prince and Master Poins anon; and they / will put on two of our jerkins and aprons; and Sir John must / not know of it: Bardolph hath brought word.
Listen, the Prince and Master Poins will be here soon, and they'll put on two of our jackets and aprons, and Sir John mustn't know about it. Bardolph has brought word.
By the mass, here will be old Utis: it will be an excellent / stratagem.
By the mass, we'll have a grand old time. It'll be an excellent trick.
I'll see if I can find out Sneak.
I'll see if I can find Sneak.

I' faith, sweetheart, methinks now you are in an excellent good / temperality: your pulsidge beats as extraordinarily as heart would / desire; and your colour, I warrant you, is as red as any rose, in / good truth, la! But, i' faith, you have drunk too much canaries; and / that's a marvellous searching wine, and it perfumes the blood ere one / can say "What's this?" How do you now?

Honestly, sweetheart, I think you're in an excellent good temper now. Your pulse is beating as extraordinarily as anyone could wish, and your colour, I promise you, is as red as any rose, truly! But honestly, you've drunk too much Canary wine, and that's a wonderfully penetrating wine; it perfumes the blood before you can say "What's this?" How are you now?
Why, that's well said; a good heart's worth gold. Lo, here / comes Sir John.
Well, that's good to hear; a good heart's worth gold. Look, here comes Sir John.
[Singing] "When Arthur first in court"—Empty the jordan. / [Exit First Drawer]—[Singing] "And was a worthy king." / How now, Mistress Doll!
(Singing) "When Arthur first in court" — Empty the chamber pot. (Exit First Drawer) — (Singing) "And was a worthy king." How are you, Mistress Doll?
Sick of a calm; yea, good faith.
Sick from too much calm; yes, truly.
So is all her sect; an they be once in a calm, they are sick.
So are all women of her sort: once they're calm, they're sick.
You muddy rascal, is that all the comfort you give me?
You dirty rascal, is that all the comfort you give me?
You make fat rascals, Mistress Doll.
You make rascals fat, Mistress Doll.
I make them! gluttony and diseases make them; I make them not.
I make them! Gluttony and diseases make them; I don't.
If the cook help to make the gluttony, you help to make the diseases, / Doll: we catch of you, Doll, we catch of you; grant that, my poor / virtue, grant that.
If the cook helps cause the gluttony, you help cause the diseases, Doll. We catch them from you, Doll, we catch them from you. Admit it, my poor virtue, admit it.
Yea, joy, our chains and our jewels.
Yes, my darling, you catch our chains and our jewels.

"Your brooches, pearls, and ouches:" for to serve bravely is to come / halting off, you know: to come off the breach with his pike bent / bravely, and to surgery bravely; to venture upon the charged chambers / bravely,—

"Your brooches, pearls and ornaments" — because to serve bravely, you know, is to come away limping: to come away from the breach with your pike bravely bent, and bravely off to the surgeon, to venture bravely against loaded guns —
Hang yourself, you muddy conger, hang yourself!
Go hang yourself, you slimy eel, hang yourself!

By my troth, this is the old fashion; you two never meet but you / fall to some discord: you are both, i' good truth, as rheumatic / as two dry toasts; you cannot one bear with another's confirmities. / What the good-year! one must bear, and that must be you: you are the / weaker vessel, as as they say, the emptier vessel.

Honestly, it's the same old story. You two never meet without falling out. Truly, you're both as irritable as two dry pieces of toast; you can't put up with each other's infirmities. What the devil! One of you has to put up with it, and it has to be you. You're the weaker vessel, as they say, the emptier vessel.

Can a weak empty vessel bear such a huge full hogshead? there's a whole / merchant's venture of Bourdeaux stuff in him; you have not seen a hulk / better stuffed in the hold. Come, I'll be friends with thee, Jack: / thou art going to the wars; and whether I shall ever see thee again or / no, there is nobody cares.

Can a weak empty vessel carry such a huge full barrel? There's a whole merchant's cargo of Bordeaux wine in him; you've never seen a ship's hold better stuffed. Come on, I'll be friends with you, Jack. You're going off to the wars, and whether I'll ever see you again or not, nobody cares.
Sir, Ancient Pistol's below, and would speak with you.
Sir, Ensign Pistol's downstairs and wants to speak to you.
Hang him, swaggering rascal! let him not come hither: it is the / foul-mouthed'st rogue in England.
Hang him, the swaggering rascal! Don't let him come up here. He's the foulest-mouthed rogue in England.

If he swagger, let him not come here: no, by my faith; I must live / among my neighbours; I'll no swaggerers: I am in good name and fame / with the very best: shut the door; there comes no swaggerers here: / I have not lived all this while, to have swaggering now: shut the / door, I pray you.

If he swaggers, don't let him come in here. No, by my faith; I have to live among my neighbours. I won't have swaggerers. I have a good name and reputation with the very best people. Shut the door. No swaggerers come in here. I haven't lived all this time to have swaggering now. Shut the door, please.
Pray ye, pacify yourself, Sir John: there comes no swaggerers here.
Please calm yourself, Sir John. No swaggerers come in here.
Dost thou hear? it is mine ancient.
Are you listening? He's my ensign.

Tilly-fally, Sir John, ne'er tell me: your ancient swaggerer comes / not in my doors. I was before Master Tisick, the debuty, t'other day; / and, as he said to me, 'twas no longer ago than Wednesday last, / "I' good faith, neighbour Quickly," says he; Master Dumbe, our / minister, was by then; "neighbour Quickly," says he, "receive those / that are civil; for" said he "you are in an ill name:" now a' said / so, I can tell whereupon; "for," says he, "you are an honest woman, / and well thought on; therefore take heed what guests you receive: / receive," says he, "no swaggering companions." There comes none here: / you would bless you to hear what he said: no, I'll no swaggerers.

Fiddlesticks, Sir John, don't tell me. Your ensign swaggerer isn't coming through my doors. I was up before Master Tisick, the deputy, the other day, and he said to me — it was no longer ago than last Wednesday — "Honestly, neighbour Quickly," he says (Master Dumbe, our minister, was there at the time), "neighbour Quickly," he says, "only let in people who are civil, because," he said, "you have a bad name." Now, he said that, I can tell you why. "Because," he says, "you're an honest woman and well thought of, so be careful what guests you let in. Don't let in," he says, "any swaggering fellows." None come in here. You'd be amazed to hear what he said. No, I won't have swaggerers.

He's no swaggerer, hostess; a tame cheater, i' faith; you may stroke / him as gently as a puppy greyhound: he'll not swagger with a Barbary / hen, if her feathers turn back in any show of resistance. Call / him up, drawer.

He's no swaggerer, hostess. He's a tame cardsharp, honestly; you can stroke him as gently as a greyhound puppy. He wouldn't swagger at a guinea hen if her feathers stood up as though she meant to fight. Call him up, waiter.

Cheater, call you him? I will bar no honest man my house, nor no / cheater: but I do not love swaggering, by my troth; I am the worse, / when one says swagger: feel, masters, how I shake; look you, I / warrant you.

Cheater, you call him? I won't bar any honest man from my house, nor any escheator. But I don't like swaggering, honestly; I feel worse when anyone says "swagger". Feel how I'm shaking, gentlemen. Look, I promise you.
Do I? yea, in very truth, do I, an 'twere an aspen leaf: I / cannot abide swaggerers.
Am I? Yes, in very truth I am, like an aspen leaf. I can't stand swaggerers.
Welcome, Ancient Pistol. Here, Pistol, I charge you with / a cup of sack: do you discharge upon mine hostess.
Welcome, Ensign Pistol. Here, Pistol, I load you with a cup of sack: you fire it off at my hostess.
I will discharge upon her, Sir John, with two bullets.
I will fire at her, Sir John, with two bullets.
She is pistol-proof, sir; you shall hardly offend her.
She's pistol-proof, sir. You'll hardly hurt her.
Come, I'll drink no proofs nor no bullets: I'll drink no / more than will do me good, for no man's pleasure, I.
Come on, I won't drink any proofs or bullets. I'll drink no more than does me good, for no man's pleasure, not I.
Then to you, Mistress Dorothy; I will charge you.
Then to you, Mistress Dorothy; I'll charge you.
Charge me! I scorn you, scurvy companion. What! you poor, / base, rascally, cheating, lack-linen mate! Away, you mouldy / rogue, away! / I am meat for your master.
Charge me! I scorn you, you scabby fellow. What! You poor, low, rascally, cheating, shirtless mate! Get away, you mouldy rogue, get away! I'm meat for your master.

Away, you cut-purse rascal! you filthy bung, away! by this wine, / I'll thrust my knife in your mouldy chaps, an you play the saucy / cuttle with me. Away, you bottle-ale rascal! you basket-hilt stale / juggler, you! Since when, I pray you, sir? God's light, with two / points on your shoulder? much!

Get away, you pickpocket rascal! You filthy purse, get away! By this wine, I'll stick my knife in your mouldy jaws if you play the cheeky cutthroat with me. Get away, you flat-beer rascal! You worn-out sword-swinging fraud! Since when, may I ask, sir? God's light, with two laces on your shoulder? Really!
God let me not live, but I will murder your ruff for this.
God strike me dead if I don't tear your ruff to pieces for this.
No more, Pistol; I would not have you go off here: / discharge yourself of our company, Pistol.
No more, Pistol. I don't want you going off in here. Discharge yourself from our company, Pistol.
No, good Captain Pistol; not here, sweet captain.
No, good Captain Pistol; not here, sweet captain.

Captain! thou abominable damned cheater, art thou not ashamed / to be called captain? An captains were of my mind, they would / truncheon you out, for taking their names upon you before you / have earned them. You a captain! you slave, for what? for tearing / a poor whore's ruff in a bawdy-house? He a captain! hang him, / rogue! he lives upon mouldy stewed prunes and dried cakes. A / captain! God's light, these villains will make the word as odious / as the word "occupy;" which was an excellent good word before it / was ill sorted: therefore captains had need look to't.

Captain! You disgusting damned cheat, aren't you ashamed to be called captain? If captains thought like me, they'd beat you out with their batons for taking their title before you've earned it. You, a captain! You slave, for what? For tearing a poor whore's ruff in a brothel? Him, a captain! Hang him, the rogue! He lives on mouldy stewed prunes and stale cakes. A captain! God's light, these villains will make the word as disgusting as the word "occupy", which was an excellent good word before it got into bad company. So captains had better watch out.
Pray thee, go down, good ancient.
Not I: I tell thee what, Corporal Bardolph, I could tear / her: I'll be revenged of her.
Not me. I tell you what, Corporal Bardolph, I could tear her apart. I'll get my revenge on her.

I'll see her damned first; to Pluto's damned lake, by this / hand, to the infernal deep, with Erebus and tortures vile also. / Hold hook and line, say I. Down, down, dogs! down, faitors! / Have we not Hiren here?

I'll see her damned first — to Pluto's damned lake, by this hand, to the bottomless pit, with Erebus and vile tortures too. Hold the hook and line, I say! Down, down, dogs! Down, traitors! Haven't we got Irene here?
Good Captain Peesel, be quiet; 'tis very late, i' faith: I / beseek you now, aggravate your choler.
Good Captain Peesel, be quiet. It's very late, honestly. I beg you now, aggravate your anger.

These be good humours, indeed! Shall packhorses / And hollow pamper'd jades of Asia, / Which cannot go but thirty mile a-day, / Compare with Caesars, and with Cannibals, / And Trojan Greeks? nay, rather damn them with / King Cerberus; and let the welkin roar. / Shall we fall foul for toys?

These are fine moods indeed! Shall packhorses and hollow pampered nags of Asia, which can't go more than thirty miles a day, compare themselves with Caesars, and with Cannibals, and Trojan Greeks? No, rather damn them with King Cerberus, and let the heavens roar. Shall we fall out over trifles?
By my troth, captain, these are very bitter words.
Honestly, captain, these are very bitter words.
Be gone, good ancient: this will grow to a brawl anon.
Go, good ensign. This will turn into a brawl in a moment.
Die men like dogs! give crowns like pins! Have we not Hiren / here?
Let men die like dogs! Give away crowns like pins! Haven't we got Irene here?
O' my word, captain, there's none such here. What the / good-year! do you think I would deny her? For God's sake, be / quiet.
On my word, captain, there's no one like that here. What the devil! Do you think I'd deny her? For God's sake, be quiet.

Then feed, and be fat, my fair Calipolis. / Come, give's some sack. / "Si fortune me tormente, sperato me contento." / Fear we broadsides? no, let the fiend give fire: / Give me some sack: and, sweetheart, lie thou there.

Then eat and grow fat, my fair Calipolis. Come, give us some sack. "If fortune torments me, hope contents me." Are we afraid of broadsides? No, let the devil fire! Give me some sack. And, sweetheart, you lie there.
Come we to full points here, and are etceteras nothing?
Have we come to a full stop here, and are "et ceteras" nothing?
Sweet knight, I kiss thy neif: what! we have seen the seven / stars.
Sweet knight, I kiss your fist. What! We've seen the seven stars together.
For God's sake, thrust him down stairs: I cannot endure such a / fustian rascal.
For God's sake, throw him downstairs. I can't stand such a ranting rascal.
Thrust him down stairs! know we not Galloway nags?
Throw him downstairs! Don't we know the Galloway ponies?
Quoit him down, Bardolph, like a shove-groat shilling: / nay, an a' do nothing but speak nothing, a' shall be nothing / here.
Slide him down, Bardolph, like a coin in shove-ha'penny. No, if he does nothing but talk nonsense, he'll be nothing here.
What! shall we have incision? shall we imbrue?
What! Shall we have cutting? Shall we draw blood?
Then death rock me asleep, abridge my doleful days! / Why, then, let grievous, ghastly, gaping wounds / Untwine the Sisters Three! Come, Atropos, I say!
Then let death rock me to sleep and cut short my miserable days! Why then, let grievous, ghastly, gaping wounds untwist the thread of the three Fates! Come, Atropos, I say!
I pray thee, Jack, I pray thee, do not draw.
Here's a goodly tumult! I'll forswear keeping house, afore / I'll be in these tirrits and frights. So; murder, I warrant now. / Alas, alas! put up your naked weapons, put up your naked weapons.

Here's a fine uproar! I'll give up keeping a tavern before I'll have these terrors and frights. There, murder, I'm sure of it now. Alas, alas! Put away your naked weapons, put away your naked weapons.
I pray thee, Jack, be quiet; the rascal's gone. Ah, you whoreson / little valiant villain, you!
Please, Jack, be calm. The rascal's gone. Oh, you son-of-a-whore brave little villain, you!
Are you not hurt i' the groin? methought a' made a shrewd / thrust at your belly.
Aren't you hurt in the groin? I thought he made a nasty thrust at your belly.
Have you turned him out o' doors?
Yea, sir. The rascal's drunk: you have hurt him, sir, i' / the shoulder.
Yes, sir. The rascal's drunk. You've wounded him, sir, in the shoulder.

Ah, you sweet little rogue, you! Alas, poor ape, how thou / sweatest! come, let me wipe thy face; come on, you whoreson chops: / ah, rogue! i' faith, I love thee: thou art as valorous as Hector / of Troy, worth five of Agamemnon, and ten times better than the Nine / Worthies: ah, villain!

Oh, you sweet little rogue, you! Alas, poor monkey, how you're sweating! Come, let me wipe your face. Come on, you son-of-a-whore fat cheeks. Oh, rogue! Honestly, I love you. You're as brave as Hector of Troy, worth five Agamemnons, and ten times better than the Nine Worthies. Oh, villain!
A rascally slave! I will toss the rogue in a blanket.
A rascally slave! I'll toss the rogue in a blanket.
Do, an thou darest for thy heart: an thou dost, I'll canvass / thee between a pair of sheets.
Do it, if you dare for your life. If you do, I'll toss you between a pair of sheets.
Let them play. Play, sirs. Sit on my knee, Doll. A rascal / bragging slave! The rogue fled from me like quicksilver.
Let them play. Play, gentlemen. Sit on my knee, Doll. A rascally bragging slave! The rogue ran away from me like quicksilver.

I' faith, and thou followedst him like a church. Thou whoreson / little tidy Bartholomew boar-pig, when wilt thou leave fighting / o' days and foining o' nights, and begin to patch up thine old body / for heaven?

Honestly, and you chased him like a church. You son-of-a-whore neat little roast piglet from Bartholomew Fair, when are you going to stop fighting by day and thrusting by night, and start patching up your old body for heaven?
Peace, good Doll! do not speak like a death's-head; do / not bid me remember mine end.
Quiet, good Doll! Don't talk like a skull; don't tell me to remember my death.
Sirrah, what humour's the prince of?
Tell me, what sort of man is the Prince?
A good shallow young fellow: 'a would have made a good / pantler; a' would ha' chipped bread well.
A good shallow young fellow. He'd have made a good pantry servant; he'd have cut the crusts off bread well.
They say Poins has a good wit.
They say Poins has a good wit.
He a good wit! hang him, baboon! his wit's as thick as / Tewksbury mustard; there's no more conceit in him than is in a / mallet.
Him, a good wit! Hang him, the baboon! His wit's as thick as Tewkesbury mustard. There's no more imagination in him than in a mallet.
Why does the prince love him so, then?
Then why does the Prince love him so much?

Because their legs are both of a bigness, and a' plays at quoits / well, and eats conger and fennel, and drinks off candles' ends for / flap-dragons, and rides the wild-mare with the boys, and jumps upon / joined-stools, and swears with a good grace, and wears his boots very / smooth, like unto the sign of the leg, and breeds no bate with telling / of discreet stories; and such other gambol faculties a' has, that show / a weak mind and an able body, for the which the prince admits him: for / the prince himself is such another; the weight of a hair will turn the / scales between their avoirdupois.

Because their legs are both the same size, and he plays quoits well, and eats eel and fennel, and drinks off burning candle-ends in flaming brandy, and rides piggyback with the boys, and jumps over stools, and swears elegantly, and wears his boots very smooth, like the sign over a bootmaker's shop, and causes no trouble by telling tactful stories; and he has other such playful skills that show a weak mind and a fit body, and that's why the Prince puts up with him. Because the Prince is just the same: a hair's weight would tip the scales between them.
Would not this nave of a wheel have his ears cut off?
Shouldn't this hub of a wheel have his ears cut off?
Let's beat him before his whore.
Let's beat him in front of his whore.
Look, whether the withered elder hath not his poll clawed / like a parrot.
Look at the withered old tree having his head scratched like a parrot.
Is it not strange that desire should so many years outlive / performance?
Isn't it strange that desire should outlive performance by so many years?
Saturn and Venus this year in conjunction! what says the / almanac to that?
Saturn and Venus in conjunction this year! What does the almanac say about that?
And, look, whether the fiery Trigon, his man, be not lisping / to his master's old tables, his note-book, his counsel-keeper.
And look how his man, the fiery triangle, is whispering to his master's old notebook, his diary, his confidante.
Thou dost give me flattering busses.
By my troth, I kiss thee with a most constant heart.
Honestly, I kiss you with a completely faithful heart.
I am old, I am old.
I love thee better than I love e'er a scurvy young boy of / them all.
I love you better than any scabby young boy of them all.
What stuff wilt have a kirtle of? I shall receive money o' / Thursday: shalt have a cap to-morrow. A merry song, come: it / grows late; we'll to bed. Thou'lt forget me when I am gone.
What material do you want a skirt made of? I'll get some money on Thursday; you'll have a cap tomorrow. A merry song, come on. It's getting late; we'll go to bed. You'll forget me when I've gone.
By my troth, thou'lt set me a-weeping, an thou sayest so: / prove that ever I dress myself handsome till thy return: well, / hearken at the end.
Honestly, you'll make me cry if you say that. See if I ever dress myself up nicely before you come back. Well, wait and see how it ends.
Ha! a bastard son of the king's? And art thou not Poins / his brother?
Ha! A bastard son of the King's? And aren't you Poins's brother?
Why, thou globe of sinful continents, what a life dost thou lead!
Why, you globe of sinful continents, what a life you lead!
A better than thou: I am a gentleman; thou art a drawer.
A better one than yours. I'm a gentleman; you're a waiter.
Very true, sir; and I come to draw you out by the ears.
Very true, sir, and I've come to draw you out by the ears.
O, the Lord preserve thy grace! by my troth, welcome to / London. Now, the Lord bless that sweet face of thine! O Jesu, / are you come from Wales?
Oh, the Lord preserve your grace! Honestly, welcome to London. Now the Lord bless that sweet face of yours! Oh Jesus, have you come from Wales?
Thou whoreson mad compound of majesty, by this light / flesh and corrupt blood, thou art welcome.
You son-of-a-whore mad mixture of majesty, by this light — flesh and corrupt blood — you're welcome.
How, you fat fool! I scorn you.
What, you fat fool! I scorn you.
My lord, he will drive you out of your revenge and turn all / to a merriment, if you take not the heat.
My lord, he'll talk you out of your revenge and turn it all into a joke if you don't strike while the iron's hot.
You whoreson candle-mine, you, how vilely did you speak of / me even now before this honest, virtuous, civil gentlewoman!
You son-of-a-whore tallow mine, you, how vilely you talked about me just now in front of this honest, virtuous, respectable gentlewoman!
God's blessing of your good heart! and so she is, by my troth.
God bless your good heart! And so she is, honestly.
Yea, and you knew me, as you did when you ran away by / Gad's-hill: you knew I was at your back, and spoke it on purpose / to try my patience.
Yes, and you knew it was me, just as you did when you ran away at Gad's Hill. You knew I was behind you and said it on purpose to test my patience.
No, no, no; not so; I did not think thou wast within hearing.
No, no, no, not so. I didn't think you were within earshot.
I shall drive you then to confess the wilful abuse; and then I / know how to handle you.
Then I'll force you to confess the deliberate insult, and then I'll know how to deal with you.
No abuse, Hal, o' mine honour; no abuse.
No insult, Hal, on my honour, no insult.
Not to dispraise me, and call me pantler and bread-chipper and I / know not what!
Not to run me down, and call me a pantry boy and a bread-cutter and I don't know what!

No abuse, Ned, i' the world; honest Ned, none. I dispraised him before / the wicked, that the wicked might not fall in love with him; in which / doing, I have done the part of a careful friend and a true subject, / and thy father is to give me thanks for it. No abuse, Hal: none, / Ned, none: no, faith, boys, none.

No insult in the world, Ned; honest Ned, none. I ran him down in front of the wicked so that the wicked wouldn't fall in love with him. In doing that I've acted as a caring friend and a loyal subject, and your father ought to thank me for it. No insult, Hal; none, Ned, none. No, honestly, boys, none.

See now, whether pure fear and entire cowardice doth not make thee / wrong this virtuous gentlewoman to close with us. Is she of the wicked? / is thine hostess here of the wicked? or is thy boy of the wicked? / or honest Bardolph, whose zeal burns in his nose, of the wicked?

Now see whether pure fear and total cowardice don't make you wrong this virtuous gentlewoman to make it up with us. Is she one of the wicked? Is your hostess here one of the wicked? Or is your boy one of the wicked? Or honest Bardolph, whose zeal burns in his nose, one of the wicked?
Answer, you dead elm tree, answer.

The fiend hath pricked down Bardolph irrecoverable; and his / face is Lucifer's privy-kitchen, where he doth nothing but roast / malt-worms. / For the boy, there is a good angel about him; but the devil / outbids him too.

The devil has marked Bardolph down as past saving, and his face is Lucifer's private kitchen, where he does nothing but roast drunkards. As for the boy, he has a good angel with him, but the devil outbids him too.
For one of them, she is in hell already, and burns poor souls. / For the other, I owe her money; and whether she be damned for / that, I know not.
One of them is in hell already, and burns poor souls with disease. As for the other, I owe her money, and whether she's damned for that I don't know.

No, I think thou art not; I think thou art quit for that. Marry, there / is another indictment upon thee, for suffering flesh to be eaten in / thy house, contrary to the law; for the which I think thou wilt howl.

No, I don't think you are; I think you're let off for that. But there's another charge against you, for allowing meat to be eaten in your house during Lent, against the law. I think you'll howl for that.
All victuallers do so: what's a joint of mutton or two in a / whole Lent?
All innkeepers do it. What's a joint of mutton or two in a whole Lent?
His grace says that which his flesh rebels against.
His grace says what his flesh rebels against.
Who knocks so loud at door? Look to the door there, Francis.
Who's knocking so loud at the door? See to the door there, Francis.

The king your father is at Westminster; / And there are twenty weak and wearied posts / Come from the north: and, as I came along, / I met and overtook a dozen captains, / Bare-headed, sweating, knocking at the taverns, / And asking every one for Sir John Falstaff.

The King your father is at Westminster, and twenty weak and exhausted messengers have come from the north. And on my way here I met and passed a dozen captains, bare-headed and sweating, knocking at the taverns and asking everyone for Sir John Falstaff.

By heaven, Poins, I feel me much to blame, / So idly to profane the precious time, / When tempest of commotion, like the south / Borne with black vapour, doth begin to melt / And drop upon our bare unarmed heads. / Give me my sword and cloak. Falstaff, good night.

By heaven, Poins, I feel very much to blame for wasting precious time so idly, when a storm of rebellion, like the south wind loaded with black cloud, is starting to melt and pour down on our bare, unarmed heads. Give me my sword and cloak. Falstaff, good night.
Now comes in the sweetest morsel of the night, and we must / hence, and leave it unpicked. / [Knocking within] More knocking at the door!
Now comes the sweetest morsel of the night, and we have to go and leave it untasted. (Knocking within) More knocking at the door!
You must away to court, sir, presently; / A dozen captains stay at door for you.
You have to go to court at once, sir. A dozen captains are waiting at the door for you.

[To the Page] Pay the musicians, sirrah. Farewell, hostess; farewell, Doll. / You see, my good wenches, how men of merit are sought after: / the undeserver may sleep, when the man of action is called on. / Farewell, good wenches: if I be not sent away post, I will see / you again ere I go.

(To the Page) Pay the musicians, boy. Farewell, hostess; farewell, Doll. You see, my good girls, how men of merit are sought after. The undeserving can sleep, while the man of action gets called. Farewell, good girls. If I'm not sent off at once, I'll see you again before I go.
I cannot speak; if my heart be not ready to burst,—well, sweet / Jack, have a care of thyself.
I can't speak. If my heart isn't ready to burst — well, sweet Jack, take care of yourself.
Well, fare thee well: I have known thee these twenty-nine years, / come peascod-time; but an honester and truer-hearted man,—— / well, fare thee well.
Well, goodbye to you. I've known you twenty-nine years, come pea-pod time, but a more honest and truer-hearted man — well, goodbye to you.
[Within] Bid Mistress Tearsheet come to my master.
(Offstage) Tell Mistress Tearsheet to come to my master.
O, run, Doll, run; run, good Doll: come. [She comes blubbered] / Yea, will you come, Doll?
Oh, run, Doll, run. Run, good Doll. Come on. (She comes in, her face swollen with tears) Yes, will you come, Doll?
Go call the Earls of Surrey and of Warwick; / But, ere they come, bid them o'er-read these letters, / And well consider of them: make good speed.
Go and call the Earls of Surrey and Warwick. But before they come, tell them to read these letters through and think them over carefully. Be quick.

How many thousands of my poorest subjects / Are at this hour asleep! O sleep, O gentle sleep, / Nature's soft nurse, how have I frighted thee, / That thou no more wilt weigh my eyelids down / And steep my senses in forgetfulness? / Why rather, sleep, liest thou in smoky cribs, / Upon uneasy pallets stretching thee / And hush'd with buzzing night-flies to thy slumber / Than in the perfumed chambers of the great, / Under the canopies of costly state, / And lull'd with sound of sweetest melody? / O thou dull god, why liest thou with the vile / In loathsome beds, and leavest the kingly couch / A watch-case or a common 'larum-bell? / Wilt thou upon the high and giddy mast / Seal up the ship-boy's eyes, and rock his brains / In cradle of the rude imperious surge / And in the visitation of the winds, / Who take the ruffian billows by the top, / Curling their monstrous heads and hanging them / With deafening clamour in the slippery clouds, / That, with the hurly, death itself awakes? / Canst thou, O partial sleep, give thy repose / To the wet sea-boy in an hour so rude; / And in the calmest and most stillest night, / With all appliances and means to boot, / Deny it to a king? Then happy low, lie down! / Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.

How many thousands of my poorest subjects are asleep at this hour! Oh sleep, oh gentle sleep, nature's soft nurse, how have I frightened you, that you'll no longer weigh my eyelids down and soak my senses in forgetfulness? Why, sleep, do you prefer to lie in smoky hovels, stretched out on uncomfortable straw beds and lulled to sleep by buzzing night-flies, rather than in the perfumed rooms of great men, under expensive canopies, lulled by the sound of the sweetest music? Oh, you dull god, why do you lie with the lowly in their disgusting beds and leave the king's bed like a sentry box or an alarm bell? Will you seal the ship's boy's eyes on top of the high, swaying mast, and rock his brain in the cradle of the rough, overpowering sea, in the onslaught of the winds, which seize the violent waves by the crests, curling their monstrous heads and hanging them in the slippery clouds with such a deafening roar that the uproar wakes death itself? Can you, unfair sleep, give your rest to the soaked ship's boy in such a violent hour, and in the calmest, stillest night, with every comfort and aid besides, deny it to a king? Then lie down, you happy humble people! The head that wears a crown lies uneasy.
Many good morrows to your majesty!
Many good mornings to your Majesty!
Why then, good morrow to you all, my lords. / Have you read o'er the letters that I sent you?
Well then, good morning to you all, my lords. Have you read through the letters I sent you?
Then you perceive the body of our kingdom / How foul it is; what rank diseases grow, / And with what danger, near the heart of it.
Then you see how diseased the body of our kingdom is, what rotten illnesses are growing in it, and how dangerously close to its heart.
It is but as a body yet distemper'd; / Which to his former strength may be restored / With good advice and little medicine: / My Lord Northumberland will soon be cool'd.
It's only like a body that's out of sorts, which can be restored to its former strength with good advice and a little medicine. My Lord Northumberland will soon be cooled down.

O God! that one might read the book of fate, / And see the revolution of the times / Make mountains level, and the continent, / Weary of solid firmness, melt itself / Into the sea! and, other times, to see / The beachy girdle of the ocean / Too wide for Neptune's hips; how chances mock, / And changes fill the cup of alteration / With divers liquors! O, if this were seen, / The happiest youth, viewing his progress through, / What perils past, what crosses to ensue, / Would shut the book, and sit him down and die. / 'Tis not ten years gone / Since Richard and Northumberland, great friends, / Did feast together, and in two years after / Were they at wars: it is but eight years since / This Percy was the man nearest my soul, / Who like a brother toil'd in my affairs / And laid his love and life under my foot, / Yea, for my sake, even to the eyes of Richard / Gave him defiance. But which of you was by— / You, cousin Nevil, as I may remember—

Oh God! If only one could read the book of fate and see how the turning of the times makes mountains flat, and the dry land, tired of being solid, melt into the sea; and at other times see the sandy belt of the shore grow too wide for the sea-god's hips; see how chance mocks us, and how changes fill the cup of alteration with different drinks! Oh, if this could be seen, the happiest young man, looking through the course of his life, what dangers past, what troubles still to come, would shut the book, sit down and die. It's not ten years ago that Richard and Northumberland were great friends and feasted together, and two years after that they were at war. It's only eight years since this Percy was the man closest to my heart, who worked like a brother on my behalf and laid his love and life at my feet — yes, and for my sake even defied Richard to his face. But which of you was there — you, cousin Nevil, as I remember —

When Richard, with his eye brimful of tears, / Then check'd and rated by Northumberland, / Did speak these words, now proved a prophecy? / "Northumberland, thou ladder by the which / My cousin Bolingbroke ascends my throne;" / Though then, God knows, I had no such intent, / But that necessity so bow'd the state / That I and greatness were compell'd to kiss: / "The time shall come," thus did he follow it, / "The time will come, that foul sin, gathering head, / Shall break into corruption:" so went on, / Foretelling this same time's condition / And the division of our amity.

when Richard, his eyes brimming with tears, being rebuked and scolded by Northumberland, spoke these words, which have now proved a prophecy? "Northumberland, you ladder by which my cousin Bolingbroke climbs to my throne" — though at that time, God knows, I had no such intention, except that necessity so bent the state that greatness and I were forced to kiss. "The time will come," he went on, "the time will come when foul sin, coming to a head, will burst into rottenness." And so he went on, foretelling the state of things now and the breaking of our friendship.

There is a history in all men's lives, / Figuring the natures of the times deceased; / The which observed, a man may prophesy, / With a near aim, of the main chance of things / As yet not come to life, who in their seeds / And weak beginning lie intreasured. / Such things become the hatch and brood of time; / And by the necessary form of this / King Richard might create a perfect guess / That great Northumberland, then false to him, / Would of that seed grow to a greater falseness; / Which should not find a ground to root upon, / Unless on you.

There's a pattern in every man's life that reflects the nature of times gone by. By observing it, a man can predict fairly accurately the likely course of things that haven't yet come to life, which lie stored up in their seeds and weak beginnings. Such things are hatched and bred by time. And from this inevitable pattern King Richard could make a perfect guess that great Northumberland, false to him then, would grow from that seed to a greater falseness, which would find no ground to take root in except you.
Are these things then necessities? / Then let us meet them like necessities: / And that same word even now cries out on us: / They say the bishop and Northumberland / Are fifty thousand strong.
Are these things necessities, then? Then let's face them as necessities. And that same word is calling out to us now. They say the Bishop and Northumberland are fifty thousand strong.

It cannot be, my lord; / Rumour doth double, like the voice and echo, / The numbers of the fear'd. Please it your grace / To go to bed. Upon my soul, my lord, / The powers that you already have sent forth / Shall bring this prize in very easily. / To comfort you the more, I have received / A certain instance that Glendower is dead. / Your majesty hath been this fortnight ill, / And these unseason'd hours perforce must add / Unto your sickness.

That can't be so, my lord. Rumour doubles the numbers of the people we fear, like a voice and its echo. Please, your grace, go to bed. Upon my soul, my lord, the forces you've already sent out will win this prize very easily. To comfort you further, I've received reliable news that Glendower is dead. Your Majesty has been ill this fortnight, and these late hours are bound to make your sickness worse.
I will take your counsel: / And were these inward wars once out of hand, / We would, dear lords, unto the Holy Land.
I'll take your advice. And once these civil wars were dealt with, dear lords, we would go to the Holy Land.
Come on, come on, come on, sir; give me your hand, sir, / give me your hand, sir: an early stirrer, by the rood! And how / doth my good cousin Silence?
Come on, come on, come on, sir. Give me your hand, sir, give me your hand, sir. An early riser, by the cross! And how's my good cousin Silence?
And how doth my cousin, your bedfellow? and your fairest / daughter and mine, my god-daughter Ellen?
And how's my cousin, your wife? And your lovely daughter and mine, my god-daughter Ellen?
Alas, a black ousel, cousin Shallow!
Alas, as dark as a blackbird, cousin Shallow!
By yea and nay, sir, I dare say my cousin William is become / a good scholar: he is at Oxford still, is he not?
By yes and no, sir, I'd say my cousin William has become a good scholar. He's still at Oxford, isn't he?
He is, sir, at my expense.
A' must, then, to the inns o' court shortly. I was once of / Clement's Inn, where I think they will talk of mad Shallow yet.
Then he'll have to go to the law schools in London soon. I was at Clement's Inn once, where I think they still talk about mad Shallow.
You were called "lusty Shallow" then, cousin.
You were called "lusty Shallow" then, cousin.

By the mass, I was called any thing; and I would have done any thing / indeed too, and roundly too. There was I, and little John Doit of / Staffordshire, and black George Barnes, and Francis Pickbone, and / Will Squele, a Cotswold man; you had not four such swinge-bucklers in / all the inns o' court again: and I may say to you, we knew where the / bona-robas were and had the best of them all at commandment. Then was / Jack Falstaff, now Sir John, boy, and page to Thomas Mowbray, Duke of / Norfolk.

By the mass, I was called anything, and I'd have done anything too, and boldly. There was me, and little John Doit of Staffordshire, and black George Barnes, and Francis Pickbone, and Will Squele, a Cotswold man; you'd never find four such swashbucklers in all the law schools again. And I can tell you, we knew where the best whores were and had the pick of them at our command. Jack Falstaff, now Sir John, was a boy then, page to Thomas Mowbray, Duke of Norfolk.
This Sir John, cousin, that comes hither anon about soldiers?
This Sir John, cousin, who's coming here soon about soldiers?

The same Sir John, the very same. I see him break Skogan's head at the / court-gate, when a' was a crack not thus high: and the very same / day did I fight with one Sampson Stockfish, a fruiterer, behind / Gray's Inn. / Jesu, Jesu, the mad days that I have spent! and to see how many of my / old acquaintance are dead!

The same Sir John, the very same. I saw him crack Skogan's head at the court gate when he was a little lad this high. And that very same day I fought a fruit-seller called Sampson Stockfish behind Gray's Inn. Jesus, Jesus, the mad days I've spent! And to see how many of my old friends are dead!
Certain, 'tis certain; very sure, very sure: death, as the Psalmist / saith, is certain to all; all shall die. How a good yoke of bullocks at / Stamford fair?
Certainly, it's certain; very sure, very sure. Death, as the Psalmist says, is certain for everyone; everyone will die. How much is a good pair of bullocks at Stamford fair?
By my troth, I was not there.
Death is certain. Is old Double of your town living yet?
Death is certain. Is old Double from your town still alive?

Jesu, Jesu, dead! a' drew a good bow; and dead! a' shot a fine shoot: / John a Gaunt loved him well, and betted much money on his head. / Dead! a' would have clapped i' the clout at twelve score; and carried / you a forehand shaft a fourteen and fourteen and a half, that it / would have done a man's heart good to see. How a score of ewes now?

Jesus, Jesus, dead! He drew a good bow, and dead! He shot a fine shot. John of Gaunt was very fond of him and bet a lot of money on him. Dead! He'd hit the bull's-eye at two hundred and forty yards, and shoot a straight arrow two hundred and eighty or two hundred and ninety yards, so it would do your heart good to see it. How much is a score of ewes now?
Thereafter as they be: a score of good ewes may be worth ten / pounds.
That depends on what they're like. A score of good ewes might be worth ten pounds.
Here come two of Sir John Falstaffs men, as I think.
Here come two of Sir John Falstaff's men, I think.
Good morrow, honest gentlemen: I beseech you, which is justice / Shallow?
Good morning, honest gentlemen. Please, which of you is Justice Shallow?
I am Robert Shallow, sir; a poor esquire of this county, and one / of the king's justices of the peace: what is your good pleasure / with me?
I'm Robert Shallow, sir, a poor gentleman of this county and one of the King's justices of the peace. What can I do for you?
My captain, sir, commends him to you; my captain, Sir John / Falstaff, a tall gentleman, by heaven, and a most gallant leader.
My captain, sir, sends you his regards: my captain, Sir John Falstaff, a fine brave gentleman, by heaven, and a most gallant leader.
He greets me well, sir. I knew him a good backsword man. How / doth the good knight? may I ask how my lady his wife doth?
That's kind of him, sir. I knew him as a good swordsman with the broadsword. How is the good knight? May I ask how my lady his wife is?
Sir, pardon; a soldier is better accommodated than with a wife.
Excuse me, sir, a soldier is better accommodated than with a wife.

It is well said, in faith, sir; and it is well said indeed too. / Better accommodated! it is good; yea, indeed, is it: good phrases are / surely, and ever were, very commendable. Accommodated! it comes of / "accommodo:" very good; a good phrase.

Well said, sir, honestly; very well said indeed. "Better accommodated"! That's good; yes, it is indeed. Good phrases are certainly, and always were, very admirable. "Accommodated"! It comes from "accommodo". Very good; a good phrase.

Pardon me, sir; I have heard the word. Phrase call you it? By this / day, I know not the phrase; but I will maintain the word with my sword / to be a soldier-like word, and a word of exceeding good command, by / heaven. / Accommodated; that is, when a man is, as they say, accommodated; or / when a man is, being, whereby a' may be thought to be accommodated; / which is an excellent thing.

Pardon me, sir, I've heard the word. Do you call it a phrase? By this day, I don't know about phrases, but I'll defend the word with my sword as a soldierly word, a word of extremely good command, by heaven. "Accommodated": that is, when a man is, as they say, accommodated; or when a man is, being — whereby he may be thought to be accommodated — which is an excellent thing.
Look, here comes good Sir John. Give me your good hand, give me your / worship's good hand: by my troth, you like well and bear your years / very well: welcome, good Sir John.
Look, here comes good Sir John. Give me your good hand, give me your worship's good hand. Honestly, you look well and carry your years very well. Welcome, good Sir John.
I am glad to see you well, good Master Robert Shallow: Master / Surecard, as I think?
I'm glad to see you well, good Master Robert Shallow. Master Surecard, I think?
No, Sir John; it is my cousin Silence, in commission with me.
No, Sir John, it's my cousin Silence, who's a magistrate with me.
Good Master Silence, it well befits you should be of the peace.
Good Master Silence, it's very fitting that you should be a justice of the peace.
Fie! this is hot weather, gentlemen. Have you provided me here / half a dozen sufficient men?
Phew! This is hot weather, gentlemen. Have you got me half a dozen suitable men here?
Marry, have we, sir. Will you sit?
Indeed we have, sir. Will you sit down?
Let me see them, I beseech you.

Where's the roll? where's the roll? where's the roll? Let me see, / let me see, let me see. / So, so, so, so, so, so, so: yea, marry, sir: Ralph Mouldy! / Let them appear as I call; let them do so, let them do so. / Let me see; where is Mouldy?

Where's the list? Where's the list? Where's the list? Let me see, let me see, let me see. So, so, so, so, so, so, so. Yes, indeed, sir. Ralph Mouldy! Let them come forward as I call them; let them do that, let them do that. Let me see, where's Mouldy?
What think you, Sir John? a good-limbed fellow; young, strong, / and of good friends.
What do you think, Sir John? A well-built fellow: young, strong, and from a good family.
'Tis the more time thou wert used.
Then it's high time you were used.
Ha, ha, ha! most excellent, i' faith! things that are mouldy lack use: / very singular good! in faith, well said, Sir John, very well said.
Ha, ha, ha! Most excellent, honestly! Things that are mouldy haven't been used. Exceptionally good! Honestly, well said, Sir John, very well said.

I was prick'd well enough before, an you could have let me alone: / my old dame will be undone now for one to do her husbandry and her / drudgery: you need not to have pricked me; there are other men fitter / to go out than I.

I was pricked often enough before, if you'd just left me alone. My old woman will be ruined now, with no one to do her farm work and her chores. You didn't need to pick me; there are other men better suited to go than me.
Go to: peace, Mouldy; you shall go. Mouldy, it is time you were spent.
Come on, quiet, Mouldy. You'll go. Mouldy, it's time you were used up.
Peace, fellow, peace; stand aside: know you where you are? For / the other, Sir John: let me see: Simon Shadow!
Quiet, fellow, quiet. Stand aside. Do you know where you are? Now for the next one, Sir John. Let me see: Simon Shadow!
Yea, marry, let me have him to sit under: he's like to be a / cold soldier.
Yes, indeed, let me have him to sit under. He's likely to be a cool soldier.
Thy mother's son! like enough; and thy father's shadow: so the son of / the female is the shadow of the male: it is often so indeed; but / much of the father's substance!
Your mother's son! Likely enough, and your father's shadow. So the son of the female is the shadow of the male. That's often true indeed, but not much of the father's substance!
Do you like him, Sir John?
Do you like him, Sir John?
Shadow will serve for summer; prick him; for we have a number of / shadows to fill up the muster-book.
Shadow will do for summer. Tick him, because we have a number of shadows to fill up the roll.
Thou art a very ragged wart.
Shall I prick him down, Sir John?
Shall I tick him, Sir John?
It were superfluous; for his apparel is built upon his back and / the whole frame stands upon pins: prick him no more.
That would be unnecessary, because his clothes are built on his back and the whole structure is held together with pins. Don't prick him any more.
Ha, ha, ha! you can do it, sir; you can do it: I commend you / well. / Francis Feeble!
Ha, ha, ha! You can do it, sir, you can do it. I congratulate you. Francis Feeble!
You may: but if he had been a man's tailor, he'ld ha' prick'd you. / Wilt thou make as many holes in an enemy's battle as thou hast done in / a woman's petticoat?
You may. But if he'd been a men's tailor, he'd have pricked you. Will you make as many holes in an enemy army as you've made in a woman's petticoat?
I will do my good will, sir; you can have no more.
I'll do my best, sir. You can't ask for more.

Well said, good woman's tailor! well said, courageous Feeble! thou wilt / be as valiant as the wrathful dove or most magnanimous mouse. / Prick the woman's tailor: well, Master Shallow, deep, Master Shallow.
Well said, good ladies' tailor! Well said, courageous Feeble! You'll be as brave as the furious dove or the most noble mouse. Tick the ladies' tailor — firmly, Master Shallow, deep, Master Shallow.
I would Wart might have gone, sir.
I wish Wart could have gone, sir.

I would thou wert a man's tailor, that thou mightst mend him and make / him fit to go. I cannot put him to a private soldier that is the leader / of so many thousands; let that suffice, most forcible Feeble.
I wish you were a men's tailor, so you could mend him and make him fit to go. I can't make a common soldier of a man who leads so many thousands of lice. Let that be enough, most forcible Feeble.
I am bound to thee, reverend Feeble. Who is next?
I'm obliged to you, reverend Feeble. Who's next?
Peter Bullcalf from the village green!
'Fore God, a likely fellow! Come, prick me Bullcalf till he roar / again.
By God, a likely fellow! Come, tick Bullcalf until he bellows.
O Lord! good my lord captain,—
Oh Lord! My good lord captain —
What, dost thou roar before thou art prick'd?
What, are you bellowing before you're pricked?
O Lord, sir! I am a diseased man.
Oh Lord, sir! I'm a sick man.
A whoreson cold, sir, a cough, sir, which I caught with ringing / in the king's affairs upon his coronation-day, sir.
A damned cold, sir, a cough, sir, which I caught bell-ringing in the King's service on his coronation day, sir.
Come, thou shalt go to the wars in a gown; we will have away thy cold; / and I will take such order that thy friends shall ring for thee. / Is here all?
Come, you'll go to the wars in a dressing gown. We'll get rid of your cold, and I'll make sure your friends ring the bells for your funeral. Is this everyone?
Here is two more called than your number; you must have but four here, / sir; and so, I pray you, go in with me to dinner.
Two more have been called than your quota. You're only to have four here, sir. And so, please, come in and have dinner with me.
Come, I will go drink with you, but I cannot tarry dinner. I am / glad to see you, by my troth, Master Shallow.
Come, I'll go and have a drink with you, but I can't stay for dinner. I'm glad to see you, honestly, Master Shallow.
O, Sir John, do you remember since we lay all night in the windmill / in Saint George's field?
Oh, Sir John, do you remember when we spent the whole night in the windmill in St George's Fields?
No more of that, Master Shallow, no more of that.
No more of that, Master Shallow, no more of that.
Ha, 'twas a merry night. And is Jane Nightwork alive?
Ha, it was a merry night. And is Jane Nightwork still alive?
She never could away with me.
She never could put up with me.
Never, never; she would always say she could not abide Master / Shallow.
Never, never. She always used to say she couldn't stand Master Shallow.
By the mass, I could anger her to the heart. She was then a bona-roba. / Doth she hold her own well?
By the mass, I could make her furious. She was a fine-looking whore then. Is she keeping well?
Nay, she must be old; she cannot choose but be old; certain she's old; / and had Robin Nightwork by old Nightwork before I came to Clement's Inn.
Well, she must be old; she can't help being old. Certainly she's old. She had Robin Nightwork by old Nightwork before I went to Clement's Inn.
Ha, cousin Silence, that thou hadst seen that that this knight and I / have seen! Ha, Sir John, said I well?
Ha, cousin Silence, if only you'd seen what this knight and I have seen! Ha, Sir John, am I right?
We have heard the chimes at midnight, Master Shallow.
We've heard the chimes at midnight, Master Shallow.
That we have, that we have, that we have; in faith, Sir John, we have: / our watchword was "Hem boys!" Come, let's to dinner; come, let's / to dinner: Jesus, the days that we have seen! Come, come.
That we have, that we have, that we have. Honestly, Sir John, we have. Our watchword was "Hey, boys!" Come, let's go to dinner; come, let's go to dinner. Jesus, the days we've seen! Come, come.

Good Master Corporate Bardolph, stand my friend; and here's four / Harry ten shillings in French crowns for you. / In very truth, sir, I had as lief be hanged, sir, as go: and yet, / for mine own part, sir, I do not care; but rather, because I am / unwilling, and, for mine own part, have a desire to stay with my / friends; else, sir, I did not care, for mine own part, so much.

Good Master Corporate Bardolph, be my friend. Here's forty shillings in French crowns for you. In very truth, sir, I'd as soon be hanged, sir, as go. And yet, for my own part, sir, I don't care; but rather because I'm unwilling and, for my own part, want to stay with my friends. Otherwise, sir, I didn't care so much, for my own part.

And, good master corporal captain, for my old dame's sake, stand my / friend: she has nobody to do any thing about her when I am gone; / and she is old, and cannot help herself: you shall have forty, sir.

And, good master corporal captain, for my old woman's sake, be my friend. She'll have nobody to do anything for her when I'm gone, and she's old and can't help herself. You'll have forty shillings, sir.

By my troth, I care not; a man can die but once; we owe God a death: / I'll ne'er bear a base mind: an 't be my destiny, so; an 't be not, so: / no man's too good to serve's prince; and let it go which way it will, he / that dies this year is quit for the next.

Honestly, I don't care. A man can only die once. We owe God a death. I'll never have a cowardly mind. If it's my destiny, so be it; if it isn't, so be it. No man's too good to serve his prince, and whichever way it goes, a man who dies this year is let off for the next.
Well said; th'art a good fellow.
Well said. You're a good fellow.
Faith, I'll bear no base mind.
Honestly, I won't have a cowardly mind.
Come, sir, which men shall I have?
Come, sir, which men shall I have?
Sir, a word with you: I have three pound to free Mouldy and / Bullcalf.
Sir, a word with you. I've got three pounds to let Mouldy and Bullcalf off.
Come, Sir John, which four will you have?
Come, Sir John, which four will you have?
Marry, then, Mouldy, Bullcalf, Feeble, and Shadow.
Well then: Mouldy, Bullcalf, Feeble and Shadow.
Mouldy and Bullcalf: for you, Mouldy, stay at home till you are past / service; and for your part, Bullcalf, grow till you come unto it: / I will none of you.
Mouldy and Bullcalf. As for you, Mouldy, stay at home till you're too old to serve; and as for you, Bullcalf, grow until you're old enough. I'll have neither of you.
Sir John, Sir John, do not yourself wrong: they are your likeliest / men, and I would have you served with the best.
Sir John, Sir John, don't do yourself wrong. They're your most promising men, and I want you served by the best.

Will you tell me, Master Shallow, how to choose a man? Care I for the / limb, the thewes, the stature, bulk, and big assemblance of a man! / Give me the spirit, Master Shallow. Here's Wart; you see what a ragged / appearance it is: a' shall charge you and discharge you with the / motion of a pewterer's hammer, come off and on swifter than he that / gibbets on the brewer's bucket. / And this same half-faced fellow, Shadow; give me this man: he / presents no mark to the enemy; the foeman may with as great aim level / at the edge of a penknife. / And for a retreat; how swiftly will this Feeble the woman's tailor / run off! O, give me the spare men, and spare me the great ones. / Put me a caliver into Wart's hand, Bardolph.

Are you going to tell me how to choose a man, Master Shallow? Do I care about a man's limbs, muscles, height, size and big appearance? Give me spirit, Master Shallow. Here's Wart; you see how scruffy he looks. He'll load and fire for you as fast as a pewterer's hammer, advance and retreat faster than the man who hangs the brewer's buckets on the yoke. And this half-faced fellow, Shadow: give me this man. He gives the enemy no target; the enemy might as well aim at the edge of a penknife. And as for a retreat, how fast this Feeble the ladies' tailor will run! Oh, give me the thin men and spare me the big ones. Put a musket in Wart's hand, Bardolph.
Hold, Wart, traverse; thus, thus, thus.
Here, Wart, march; like this, like this, like this.

Come, manage me your caliver. So: very well: go to: very good, / exceeding good. O, give me always a little, lean, old, chapt, / bald shot. Well said, i' faith, Wart; thou'rt a good scab: hold, / there's a tester for thee.

Come, handle your musket. That's it. Very good. Go on. Very good, excellent. Oh, always give me a little, thin, old, wrinkled, bald gunner. Well done, honestly, Wart; you're a good scab. Here's sixpence for you.

He is not his craft's master; he doth not do it right. I remember at / Mile-end Green, when I lay at Clement's Inn,—I was then Sir Dagonet in / Arthur's show,—there was a little quiver fellow, and a' would manage / you his piece thus; and a' would about and about, and come you in and / come you in: "rah, tah, tah," would a' say; "bounce" would a' say; and / away again would a' go, and again would 'a come: I shall ne'er see / such a fellow.

He's not a master of his craft; he doesn't do it right. I remember at Mile End Green, when I was at Clement's Inn — I played Sir Dagonet in the Arthur pageant then — there was a nimble little fellow, and he'd handle his gun like this, and he'd turn about and about, and come in and come in: "rah, tah, tah," he'd say; "bang," he'd say; and away he'd go again, and back he'd come again. I'll never see such a fellow again.

These fellows will do well. Master Shallow, God keep you, Master Silence: / I will not use many words with you. Fare you well, gentlemen both: / I thank you: I must a dozen mile to-night. Bardolph, give the soldiers / coats.

These fellows will do well. Master Shallow, God keep you. Master Silence, I won't waste many words on you. Goodbye, gentlemen both. Thank you. I must do a dozen miles tonight. Bardolph, give the soldiers uniforms.
Sir John, the Lord bless you! God prosper your affairs! God send us / peace! At your return visit our house; let our old acquaintance be / renewed: peradventure I will with ye to the court.
Sir John, the Lord bless you! God prosper your business! God send us peace! When you come back, visit our house and let's renew our old friendship. Perhaps I'll go with you to court.
By God, I wish you would.
Go to; I have spoke at a word. God keep you.
Go on, I mean what I say. God keep you.
On, Bardolph; lead the men away.
On, Bardolph; lead the men away.

As I return, I will fetch off these justices: I do see the bottom / of Justice Shallow. / Lord, Lord, how subject we old men are to this vice of lying! / This same starved justice hath done nothing but prate to me of the / wildness of his youth, and the feats he hath done about Turnbull / Street; and every third word a lie, duer paid to the hearer than the / Turk's tribute. I do remember him at Clement's Inn like a man made / after supper of a cheese-paring: when a' was naked, he was, for all / the world, like a fork'd radish, with a head fantastically carved upon / it with a knife: a' was so forlorn, that his dimensions to any thick / sight were invincible: a' was the very genius of famine; yet lecherous / as a monkey, and the whores called him mandrake: a' came ever in the / rearward of the fashion, and sung those tunes to the overscutch'd / huswifes that he heard the carmen whistle, and sware they were his / fancies or his good-nights. / And now is this Vice's dagger become a squire, and talks as familiarly / of John a Gaunt as if he had been sworn brother to him; and I'll be / sworn a' ne'er saw him but once in the Tilt-yard; and then he burst / his head for crowding among the marshal's men. / I saw it, and told John a Gaunt he beat his own name; for you might / have thrust him and all his apparel into an eel-skin; the case of a / treble hautboy was a mansion for him, a court: and now has he land / and beefs. / Well, I'll be acquainted with him, if I return; and it shall go hard / but I'll make him a philosopher's two stones to me: if the young dace / be a bait for the old pike, I see no reason in the law of nature but I / may snap at him. / Let time shape, and there an end.

On my way back I'll fleece these justices. I can see right to the bottom of Justice Shallow. Lord, Lord, how prone we old men are to this vice of lying! This starved justice has done nothing but babble to me about the wildness of his youth and the things he did around Turnbull Street, and every third word a lie, paid to the listener more punctually than the Sultan's taxes. I remember him at Clement's Inn looking like a man carved out of a cheese-rind after supper. When he was naked he was for all the world like a forked radish with a head fantastically carved on it with a knife. He was so scrawny that anyone with poor eyesight couldn't see him at all. He was the very spirit of famine, yet as lecherous as a monkey, and the whores called him "mandrake". He was always behind the fashion, and he sang tunes he'd heard the carters whistle to worn-out hussies and swore they were his own compositions or serenades. And now this stage clown's wooden dagger has become a squire and talks as familiarly about John of Gaunt as if he'd been his sworn brother, and I'll swear he only ever saw him once, at the jousting ground, and then he got his head cracked for pushing in among the marshal's guards. I saw it, and told John of Gaunt he was beating his own name, gaunt, because you could have stuffed Shallow and all his clothes into an eel-skin; the case of a treble oboe was a mansion for him, a palace. And now he has land and cattle. Well, I'll get to know him if I come back, and I'll make him my philosopher's stone, turning everything to gold for me, or my name's not Falstaff. If the young fish is bait for the old pike, I see no reason in the law of nature why I shouldn't snap at him. Let time decide, and that's the end of it.
'Tis Gaultree Forest, an 't shall please your grace.
It's Gaultree Forest, if it please your grace.
Here stand, my lords; and send discoverers forth / To know the numbers of our enemies.
Stop here, my lords, and send scouts out to find out how many enemies there are.

'Tis well done. / My friends and brethren in these great affairs, / I must acquaint you that I have received / New-dated letters from Northumberland; / Their cold intent, tenour and substance, thus: / Here doth he wish his person, with such powers / As might hold sortance with his quality, / The which he could not levy; whereupon / He is retired, to ripe his growing fortunes, / To Scotland: and concludes in hearty prayers / That your attempts may overlive the hazard / And fearful meeting of their opposite.

That's well done. My friends and brothers in this great enterprise, I have to tell you that I've received recently dated letters from Northumberland. Their cold message, gist and substance is this: he wishes he were here in person, with an army fitting his rank, which he couldn't raise. So he has withdrawn to Scotland to let his growing fortunes ripen, and he ends with heartfelt prayers that your efforts may survive the danger of a fearful meeting with the enemy.
Thus do the hopes we have in him touch ground / And dash themselves to pieces.
So the hopes we had in him hit the ground and smash to pieces.
West of this forest, scarcely off a mile, / In goodly form comes on the enemy; / And, by the ground they hide, I judge their number / Upon or near the rate of thirty thousand.
West of this forest, barely a mile away, the enemy is advancing in good order, and judging by the ground they cover, I'd put their number at or near thirty thousand.
The just proportion that we gave them out. / Let us sway on and face them in the field.
Exactly the number we estimated. Let's move forward and face them in the field.
What well-appointed leader fronts us here?
What well-equipped leader is coming to meet us here?
I think it is my Lord of Westmoreland.
I think it's my Lord of Westmoreland.
Health and fair greeting from our general, / The prince, Lord John and Duke of Lancaster.
Health and kind greetings from our general, the Prince, Lord John, Duke of Lancaster.
Say on, my Lord of Westmoreland, in peace: / What doth concern your coming?
Speak on in peace, my Lord of Westmoreland. What is the reason for your coming?

Then, my lord, / Unto your grace do I in chief address / The substance of my speech. If that rebellion / Came like itself, in base and abject routs, / Led on by bloody youth, guarded with rags, / And countenanced by boys and beggary, / I say, if damn'd commotion so appear'd, / In his true, native, and most proper shape, / You, reverend father, and these noble lords / Had not been here, to dress the ugly form / Of base and bloody insurrection / With your fair honours. You, lord archbishop, / Whose see is by a civil peace maintain'd, / Whose beard the silver hand of peace hath touch'd, / Whose learning and good letters peace hath tutor'd, / Whose white investments figure innocence, / The dove and very blessed spirit of peace, / Wherefore you do so ill translate yourself / Out of the speech of peace that bears such grace, / Into the harsh and boisterous tongue of war; / Turning your books to graves, your ink to blood, / Your pens to lances and your tongue divine / To a loud trumpet and a point of war?

Then, my lord, I address my speech chiefly to your grace. If rebellion came looking like itself, in low, wretched mobs led by violent youths, dressed in rags and supported by boys and beggars — I say, if damned rebellion appeared like that, in its true, natural and proper shape, you, reverend father, and these noble lords wouldn't be here dressing up the ugly shape of low and bloody revolt with your honourable reputations. You, lord Archbishop, whose diocese is kept up by civil peace, whose beard the silver hand of peace has touched, whose learning and scholarship peace has taught, whose white robes stand for innocence, the dove and the very blessed spirit of peace — why do you so badly translate yourself out of the gracious language of peace into the harsh, noisy tongue of war, turning your books into graves, your ink into blood, your pens into lances and your holy tongue into a loud trumpet sounding the call to battle?

Wherefore do I this? so the question stands. / Briefly to this end: we are all diseased, / And with our surfeiting and wanton hours / Have brought ourselves into a burning fever, / And we must bleed for it; of which disease / Our late king, Richard, being infected, died. / But, my most noble Lord of Westmoreland, / I take not on me here as a physician, / Nor do I as an enemy to peace / Troop in the throngs of military men; / But rather show awhile like fearful war, / To diet rank minds sick of happiness, / And purge the obstructions which begin to stop / Our very veins of life.
