Hear me more plainly. / I have in equal balance justly weigh'd / What wrongs our arms may do, what wrongs we suffer, / And find our griefs heavier than our offences. / We see which way the stream of time doth run, / And are enforced from our most quiet there / By the rough torrent of occasion; / And have the summary of all our griefs, / When time shall serve, to show in articles; / Which long ere this we offer'd to the king, / And might by no suit gain our audience: / When we are wrong'd and would unfold our griefs, / We are denied access unto his person / Even by those men that most have done us wrong. / The dangers of the days but newly gone, / Whose memory is written on the earth / With yet appearing blood, and the examples / Of every minute's instance, present now, / Hath put us in these ill-beseeming arms, / Not to break peace or any branch of it, / But to establish here a peace indeed, / Concurring, both in name and quality.

Why am I doing this? That's the question. Briefly, for this reason: we are all diseased, and with our overeating and our wild hours we have brought ourselves into a burning fever, and we must be bled for it. Our late King Richard caught this disease and died of it. But, my most noble Lord of Westmoreland, I'm not setting myself up here as a doctor, nor do I march among crowds of soldiers as an enemy of peace. Rather, I put on the look of fearful war for a while, to put on a diet minds that are swollen and sick of too much happiness, and to clear the blockages that are beginning to stop our very veins of life. Let me speak more plainly. I have weighed fairly in the balance the wrongs our army may do and the wrongs we suffer, and I find our grievances heavier than our offences. We see which way the current of the times is running, and we're forced out of our peaceful lives by the rough torrent of events. We have a list of all our grievances, to show in written articles when the time comes, which we offered to the King long ago and could get no hearing for, however we pleaded. When we are wronged and want to set out our grievances, we're refused access to him by the very men who have wronged us most. The dangers of the days just past, whose memory is still written on the earth in blood that can be seen, and the examples that every minute now presents, have put us in this unfitting armour — not to break the peace or any branch of it, but to set up here a real peace, true both in name and in substance.

When ever yet was your appeal denied? / Wherein have you been galled by the king? / What peer hath been suborn'd to grate on you, / That you should seal this lawless bloody book / Of forged rebellion with a seal divine / And consecrate commotion's bitter edge?

When was your appeal ever refused? How has the King hurt you? What lord has been bribed to harass you, that you should seal this lawless, bloody book of fraudulent rebellion with a holy seal and bless the bitter edge of rebellion?
My brother general, the commonwealth, / To brother born an household cruelty, / I make my quarrel in particular.
I make it my personal quarrel on behalf of my brother, the people, and the cruelty done at home to my born brother.
There is no need of any such redress; / Or if there were, it not belongs to you.
There's no need for any such remedy; or if there were, it isn't your business.
Why not to him in part, and to us all / That feel the bruises of the days before, / And suffer the condition of these times / To lay a heavy and unequal hand / Upon our honours?
Why isn't it partly his, and all of ours, who feel the bruises of the days gone by and suffer under these times, which lay a heavy and unjust hand on our honours?

O, my good Lord Mowbray, / Construe the times to their necessities, / And you shall say indeed, it is the time, / And not the king, that doth you injuries. / Yet for your part, it not appears to me / Either from the king or in the present time / That you should have an inch of any ground / To build a grief on: were you not restored / To all the Duke of Norfolk's signories, / Your noble and right well rememb'red father's?

Oh, my good Lord Mowbray, interpret the times by what they make necessary, and you'll indeed say it's the times, not the King, that are injuring you. And yet for your part, it doesn't seem to me that either the King or the present times give you an inch of ground to build a grievance on. Weren't you given back all the estates of the Duke of Norfolk, your noble and well-remembered father?

What thing, in honour, had my father lost, / That need to be revived and breathed in me? / The king that loved him, as the state stood then, / Was force perforce compell'd to banish him: / And then that Henry Bolingbroke and he, / Being mounted and both roused in their seats, / Their neighing coursers daring of the spur, / Their armed staves in charge, their beavers down, / Their eyes of fire sparkling through sights of steel, / And the loud trumpet blowing them together, / Then, then, when there was nothing could have stay'd / My father from the breast of Bolingbroke, / O, when the king did throw his warder down, / His own life hung upon the staff he threw; / Then threw he down himself and all their lives / That by indictment and by dint of sword / Have since miscarried under Bolingbroke.

What honour had my father lost that needed to be revived and breathed into me? The King who loved him was forced, against his will, by the state of things at the time, to banish him. And then, when Henry Bolingbroke and he were mounted and both braced in their saddles, their neighing horses daring the spur, their lances levelled, their visors down, their fiery eyes sparkling through the slits of their steel helmets, and the loud trumpet blowing them together — then, then, when nothing could have stopped my father's lance from reaching Bolingbroke's chest, oh, when the King threw his staff down, his own life hung on the staff he threw. He threw down himself and the lives of all those who since then, by legal charges and by the sword, have been destroyed under Bolingbroke.

You speak, Lord Mowbray, now you know not what. / The Earl of Hereford was reputed then / In England the most valiant gentleman: / Who knows on whom fortune would then have smiled? / But if your father had been victor there, / He ne'er had borne it out of Coventry: / For all the country in a general voice / Cried hate upon him; and all their prayers and love / Were set on Hereford, whom they doted on / And bless'd and graced indeed, more than the king. / But this is mere digression from my purpose. / Here come I from our princely general / To know your griefs; to tell you from his grace / That he will give you audience; and wherein / It shall appear that your demands are just, / You shall enjoy them, everything set off / That might so much as think you enemies.

You don't know what you're saying now, Lord Mowbray. The Earl of Hereford was then thought the bravest gentleman in England. Who knows which of them fortune would have smiled on? But if your father had won there, he would never have got out of Coventry alive, because the whole country with one voice cried out its hatred of him, and all their prayers and love were set on Hereford, whom they adored and blessed and honoured more than the King. But this is just a digression from my purpose. I've come from our princely general to hear your grievances and to tell you from his grace that he will give you a hearing, and wherever your demands are shown to be just you shall have them, with everything set aside that might make you seem enemies.
But he hath forc'd us to compel this offer; / And it proceeds from policy, not love.
But he's been forced by us to make this offer, and it comes from cunning, not love.

Mowbray, you overween to take it so; / This offer comes from mercy, not from fear: / For, lo! within a ken our army lies, / Upon mine honour, all too confident / To give admittance to a thought of fear. / Our battle is more full of names than yours, / Our men more perfect in the use of arms, / Our armour all as strong, our cause the best; / Then reason will our hearts should be as good: / Say you not then our offer is compell'd.

Mowbray, you're being arrogant to take it that way. This offer comes from mercy, not fear. Look, our army lies within sight, upon my honour far too confident to let in a thought of fear. Our army has more famous names in it than yours, our men are more skilled with weapons, our armour as strong, our cause the best; so reason says our courage should be as good. Don't say, then, that our offer is forced.
Well, by my will we shall admit no parley.
Well, if I have my way we'll have no negotiation.
That argues but the shame of your offence: / A rotten case abides no handling.
That only proves how shameful your crime is. A rotten case can't bear handling.
Hath the Prince John a full commission, / In very ample virtue of his father, / To hear and absolutely to determine / Of what conditions we shall stand upon?
Does Prince John have full authority, fully representing his father, to hear and to decide absolutely on the conditions we will insist on?
That is intended in the general's name: / I muse you make so slight a question.
That's implied in the title of general. I'm surprised you ask such a trivial question.

Then take, my Lord of Westmoreland, this schedule, / For this contains our general grievances: / Each several article herein redress'd, / All members of our cause, both here and hence, / That are insinew'd to this action, / Acquitted by a true substantial form / And present execution of our wills / To us and to our purposes confined, / We come within our awful banks again / And knit our powers to the arm of peace.

Then take this document, my Lord of Westmoreland, because it contains our general grievances. If each separate article in it is put right, and all those who share our cause, both here and elsewhere, who are bound up in this action, are pardoned in a proper, binding form, and our demands, as they concern us and our aims, are carried out at once, we will come back within our respectful bounds and join our forces to the arm of peace.

This will I show the general. Please you, lords, / In sight of both our battles we may meet; / And either end in peace, which God so frame! / Or to the place of difference call the swords / Which must decide it.
I'll show this to the general. If you please, lords, we can meet in sight of both our armies, and either end in peace, which God grant, or call the swords to the field that must settle our quarrel.
My lord, we will do so.
There is a thing within my bosom tells me / That no conditions of our peace can stand.
Something inside me tells me that no terms of peace we make will last.
Fear you not that: if we can make our peace / Upon such large terms and so absolute / As our conditions shall consist upon, / Our peace shall stand as firm as rocky mountains.
Don't be afraid of that. If we can make our peace on such broad and absolute terms as our conditions insist on, our peace will stand as firm as rocky mountains.

Yea, but our valuation shall be such / That every slight and false-derived cause, / Yea, every idle, nice and wanton reason / Shall to the king taste of this action; / That, were our royal faiths martyrs in love, / We shall be winnow'd with so rough a wind / That even our corn shall seem as light as chaff / And good from bad find no partition.

Yes, but we'll be valued in such a way that every trivial, false excuse, yes, every idle, petty and silly reason, will remind the King of this rebellion. Even if we were martyrs in our love and loyalty to the King, we'll be winnowed by such a rough wind that even our grain will seem as light as chaff, and good will not be separated from bad.

No, no, my lord. Note this; the king is weary / Of dainty and such picking grievances: / For he hath found to end one doubt by death / Revives two greater in the heirs of life, / And therefore will he wipe his tables clean / And keep no tell-tale to his memory / That may repeat and history his loss / To new remembrance; for full well he knows / He cannot so precisely weed this land / As his misdoubts present occasion: / His foes are so enrooted with his friends / That, plucking to unfix an enemy, / He doth unfasten so and shake a friend: / So that this land, like an offensive wife / That hath enraged him on to offer strokes, / As he is striking, holds his infant up / And hangs resolved correction in the arm / That was uprear'd to execution.

No, no, my lord. Notice this: the King is tired of petty, nit-picking grievances, because he has found that ending one fear with a death brings two greater ones to life in the heirs who survive. So he'll wipe his slate clean and keep no informer by him to repeat the story of his losses and remind him of them again. He knows very well he can't weed this land as thoroughly as his suspicions suggest. His enemies are so rooted in among his friends that, in pulling up an enemy, he loosens and shakes a friend. So this land, like a quarrelsome wife who has driven him to the point of hitting her, holds up his baby just as he's about to strike, and keeps the punishment he's decided on hanging in the arm that was raised to carry it out.
Besides, the king hath wasted all his rods / On late offenders, that he now doth lack / The very instruments of chastisement: / So that his power, like to a fangless lion, / May offer, but not hold.
Besides, the King has used up all his rods on recent offenders, so that he now lacks the very means of punishment. His power, like a lion without teeth, can threaten but not hold.
'Tis very true: / And therefore be assured, my good lord marshal, / If we do now make our atonement well, / Our peace will, like a broken limb united, / Grow stronger for the breaking.
That's very true. And so be assured, my good Lord Marshal, if we make our reconciliation well now, our peace will be like a broken limb that has healed, stronger for having been broken.
Be it so. / Here is return'd my Lord of Westmoreland.
So be it. Here's my Lord of Westmoreland back.
The prince is here at hand: pleaseth your lordship / To meet his grace just distance 'tween our armies.
The Prince is close by. If your lordship pleases, meet his grace exactly halfway between our armies.
Your grace of York, in God's name then, set forward.
Your grace of York, in God's name then, go ahead.
Before, and greet his grace: my lord, we come.
Go first and greet his grace. My lord, we're coming.

You are well encounter'd here, my cousin Mowbray: / Good day to you, gentle lord Archbishop; / And so to you, Lord Hastings, and to all. / My Lord of York, it better show'd with you / When that your flock, assembled by the bell, / Encircled you to hear with reverence / Your exposition on the holy text / Than now to see you here an iron man, / Cheering a rout of rebels with your drum, / Turning the word to sword and life to death. / That man that sits within a monarch's heart, / And ripens in the sunshine of his favour, / Would he abuse the countenance of the king, / Alack, what mischiefs might he set abroach / In shadow of such greatness! With you, lord bishop, / It is even so. Who hath not heard it spoken / How deep you were within the books of God? / To us the speaker in his parliament; / To us the imagined voice of God himself; / The very opener and intelligencer / Between the grace, the sanctities of heaven / And our dull workings. O, who shall believe / But you misuse the reverence of your place, / Employ the countenance and grace of heaven, / As a false favourite doth his prince's name, / In deeds dishonourable? You have ta'en up, / Under the counterfeited zeal of God, / The subjects of his substitute, my father, / And both against the peace of heaven and him / Have here up-swarm'd them.

Well met here, my cousin Mowbray. Good day to you, noble lord Archbishop, and to you, Lord Hastings, and to everyone. My Lord of York, you looked better when your congregation, called by the bell, gathered round you to listen reverently to your sermon on the holy text, than now, seeing you here as a man of iron, encouraging a mob of rebels with your drum, turning the Word into the sword and life into death. If a man who sits in a monarch's heart and ripens in the sunshine of his favour abused the King's support, alas, what harm he could set going under cover of such greatness! It's just so with you, lord Bishop. Who hasn't heard how deeply you were in God's books? To us you were the speaker in God's parliament, the imagined voice of God himself, the very interpreter and messenger between the grace and holiness of heaven and our dull actions. Oh, who could believe anything but that you are misusing the respect owed to your position, using the favour and grace of heaven in dishonourable deeds, as a false favourite uses his prince's name? Under a pretended zeal for God, you've raised up the subjects of His deputy, my father, and swarmed them here against both the peace of heaven and the King.

Good my Lord of Lancaster, / I am not here against your father's peace; / But, as I told my Lord of Westmoreland, / The time misorder'd doth, in common sense, / Crowd us and crush us to this monstrous form / To hold our safety up. I sent your grace / The parcels and particulars of our grief, / The which hath been with scorn shoved from the court, / Whereon this Hydra son of war is born; / Whose dangerous eyes may well be charm'd asleep / With grant of our most just and right desires, / And true obedience, of this madness cured, / Stoop tamely to the foot of majesty.

My good Lord of Lancaster, I'm not here against your father's peace. But, as I told my Lord of Westmoreland, these disordered times, as anyone can see, crowd us and crush us into this monstrous shape to keep ourselves safe. I sent your grace the details and particulars of our grievances, which have been pushed out of court with scorn, and from that this many-headed Hydra, this son of war, is born. Its dangerous eyes may be charmed to sleep by granting our just and proper wishes, and true obedience, cured of this madness, will bow tamely at the feet of majesty.
If not, we ready are to try our fortunes / To the last man.
If not, we're ready to try our luck to the last man.

And though we here fall down, / We have supplies to second our attempt: / If they miscarry, theirs shall second them; / And so success of mischief shall be born / And heir from heir shall hold this quarrel up / Whiles England shall have generation.

And even if we fall here, we have reinforcements to back up our attempt. If they fail, theirs will back them up, and so a succession of trouble will be born, and heir after heir will keep this quarrel going as long as England has children.
You are too shallow, Hastings, much to shallow, / To sound the bottom of the after-times.
You're too shallow, Hastings, much too shallow, to sound the depths of the future.
Pleaseth your grace to answer them directly / How far forth you do like their articles.
If your grace pleases, answer them directly: how far do you accept their articles?

I like them all, and do allow them well, / And swear here, by the honour of my blood, / My father's purposes have been mistook, / And some about him have too lavishly / Wrested his meaning and authority. / My lord, these griefs shall be with speed redress'd; / Upon my soul, they shall. If this may please you, / Discharge your powers unto their several counties, / As we will ours; and here between the armies / Let's drink together friendly and embrace, / That all their eyes may bear those tokens home / Of our restored love and amity.

I like them all and fully accept them, and I swear here by the honour of my blood that my father's intentions have been misunderstood, and that some of those around him have too freely twisted his meaning and his authority. My lord, these grievances will be put right quickly; upon my soul, they will. If this satisfies you, send your troops home to their counties, as we'll send ours; and here between the armies let's drink together in friendship and embrace, so that all their eyes can carry home these signs of our restored love and friendship.
I take your princely word for these redresses.
I take your princely word for these remedies.
I give it you, and will maintain my word: / And thereupon I drink unto your grace.
I give it to you, and I'll keep my word. And with that, I drink to your grace.
Go, captain, and deliver to the army / This news of peace: let them have pay, and part: / I know it will please them. Hie thee, captain.
Go, captain, and give the army this news of peace. Let them be paid and go. I know it will please them. Hurry, captain.
To you, my noble Lord of Westmoreland.
To you, my noble Lord of Westmoreland.
I pledge your grace; and, if you knew what pains / I have bestow'd to breed this present peace, / You would drink freely: but my love to ye / Shall show itself more openly hereafter.
I drink to your grace. And if you knew what trouble I've taken to bring about this peace, you'd drink heartily. But my love for you will show itself more openly later.
I am glad of it. / Health to my lord and gentle cousin, Mowbray.
I'm glad of it. Health to my lord and noble cousin, Mowbray.
You wish me health in very happy season, / For I am, on the sudden, something ill.
You wish me health at a very good moment, because I've suddenly come over rather ill.
Against ill chances men are ever merry; / But heaviness foreruns the good event.
Men are always merry just before bad luck, but heaviness comes before a good outcome.
Therefore be merry, coz; since sudden sorrow / Serves to say thus, "some good thing comes tomorrow."
So be merry, cousin, since sudden sorrow means "something good will come tomorrow".
Believe me, I am passing light in spirit.
So much the worse, if your own rule be true.
All the worse, if your own rule is true.
The word of peace is render'd: hark, how they shout!
The word of peace has been given. Listen to them shout!
This had been cheerful after victory.
That would have been cheerful after a victory.
A peace is of the nature of a conquest; / For then both parties nobly are subdued, / And neither party loser.
A peace is a kind of conquest, because both sides are nobly subdued and neither side loses.
Go, my lord. / And let our army be discharged too.
Go, my lord, and let our army be dismissed too.
And, good my lord, so please you, let our trains / March by us, that we may peruse the men / We should have coped withal.
And, my good lord, if you please, let your troops march past us so we can look over the men we would have fought.
Go, good Lord Hastings, / And, ere they be dismiss'd, let them march by.
Go, good Lord Hastings, and let them march past before they're dismissed.
I trust, lords, we shall lie to-night together.
I trust, lords, we'll spend tonight together.
Now, cousin, wherefore stands our army still?
Now, cousin, why is our army standing still?
The leaders, having charge from you to stand, / Will not go off until they hear you speak.
The officers, having orders from you to stand, won't leave until they hear you say so.

My lord, our army is dispersed already: / Like youthful steers unyoked, they take their courses / East, west, north, south; or, like a school broke up, / Each hurries toward his home and sporting-place.

My lord, our army has already dispersed. Like young bullocks let out of the yoke, they're running off east, west, north and south; or, like a school let out, each one is hurrying home or to his playground.
Good tidings, my Lord Hastings; for the which / I do arrest thee, traitor, of high treason: / And you, lord archbishop, and you, Lord Mowbray, / Of capital treason I attach you both.
Good news, my Lord Hastings — and for it I arrest you, traitor, for high treason. And you, lord Archbishop, and you, Lord Mowbray, I arrest you both for treason punishable by death.
Is this proceeding just and honourable?
Is this proceeding fair and honourable?
Will you thus break your faith?
Will you break your promise like this?

I pawn'd thee none: / I promised you redress of these same grievances / Whereof you did complain; which, by mine honour, / I will perform with a most Christian care. / But for you, rebels, look to taste the due / Meet for rebellion and such acts as yours. / Most shallowly did you these arms commence, / Fondly brought here and foolishly sent hence. / Strike up our drums, pursue the scattr'd stray: / God, and not we, hath safely fought to-day. / Some guard these traitors to the block of death, / Treason's true bed and yielder up of breath.

I pledged you none. I promised you a remedy for the grievances you complained about, which, upon my honour, I will carry out with most Christian care. But as for you, rebels, expect to taste the punishment that fits rebellion and actions like yours. You started this war very shallowly, foolishly brought your forces here and foolishly sent them away. Sound our drums; pursue the scattered stragglers. God, not we, has fought safely today. Some of you, take these traitors to the block, treason's proper bed, where life is given up.
What's your name, sir? of what condition are you, and of / what place, I pray?
What's your name, sir? What's your rank, and where are you from, may I ask?
I am a knight sir; and my name is Colevile of the Dale.
I'm a knight, sir, and my name is Colevile of the Dale.

Well, then, Colevile is your name, a knight is your degree, and / your place the dale: Colevile shall be still your name, a traitor / your degree, and the dungeon your place, a place deep enough; so / shall you be still Colevile of the dale.

Well then, Colevile is your name, a knight is your rank, and your place the dale. Colevile will still be your name, a traitor your rank, and the dungeon your place, a place deep enough, so you'll still be Colevile of the dale.
Are not you Sir John Falstaff?

As good a man as he, sir, whoe'er I am. Do ye yield, sir? or shall I / sweat for you? If I do sweat, they are the drops of thy lovers, and / they weep for thy death: therefore rouse up fear and trembling, / and do observance to my mercy.

As good a man as him, sir, whoever I am. Do you surrender, sir, or must I sweat for you? If I do sweat, they're the tears of those who love you, weeping for your death. So stir up your fear and trembling and bow to my mercy.
I think you are Sir John Falstaff, and in that thought yield me.
I think you're Sir John Falstaff, and thinking so, I surrender.

I have a whole school of tongues in this belly of mine, and not a / tongue of them all speaks any other word but my name. An I had but / a belly of any indifferency, I were simply the most active fellow in / Europe: my womb, my womb, my womb undoes me. / Here comes our general.

I have a whole school of tongues in this belly of mine, and not one of them says anything but my name. If only I had a belly of ordinary size, I'd simply be the most active fellow in Europe. My belly, my belly, my belly is my ruin. Here comes our general.
The heat is past; follow no further now: / Call in the powers, good cousin Westmoreland.
The heat of battle is over. Pursue no further now. Call in the troops, good cousin Westmoreland.
Now, Falstaff, where have you been all this while? / When everything is ended, then you come: / These tardy tricks of yours will, on my life, / One time or other break some gallows' back.
Now, Falstaff, where have you been all this time? When everything's over, then you arrive. These late tricks of yours will, I swear, one day or another break some gallows' back.

I would be sorry, my lord, but it should be thus: I never knew yet / but rebuke and check was the reward of valour. Do you think me a / swallow, an arrow, or a bullet? have I, in my poor and old motion, / the expedition of thought? I have speeded hither with the very / extremest inch of possibility; I have foundered nine score and odd / posts: and here, travel-tainted as I am, have, in my pure and / immaculate valour, taken Sir John Colevile of the dale, a most furious / knight and valorous enemy. But what of that? he saw me, and yielded; / that I may justly say, with the hook-nosed fellow of Rome, "I came, / saw, and overcame."

I'd be sorry, my lord, if it were any other way. I've never known anything but scolding and rebuke to be the reward of courage. Do you think I'm a swallow, an arrow or a bullet? Do I, with my poor old movements, have the speed of thought? I've hurried here at the very utmost limit of possibility. I've worn out more than a hundred and eighty post-horses. And here, dirty from the journey as I am, in my pure, spotless courage, I've taken Sir John Colevile of the dale, a most furious knight and brave enemy. But what of it? He saw me and surrendered, so that I can fairly say, with that hook-nosed fellow from Rome, "I came, saw and conquered."
It was more of his courtesy than your deserving.
It was more his politeness than your merit.

I know not: here he is, and here I yield him: and I beseech your / grace, let it be booked with the rest of this day's deeds; or, by the / Lord, I will have it in a particular ballad else, with mine own / picture on the top on't, Colevile kissing my foot: to the which / course if I be enforced, if you do not all show like gilt twopences to / me, and I in the clear sky of fame o'ershine you as much as the full / moon doth the cinders of the element, which show like pins' heads to / her, believe not the word of the noble: therefore let me have right, / and let desert mount.

I don't know. Here he is, and here I hand him over. And I beg your grace, let it be recorded with the rest of today's deeds, or else, by the Lord, I'll have it put in a ballad of its own, with my picture at the top and Colevile kissing my foot. And if I'm forced to do that, and you don't all look like cheap gilded coins next to me, and I don't outshine you in the clear sky of fame as much as the full moon outshines the stars, which look like pinheads beside her, then don't believe a nobleman's word. So give me my due, and let merit rise.
Yours is too heavy to rise.
Yours is too dense to shine.
Let it do something, my good lord, that may do me good, and / call it what you will.
Let it do something, my good lord, that will do me some good, and call it whatever you like.
A famous rebel art thou, Colevile.
And a famous true subject took him.
And a famous loyal subject captured him.
I am, my lord, but as my betters are / That led me hither: had they been ruled by me, / You should have won them dearer than you have.
I am, my lord, only what my superiors are who led me here. If they'd taken my advice, you'd have paid a higher price for them than you have.
I know not how they sold themselves: but thou, like a kind / fellow, gavest thyself away gratis; and I thank thee for thee.
I don't know what price they sold themselves for. But you, like a kind fellow, gave yourself away for free, and I thank you for yourself.
Well, have you stopped the chase?
Retreat is made and execution stay'd.
The retreat has been sounded and the killing stopped.
Send Colevile with his confederates / To York, to present execution. / Blunt, lead him hence; and see you guard him sure.
Send Colevile and his allies to York for immediate execution. Blunt, take him away, and make sure you guard him well.

And now dispatch we toward the court, my lords: / I hear the king my father is sore sick: / Our news shall go before us to his majesty, / Which, cousin, you shall bear to comfort him, / And we with sober speed will follow you.

And now let's hurry to court, my lords. I hear the King my father is very ill. Our news will go ahead of us to his Majesty; you, cousin, will carry it to comfort him, and we'll follow you with steady speed.
My lord, I beseech you, give me leave to go through Gloucestershire: / and, when you come to court, stand my good lord, pray, in your good / report.
My lord, please give me permission to go through Gloucestershire, and when you get to court, please be my good lord in your report.
Fare you well, Falstaff: I, in my condition, / Shall better speak of you than you deserve.
Goodbye, Falstaff. In my position, I'll speak better of you than you deserve.

I would you had but the wit: 'twere better than your dukedom. / Good faith, this same young sober-blooded boy doth not love me; / nor a man cannot make him laugh; but that's no marvel, he drinks / no wine. There's never none of these demure boys come to any proof; / for thin drink doth so over-cool their blood, and making many / fish-meals, that they fall into a kind of male green-sickness; and / then, when they marry, they get wenches: they are generally fools / and cowards; which some of us should be too, but for inflammation. / A good sherris-sack hath a two-fold operation in it. It ascends me / into the brain; dries me there all the foolish and dull and crudy / vapours which environ it; makes it apprehensive, quick, forgetive, / full of nimble fiery and delectable shapes; which, delivered o'er to / the voice, the tongue, which is the birth, becomes excellent wit. / The second property of your excellent sherris is, the warming of the / blood; which, before cold and settled, left the liver white and pale, / which is the badge of pusillanimity and cowardice; but the sherris / warms it and makes it course from the inwards to the parts extremes: / it illumineth the face, which as a beacon gives warning to all / the rest of this little kingdom, man, to arm; and then the vital / commoners and inland petty spirits muster me all to their captain, the / heart, who, great and puffed up with this retinue, doth any deed of / courage; and this valour comes of sherris. So that skill in the weapon / is nothing without sack, for that sets it a-work; and learning a mere / hoard of gold kept by a devil, till sack commences it and sets it in / act and use. Hereof comes it that Prince Harry is valiant; for the / cold blood he did naturally inherit of his father, he hath, like lean, / sterile and bare land, manured, husbanded and tilled with excellent / endeavour of drinking good and good store of fertile sherris, that he / is become very hot and valiant. If I had a thousand sons, the first / humane principle I would teach them should be, to forswear thin / potations and to addict themselves to sack.

I wish you had the wit to; it would be worth more than your dukedom. Honestly, this sober-blooded boy doesn't love me, and no one can make him laugh. But that's no wonder: he drinks no wine. None of these well-behaved boys ever amount to anything, because weak drink cools their blood so much, and with eating so much fish they fall into a kind of male anaemia, and then when they marry they father girls. They're generally fools and cowards, as some of us would be too, if it weren't for drink heating us up. A good sherry has a double effect. It climbs into the brain and dries up all the foolish, dull, sluggish vapours surrounding it; it makes the brain quick, lively and inventive, full of nimble, fiery, delightful images, which, passed on to the voice, the tongue, which gives them birth, become excellent wit. The second quality of your excellent sherry is that it warms the blood, which, being cold and still before, left the liver white and pale, which is the sign of faint-heartedness and cowardice. But the sherry warms it and makes it run from the inner organs to the extremities. It lights up the face, which like a beacon warns all the rest of this little kingdom, man, to arm; and then all the vital common people and minor spirits inside gather to their captain, the heart, which, great and swollen with this following, will do any brave deed. And this courage comes from sherry. So skill with weapons is nothing without sack, because sack sets it working, and learning is just a hoard of gold guarded by a devil until sack sets it going and puts it to use. That's why Prince Harry is brave: the cold blood he naturally inherited from his father he has manured, farmed and ploughed, like poor, barren, bare land, with the excellent labour of drinking plenty of good fertile sherry, so that he has become very hot and brave. If I had a thousand sons, the first human principle I'd teach them would be to give up weak drinks and devote themselves to sack.
The army is discharged all and gone.
The whole army has been discharged and gone.

Let them go. I'll through Gloucestershire; and there will I visit / Master Robert Shallow, esquire: I have him already tempering between / my finger and my thumb, and shortly will I seal with him. Come away.

Let them go. I'll go through Gloucestershire, and there I'll visit Master Robert Shallow, esquire. I've already got him softening like wax between my finger and thumb, and soon I'll seal my bargain with him. Come on.

Now, lords, if God doth give successful end / To this debate that bleedeth at our doors, / We will our youth lead on to higher fields / And draw no swords but what are sanctified. / Our navy is address'd, our power collected, / Our substitutes in absence well invested, / And every thing lies level to our wish: / Only, we want a little personal strength; / And pause us, till these rebels, now afoot, / Come underneath the yoke of government.

Now, lords, if God gives a successful end to this conflict that's bleeding at our doors, we will lead our young men to higher battlefields and draw no swords except holy ones. Our navy is ready, our army gathered, our deputies for while we're away properly appointed, and everything is as we'd wish. We only lack a little bodily strength, and we must wait until these rebels who are now in the field are brought back under the yoke of government.
Both which we doubt not but your majesty / Shall soon enjoy.
We have no doubt your Majesty will soon have both of those.
Humphrey, my son of Gloucester, / Where is the prince your brother?
Humphrey, my son of Gloucester, where is the Prince your brother?
I think he's gone to hunt, my lord, at Windsor.
I think he's gone hunting at Windsor, my lord.
I do not know, my lord.
Is not his brother, Thomas of Clarence, with him?
Isn't his brother, Thomas of Clarence, with him?
No, my good lord; he is in presence here.
No, my good lord, he's here with you.
What would my lord and father?
What does my lord and father want?

Nothing but well to thee, Thomas of Clarence. / How chance thou art not with the prince thy brother? / He loves thee, and thou dost neglect him, Thomas; / Thou hast a better place in his affection / Than all thy brothers: cherish it, my boy, / And noble offices thou mayst effect / Of mediation, after I am dead, / Between his greatness and thy other brethren: / Therefore omit him not; blunt not his love, / Nor lose the good advantage of his grace / By seeming cold or careless of his will; / For he is gracious, if he be observed. / He hath a tear for pity and a hand / Open as day for melting charity: / Yet notwithstanding, being incensed, he's flint; / As humorous as winter and as sudden / As flaws congealed in the spring of day. / His temper, therefore, must be well observed: / Chide him for faults, and do it reverently, / When you perceive his blood inclined to mirth; / But, being moody, give him line and scope, / Till that his passions, like a whale on ground, / Confound themselves with working. Learn this, Thomas, / And thou shalt prove a shelter to thy friends, / A hoop of gold to bind thy brothers in, / That the united vessel of their blood, / Mingled with venom of suggestion— / As, force perforce, the age will pour it in— / Shall never leak, though it do work as strong / As aconitum or rash gunpowder.

Only good for you, Thomas of Clarence. How is it you're not with the Prince your brother? He loves you, and you neglect him, Thomas. You have a better place in his affection than all your brothers. Value it, my boy, and after I'm dead you may do noble service as a go-between between his greatness and your other brothers. So don't neglect him, don't blunt his love or lose the advantage of his favour by seeming cold or careless of what he wants, because he is gracious if he's treated with respect. He has a tear for pity and a hand as open as daylight for tender charity. And yet, when he's angry, he's flint, as changeable as winter and as sudden as the frozen gusts of early morning. So his temper must be carefully watched. Scold him for his faults, and do it respectfully, when you see he's in a merry mood; but when he's moody, give him line and room, like a fisherman, until his passions, like a stranded whale, wear themselves out with struggling. Learn this, Thomas, and you'll be a shelter to your friends, a gold hoop to bind your brothers together, so that the united vessel of their blood, mixed with the poison of evil suggestion, as the times are bound to pour it in, will never leak, even if it works as strongly as wolfsbane or gunpowder.
I shall observe him with all care and love.
I'll attend to him with all care and love.
Why art thou not at Windsor with him, Thomas?
Why aren't you with him at Windsor, Thomas?
He is not there to-day; he dines in London.
He's not there today. He's having dinner in London.
And how accompanied? canst thou tell that?
And who with? Can you tell me that?
With Poins, and other his continual followers.
With Poins and his other constant followers.

Most subject is the fattest soil to weeds; / And he, the noble image of my youth, / Is overspread with them: therefore my grief / Stretches itself beyond the hour of death: / The blood weeps from my heart when I do shape / In forms imaginary the unguided days / And rotten times that you shall look upon / When I am sleeping with my ancestors. / For when his headstrong riot hath no curb, / When rage and hot blood are his counsellors, / When means and lavish manners meet together, / O, with what wings shall his affections fly / Towards fronting peril and opposed decay!

The richest soil is most prone to weeds, and he, the noble image of my youth, is overgrown with them. So my grief stretches beyond the hour of my death. My heart weeps blood when I imagine the lawless days and rotten times you'll see when I'm asleep with my ancestors. Because when his headstrong rioting has no curb, when rage and hot blood are his advisers, when money and extravagant habits come together, oh, with what wings his desires will fly towards danger ahead and ruin in his path!

My gracious lord, you look beyond him quite: / The prince but studies his companions / Like a strange tongue, wherein, to gain the language, / 'Tis needful that the most immodest word / Be look'd upon and learn'd; which once attain'd, / Your highness knows, comes to no further use / But to be known and hated. So, like gross terms, / The prince will in the perfectness of time / Cast off his followers; and their memory / Shall as a pattern or a measure live, / By which his grace must mete the lives of other, / Turning past evils to advantages.

My gracious lord, you misjudge him completely. The Prince is only studying his companions like a foreign language, in which, to master it, it's necessary to look at and learn the most indecent words; and once he's mastered them, as your Highness knows, they're of no further use except to be recognised and hated. So, like coarse words, the Prince will in the fullness of time cast off his followers, and the memory of them will live on as a pattern or a measure by which his grace will judge other men's lives, turning past evils into advantages.
'Tis seldom when the bee doth leave her comb / In the dead carrion.
The bee rarely leaves her honeycomb in a dead carcass.

Health to my sovereign, and new happiness / Added to that that I am to deliver! / Prince John your son doth kiss your grace's hand: / Mowbray, the Bishop Scroop, Hastings and all / Are brought to the correction of your law; / There is not now a rebel's sword unsheathed, / But Peace puts forth her olive every where. / The manner how this action hath been borne / Here at more leisure may your highness read, / With every course in his particular.

Health to my sovereign, and new happiness on top of what I have to tell you! Prince John your son kisses your grace's hand. Mowbray, Bishop Scroop, Hastings and all of them have been brought to the punishment of your law. There isn't a rebel's sword drawn now; Peace holds out her olive branch everywhere. Your Highness can read here at greater leisure how this action was carried out, with every stage in detail.
O Westmoreland, thou art a summer bird, / Which ever in the haunch of winter sings / The lifting up of day.
Oh Westmoreland, you're a summer bird, who always sings of the dawn at the tail end of winter.

From enemies heaven keep your majesty; / And, when they stand against you, may they fall / As those that I am come to tell you of! / The Earl Northumberland and the Lord Bardolph, / With a great power of English and of Scots, / Are by the sheriff of Yorkshire overthrown: / The manner and true order of the fight / This packet, please it you, contains at large.

May heaven keep your Majesty from enemies, and when they stand against you, may they fall like the ones I've come to tell you about! The Earl of Northumberland and Lord Bardolph, with a great army of English and Scots, have been overthrown by the sheriff of Yorkshire. This packet, if you please, contains the full details of how the fight went.

And wherefore should these good news make me sick? / Will Fortune never come with both hands full, / But write her fair words still in foulest letters? / She either gives a stomach and no food; / Such are the poor, in health; or else a feast / And takes away the stomach; such are the rich, / That have abundance and enjoy it not. / I should rejoice now at this happy news; / And now my sight fails, and my brain is giddy: / O me! come near me; now I am much ill.

And why should this good news make me ill? Will Fortune never come with both hands full, but always write her fair words in the ugliest letters? She either gives an appetite and no food, as with the poor who are healthy, or else a feast and takes away the appetite, as with the rich, who have plenty and can't enjoy it. I should be rejoicing now at this happy news, and now my sight is failing and my head is spinning. Oh me! Come close to me. I'm very ill now.
My sovereign lord, cheer up yourself, look up.
My sovereign lord, cheer up, look up.
Be patient, princes; you do know, these fits / Are with his highness very ordinary. / Stand from him, give him air; he'll straight be well.
Be calm, princes. You know these fits are very common with his Highness. Stand back from him, give him air; he'll be well soon.
No, no, he cannot long hold out these pangs: / The incessant care and labour of his mind / Hath wrought the mure that should confine it in / So thin that life looks through and will break out.
No, no, he can't endure these pains much longer. The constant worry and work of his mind have worn the wall that should contain it so thin that life shows through and will break out.
The people fear me; for they do observe / Unfather'd heirs and loathly births of nature: / The seasons change their manners, as the year / Had found some months asleep, and leap'd them over.

The people frighten me, because they've noticed children born without fathers and monstrous births. The seasons have changed their habits, as if the year had found some months asleep and jumped over them.
The river hath thrice flow'd, no ebb between; / And the old folk, time's doting chronicles, / Say it did so a little time before / That our great-grandsire, Edward, sick'd and died.
The river has flooded three times with no ebb in between, and the old people, time's rambling history books, say it did the same shortly before our great-grandfather Edward fell ill and died.
Speak lower, princes, for the king recovers.
Speak more quietly, princes, because the King is recovering.
This apoplexy will certain be his end.
This apoplexy will certainly be the end of him.
I pray you, take me up, and bear me hence / Into some other chamber: softly, pray.
Please lift me up and carry me away into another room. Gently, please.
Let there be no noise made, my gentle friends; / Unless some dull and favourable hand / Will whisper music to my weary spirit.
Let there be no noise, my gentle friends, unless some kind hand will softly play music to my weary spirit.
Call for the music in the other room.
Call for the musicians in the other room.
Set me the crown upon my pillow here.
Put the crown on my pillow here.
His eye is hollow, and he changes much.
His eyes are sunken, and he's changing a great deal.
Who saw the Duke of Clarence?
Has anyone seen the Duke of Clarence?
I am here, brother, full of heaviness.
I'm here, brother, full of sadness.
How now! rain within doors, and none abroad! / How doth the king?
What's this? Rain indoors and none outside! How is the King?
Heard he the good news yet? Tell it him.
Has he heard the good news yet? Tell him.
He alt'red much upon the hearing it.
He changed a great deal when he heard it.
If he be sick with joy, he'll recover without physic.
If he's sick with joy, he'll recover without medicine.
Not so much noise, my lords: sweet prince, speak low; / The king your father is disposed to sleep.
Not so much noise, my lords. Sweet prince, speak quietly. The King your father wants to sleep.
Let us withdraw into the other room.
Let's withdraw into the other room.
Will't please your grace to go along with us?
Will your grace come with us?
No; I will sit and watch here by the king.
No, I'll sit here and watch beside the King.

Why doth the crown lie there upon his pillow, / Being so troublesome a bedfellow? / O polish'd perturbation! golden care! / That keep'st the ports of slumber open wide / To many a watchful night! sleep with it now! / Yet not so sound and half so deeply sweet / As he whose brow with homely biggen bound / Snores out the watch of night. O majesty! / When thou dost pinch thy bearer, thou dost sit / Like a rich armour worn in heat of day, / That scalds with safety. By his gates of breath / There lies a downy feather which stirs not: / Did he suspire, that light and weightless down / Perforce must move. My gracious lord! my father! / This sleep is sound indeed; this is a sleep / That from this golden rigol hath divorced / So many English kings. Thy due from me / Is tears and heavy sorrows of the blood, / Which nature, love, and filial tenderness, / Shall, O dear father, pay thee plenteously: / My due from thee is this imperial crown, / Which, as immediate from thy place and blood, / Derives itself to me. Lo, here it sits, / Which God shall guard: and put the world's whole strength / Into one giant arm, it shall not force / This lineal honour from me: this from thee / Will I to mine leave, as 'tis left to me.

Why does the crown lie there on his pillow, when it's such a troublesome bedfellow? Oh, polished trouble! Golden worry! You keep the gates of sleep wide open through many wakeful nights. Sleep with it now! And yet not so soundly, and not half so sweetly, as the man who snores the night away with a plain nightcap tied round his head. Oh majesty! When you pinch the one who wears you, you sit like rich armour worn in the heat of the day, which scalds while it protects. At the door of his breath lies a downy feather that doesn't move. If he breathed, that light, weightless down would have to stir. My gracious lord! My father! This sleep is sound indeed. This is the sleep that has divorced so many English kings from this golden circle. What I owe you is tears and the heavy grief of my blood, which nature, love and a son's tenderness will pay you in full, oh dear father. What you owe me is this imperial crown, which comes down to me as next in your place and blood. Look, here it sits (he puts it on), and God will guard it. Even if the whole world's strength were put into one giant arm, it shall not wrench this inherited honour from me. As it's left to me by you, so I'll leave it to my heir.
What would your majesty? How fares your grace?
What does your Majesty want? How is your grace?
Why did you leave me here alone, my lords?
Why did you leave me alone here, my lords?
We left the prince my brother here, my liege, / Who undertook to sit and watch by you.
We left the Prince my brother here, my lord, who said he'd sit and watch beside you.
The Prince of Wales! Where is he? let me see him: / He is not here.
The Prince of Wales! Where is he? Let me see him. He isn't here.
This door is open; he is gone this way.
This door is open. He's gone this way.
He came not through the chamber where we stay'd.
He didn't come through the room where we were.
Where is the crown? who took it from my pillow?
Where is the crown? Who took it from my pillow?
When we withdrew, my liege, we left it here.
When we went out, my lord, we left it here.
The prince hath ta'en it hence: go, seek him out. / Is he so hasty that he doth suppose / My sleep my death? / Find him, my lord of Warwick; chide him hither.
The Prince has taken it away. Go and find him. Is he so hasty that he takes my sleep for my death? Find him, my lord of Warwick, and scold him back here.

This part of his conjoins with my disease, / And helps to end me. See, sons, what things you are! / How quickly nature falls into revolt / When gold becomes her object! / For this the foolish over-careful fathers / Have broke their sleep with thoughts, their brains with care, / Their bones with industry; / For this they have engross'd and piled up / The canker'd heaps of strange-achieved gold; / For this they have been thoughtful to invest / Their sons with arts and martial exercises; / When, like the bee, tolling from every flower / The virtuous sweets, / Our thighs pack'd with wax, our mouths with honey, / We bring it to the hive, and, like the bees, / Are murdered for our pains. This bitter taste / Yields his engrossments to the ending father.

This action of his joins forces with my illness and helps finish me off. See, sons, what you are like! How quickly nature rebels when gold becomes its goal! This is what foolish, over-anxious fathers have broken their sleep with worrying for, broken their brains with care and their bones with work. For this they have hoarded and piled up rusting heaps of gold got by strange means; for this they have taken care to give their sons learning and military training. Like the bee, we collect sweetness from every flower, our thighs packed with wax and our mouths with honey; we bring it to the hive, and, like the bees, we are murdered for our trouble. This is the bitter taste that his hoarding leaves the dying father.
Now where is he that will not stay so long / Till his friend sickness hath determin'd me?
Now where is he who can't wait until his friend sickness has finished me off?

My lord, I found the prince in the next room, / Washing with kindly tears his gentle cheeks, / With such a deep demeanour in great sorrow / That tyranny, which never quaff'd but blood, / Would, by beholding him, have wash'd his knife / With gentle eye-drops. He is coming hither.

My lord, I found the Prince in the next room, washing his gentle cheeks with loving tears, looking so deeply sorrowful that tyranny, which has never drunk anything but blood, would have washed its knife with gentle tears at the sight of him. He's coming here.
But wherefore did he take away the crown?
But why did he take away the crown?
Lo, where he comes. Come hither to me, Harry. / Depart the chamber, leave us here alone.
Look, here he comes. Come here to me, Harry. Leave the room; leave us alone here.
I never thought to hear you speak again.
I never thought I'd hear you speak again.

Thy wish was father, Harry, to that thought: / I stay too long by thee, I weary thee. / Dost thou so hunger for mine empty chair / That thou wilt needs invest thee with my honours / Before thy hour be ripe? O foolish youth! / Thou seek'st the greatness that will overwhelm thee. / Stay but a little; for my cloud of dignity / Is held from falling with so weak a wind / That it will quickly drop: my day is dim. / Thou hast stolen that which after some few hours / Were thine without offence; and at my death / Thou hast seal'd up my expectation: / Thy life did manifest thou lovedst me not, / And thou wilt have me die assured of it. / Thou hidest a thousand daggers in thy thoughts / Which thou hast whetted on thy stony heart, / To stab at half an hour of my life. / What! canst thou not forbear me half an hour? / Then get thee gone and dig my grave thyself, / And bid the merry bells ring to thine ear / That thou art crowned, not that I am dead. / Let all the tears that should bedew my hearse / Be drops of balm to sanctify thy head: / Only compound me with forgotten dust; / Give that which gave thee life unto the worms. / Pluck down my officers, break my decrees; / For now a time is come to mock at form: / Harry the Fifth is crown'd: up, vanity! / Down, royal state! all you sage counsellors, hence! / And to the English court assemble now, / From every region, apes of idleness! / Now, neighbour confines, purge you of your scum: / Have you a ruffian that will swear, drink, dance, / Revel the night, rob, murder, and commit / The oldest sins the newest kind of ways? / Be happy, he will trouble you no more; / England shall double gild his treble guilt, / England shall give him office, honour, might; / For the fifth Harry from curb'd license plucks / The muzzle of restraint, and the wild dog / Shall flesh his tooth on every innocent. / O my poor kingdom, sick with civil blows! / When that my care could not withhold thy riots, / What wilt thou do when riot is thy care? / O, thou wilt be a wilderness again, / Peopled with wolves, thy old inhabitants!

Your wish was father to that thought, Harry. I stay alive too long for you; I tire you. Are you so hungry for my empty throne that you have to dress yourself in my honours before your time is ripe? Oh, foolish young man! You're seeking the greatness that will overwhelm you. Just wait a little, because my cloud of majesty is held up by so weak a wind that it will soon fall. My day is growing dark. You've stolen what in a few hours would have been yours without wrongdoing, and at my death you've confirmed what I expected of you. Your life showed you didn't love me, and you want me to die sure of it. You're hiding a thousand daggers in your thoughts, sharpened on your stony heart, to stab at half an hour of my life. What! Can't you put up with me for half an hour? Then go and dig my grave yourself, and tell the merry bells to ring in your ear that you're crowned, not that I'm dead. Let all the tears that should fall on my coffin be drops of holy oil to anoint your head. Just mix me with forgotten dust; give the one who gave you life to the worms. Pull down my officials, break my laws, for now the time has come to mock at order. Harry the Fifth is crowned: up with vanity! Down with royal dignity! All you wise counsellors, away! And now gather at the English court from every region, you apes of idleness! Now, neighbouring countries, clear out your scum. Have you got a ruffian who will swear, drink, dance, revel all night, rob, murder and commit the oldest sins in the newest ways? Be happy: he won't trouble you any more. England will double-gild his triple guilt; England will give him office, honour and power. For the fifth Harry takes the muzzle of restraint off licence, and the wild dog will sink his teeth into every innocent. Oh, my poor kingdom, sick with the blows of civil war! When my care could not keep your disorders down, what will you do when disorder is your king's only care? Oh, you'll be a wilderness again, peopled with wolves, your old inhabitants!

O, pardon me, my liege! but for my tears, / The moist impediments unto my speech, / I had forestall'd this dear and deep rebuke / Ere you with grief had spoke and I had heard / The course of it so far. There is your crown: / And He that wears the crown immortally / Long guard it yours! If I affect it more / Than as your honour and as your renown, / Let me no more from this obedience rise, / Which my most inward true and duteous spirit / Teacheth, this prostrate and exterior bending. / God witness with me, when I here came in, / And found no course of breath within your majesty, / How cold it struck my heart! If I do feign, / O, let me in my present wildness die / And never live to show the incredulous world / The noble change that I have purposed! / Coming to look on you, thinking you dead, / And dead almost, my liege, to think you were, / I spake unto this crown as having sense, / And thus upbraided it: "The care on thee depending / Hath fed upon the body of my father; / Therefore, thou best of gold art worst of gold: / Other, less fine in carat, is more precious, / Preserving life in medicine potable; / But thou, most fine, most honour'd, most renown'd, / Hast eat thy bearer up." Thus, my most royal liege, / Accusing it, I put it on my head, / To try with it, as with an enemy / That had before my face murder'd my father, / The quarrel of a true inheritor. / But if it did infect my blood with joy, / Or swell my thoughts to any strain of pride; / If any rebel or vain spirit of mine / Did with the least affection of a welcome / Give entertainment to the might of it, / Let God for ever keep it from my head / And make me as the poorest vassal is / That doth with awe and terror kneel to it!

Oh, forgive me, my lord! If it weren't for my tears, the wet obstacles to my speech, I'd have stopped this heartfelt, deep rebuke before you'd spoken in grief and I'd heard so much of it. There's your crown, and may He who wears the crown for ever keep it yours for a long time! If I want it for any other reason than as your honour and your fame, let me never rise again from this kneeling, which my deepest, truest and most dutiful spirit teaches this outward, bowing body. God is my witness how coldly it struck my heart when I came in here and found no breath in your Majesty! If I'm pretending, oh, let me die in my present wildness and never live to show the disbelieving world the noble change I've decided on! Coming to look at you, thinking you were dead, and almost dead myself, my lord, to think you were, I spoke to this crown as if it could understand, and scolded it like this: "The care that comes with you has eaten up my father's body. So you, the best of gold, are the worst of gold. Other gold, less pure, is more precious, because it preserves life as a medicine you can drink. But you, most pure, most honoured, most famous, have eaten up the man who wore you." And so, my most royal lord, accusing it, I put it on my head to fight it, as I would an enemy who had murdered my father in front of me, as a true heir should. But if it filled my blood with joy or swelled my thoughts with any trace of pride, if any rebellious or vain part of me welcomed its power even slightly, let God keep it from my head for ever and make me like the poorest servant who kneels to it in awe and terror!

O my son, / God put it in thy mind to take it hence, / That thou mightst win the more thy father's love, / Pleading so wisely in excuse of it! / Come hither, Harry, sit thou by my bed; / And hear, I think, the very latest counsel / That ever I shall breathe. God knows, my son, / By what by-paths and indirect crook'd ways / I met this crown; and I myself know well / How troublesome it sat upon my head. / To thee it shall descend with better quiet, / Better opinion, better confirmation; / For all the soil of the achievement goes / With me into the earth. It seem'd in me / But as an honour snatch'd with boisterous hand, / And I had many living to upbraid / My gain of it by their assistances; / Which daily grew to quarrel and to bloodshed, / Wounding supposed peace: all these bold fears / Thou see'st with peril I have answered; / For all my reign hath been but as a scene / Acting that argument: and now my death / Changes the mode; for what in me was purchased, / Falls upon thee in a more fairer sort; / So thou the garland wear'st successively. / Yet, though thou stand'st more sure than I could do, / Thou art not firm enough, since griefs are green; / And all my friends, which thou must make thy friends, / Have but their stings and teeth newly ta'en out; / By whose fell working I was first advanced / And by whose power I well might lodge a fear / To be again displaced: which to avoid, / I cut them off; and had a purpose now / To lead out many to the Holy Land, / Lest rest and lying still might make them look / Too near unto my state. Therefore, my Harry, / Be it thy course to busy giddy minds / With foreign quarrels; that action, hence borne out, / May waste the memory of the former days. / More would I, but my lungs are wasted so / That strength of speech is utterly denied me. / How I came by the crown, O God, forgive; / And grant it may with thee in true peace live!

Oh, my son, God put it in your mind to take it away, so that you could win your father's love all the more by pleading so wisely in your own defence! Come here, Harry, sit by my bed and hear what I think is the very last advice I'll ever breathe. God knows, my son, by what side paths and indirect, crooked ways I came by this crown, and I myself know well how uneasily it sat on my head. It will come to you more quietly, with better reputation and firmer support, because all the dirt of getting it goes with me into the earth. In me it seemed only an honour snatched with a violent hand, and there were many alive to reproach me for having got it with their help, which every day grew into quarrels and bloodshed, wounding what was meant to be peace. You see how I have met all these bold dangers at great risk, because my whole reign has been like a play acting out that story. Now my death changes the situation, because what I got by my own action comes to you in a fairer way, so you wear the crown by right of succession. Still, though you stand more securely than I could, you're not secure enough while grievances are fresh. All my allies, whom you must make your allies, have only just had their stings and teeth pulled out. Their fierce efforts first raised me up, and I had good reason to fear their power might throw me down again. To avoid that, I cut them down, and I was planning now to lead many of them to the Holy Land, in case rest and idleness made them look too closely at my position. So, my Harry, make it your policy to keep restless minds busy with foreign wars, so that action abroad may wipe out the memory of former days. I would say more, but my lungs are so worn out that I have no strength left to speak. How I came by the crown, oh God, forgive; and grant that it may live in true peace with you!

My gracious liege, / You won it, wore it, kept it, gave it me; / Then plain and right must my possession be: / Which I with more than with a common pain / 'Gainst all the world will rightfully maintain.
My gracious lord, you won it, wore it, kept it and gave it to me. Then my possession must be clear and right, and I will defend it rightfully against the whole world with more than common effort.
Look, look, here comes my John of Lancaster.
Look, look, here comes my John of Lancaster.
Health, peace, and happiness to my royal father!
Health, peace and happiness to my royal father!

Thou bring'st me happiness and peace, son John; / But health, alack, with youthful wings is flown / From this bare wither'd trunk: upon thy sight / My worldly business makes a period. / Where is my Lord of Warwick?

You bring me happiness and peace, son John, but health, alas, has flown on young wings from this bare, withered trunk. Now that I've seen you, my worldly business comes to an end. Where is my Lord of Warwick?
Doth any name particular belong / Unto the lodging where I first did swoon?
Does the room where I first fainted have any particular name?
It's called Jerusalem, my noble lord.

Laud be to God! even there my life must end. / It hath been prophesied to me many years, / I should not die but in Jerusalem; / Which vainly I supposed the Holy Land: / But bear me to that chamber; there I'll lie; / In that Jerusalem shall Harry die.

Praise be to God! That's where my life must end. It was prophesied to me many years ago that I would die only in Jerusalem, which I foolishly thought meant the Holy Land. But carry me to that room; I'll lie there. In that Jerusalem Harry will die.
By cock and pie, sir, you shall not away to-night. / What, Davy, I say!
By cock and pie, sir, you won't go away tonight. Hey, Davy, I say!
You must excuse me, Master Robert Shallow.
You must excuse me, Master Robert Shallow.
I will not excuse you; you shall not be excused; excuses / shall not be admitted; there is no excuse shall serve; you shall / not be excused. Why, Davy!
I won't excuse you. You won't be excused. Excuses won't be allowed. No excuse will do. You won't be excused. Hey, Davy!
Davy, Davy, Davy, Davy, let me see, Davy; let me see, / Davy; let me see: yea, marry, William cook, bid him come hither. / Sir John, you shall not be excused.
Davy, Davy, Davy, Davy, let me see, Davy; let me see, Davy; let me see. Yes, of course: William the cook, tell him to come here. Sir John, you won't be excused.
Marry, sir, thus; those precepts cannot be served; and, / again, sir, shall we sow the headland with wheat?
Well, sir, it's like this: those legal summonses can't be delivered. And again, sir, shall we sow the edge of the field with wheat?
With red wheat, Davy. But for William cook: are there no / young pigeons?
With red wheat, Davy. But as for William the cook: are there any young pigeons?
Yes, sir. Here is now the smith's note for shoeing and / plough-irons.
Yes, sir. Here's the blacksmith's bill for shoeing the horses and for plough blades.
Let it be cast and paid. Sir John, you shall not be excused.
Have it added up and paid. Sir John, you won't be excused.
Now, sir, a new link to the bucket must needs be had: and, sir, do / you mean to stop any of William's wages, about the sack he lost the / other day at Hinckley fair?
Now, sir, we have to have a new link for the well-bucket chain. And, sir, do you mean to stop any of William's wages for the sack he lost the other day at Hinckley fair?
A' shall answer it. Some pigeons, Davy, a couple of short-legg'd / hens, a joint of mutton, and any pretty little tiny kickshaws, / tell William cook.
He'll pay for it. Some pigeons, Davy, a couple of short-legged hens, a joint of mutton, and any pretty little tiny fancy dishes; tell William the cook.
Doth the man of war stay all night, sir?
Is the soldier staying all night, sir?
Yea, Davy. I will use him well: a friend i' the court is better / than a penny in purse. Use his men well, Davy; for they are / arrant knaves, and will backbite.
Yes, Davy. I'll treat him well. A friend at court is better than a penny in your purse. Treat his men well, Davy, because they're out-and-out rogues and will speak ill of us behind our backs.
No worse than they are backbitten, sir; for they have marvellous / foul linen.
No worse than they're bitten in the back themselves, sir, because their shirts are wonderfully lousy.
Well conceited, Davy: about thy business, Davy.
Very witty, Davy. Get on with your work, Davy.
I beseech you, sir, to countenance William Visor of Woncot / against Clement Perkes of the hill.
Please, sir, support William Visor of Woncot in his case against Clement Perkes of the hill.
There is many complaints, Davy, against that Visor: that / Visor is an arrant knave, on my knowledge.
There are a lot of complaints against that Visor, Davy. That Visor is an out-and-out rogue, to my knowledge.

I grant your worship that he is a knave, sir; but yet, God forbid, / sir, but a knave should have some countenance at his friend's request. / An honest man, sir, is able to speak for himself, when a knave is not. / I have served your worship truly, sir, this eight years; and if I cannot / once or twice in a quarter bear out a knave against an honest man, I / have but a very little credit with your worship. / The knave is mine honest friend, sir; therefore, I beseech your worship, / let him be countenanced.

I grant your worship that he's a rogue, sir. But still, God forbid, sir, that a rogue shouldn't have a little support when his friend asks for it. An honest man, sir, can speak for himself; a rogue can't. I've served your worship faithfully for eight years, sir, and if I can't once or twice a quarter back a rogue against an honest man, I have very little credit with your worship. The rogue is my honest friend, sir, so I beg your worship, let him be supported.
Go to; I say he shall have no wrong. Look about, Davy.
Go on, I tell you he'll come to no harm. See to things, Davy.
Where are you, Sir John? Come, come, come, off with your boots. / Give me your hand, Master Bardolph.
Where are you, Sir John? Come, come, come, off with your boots. Give me your hand, Master Bardolph.
I am glad to see your worship.
I'm glad to see your worship.
I thank thee with all my heart, kind Master Bardolph: and / welcome, my tall fellow [to the Page] Come, Sir John.
I thank you with all my heart, kind Master Bardolph. And welcome, my fine fellow (to the Page). Come, Sir John.
I'll follow you, good Master Robert Shallow.
I'll follow you, good Master Robert Shallow.

If I were sawed into quantities, I should make four dozen of such / bearded hermits' staves as Master Shallow. It is a wonderful thing to / see the semblable coherence of his men's spirits and his: they, by / observing of him, do bear themselves like foolish justices: he, by / conversing with them, is turned into a justice-like serving-man: / their spirits are so married in conjunction with the participation of / society that they flock together in consent, like so many wild-geese. / If I had a suit to Master Shallow, I would humour his men with the / imputation of being near their master: if to his men, I would curry / with Master Shallow that no man could better command his servants. / It is certain that either wise bearing or ignorant carriage is / caught, as men take diseases, one of another: therefore let men take / heed of their company. I will devise matter enough out of this Shallow / to keep Prince Harry in continual laughter the wearing out of six / fashions, which is four terms, or two actions; and a' shall laugh / without intervallums. / O, it is much that a lie with a slight oath and a jest with a sad brow / will do with a fellow that never had the ache in his shoulders! / O, you shall see him laugh till his face be like a wet cloak ill laid up!

If I were sawn into pieces, I'd make four dozen bearded hermits' staffs like Master Shallow. It's a wonderful thing to see how his men's spirits match his. By watching him, they behave like foolish justices; by talking with them, he has turned into a justice-like servant. Their spirits are so married together by keeping company that they flock together in agreement like a lot of wild geese. If I wanted a favour from Master Shallow, I'd flatter his men by suggesting they were close to their master; if I wanted one from his men, I'd flatter Master Shallow that no man could command his servants better. It's certain that wise behaviour or ignorant manners are caught from one another, the way people catch diseases, so men should be careful about the company they keep. I'll make up enough material out of this Shallow to keep Prince Harry laughing for as long as it takes to wear out six fashions, which is four law terms, or two lawsuits, and he'll laugh without a break. Oh, it's amazing what a lie with a little oath, and a joke told with a straight face, will do to a young fellow who's never had aching shoulders! Oh, you'll see him laugh till his face is like a wet cloak badly folded!
I come, Master Shallow; I come, Master Shallow.
I'm coming, Master Shallow; I'm coming, Master Shallow.
How now, my lord chief-justice! whither away?
Hello, my Lord Chief Justice! Where are you going?
Exceeding well; his cares are now all ended.
Extremely well. His worries are all over now.
He's walk'd the way of nature; / And to our purposes he lives no more.
He's gone the way of nature, and as far as we're concerned he lives no longer.
I would his Majesty had call'd me with him: / The service that I truly did his life / Hath left me open to all injuries.
I wish his Majesty had called me with him. The loyal service I did him while he lived has left me exposed to every kind of injury.
Indeed I think the young king loves you not.
Indeed, I think the young King doesn't love you.
I know he doth not, and do arm myself / To welcome the condition of the time, / Which cannot look more hideously upon me / Than I have drawn it in my fantasy.
I know he doesn't, and I'm preparing myself to meet the way things are now, which can't look more hideous to me than I've pictured it in my imagination.

Here comes the heavy issue of dead Harry: / O that the living Harry had the temper / Of him, the worst of these three gentlemen! / How many nobles then should hold their places, / That must strike sail to spirits of vile sort!

Here come the sad sons of the dead Harry. Oh, if only the living Harry had the temperament of the worst of these three gentlemen! How many nobles would then keep their positions who will have to lower their sails to men of low character!
O God, I fear all will be overturn'd!
Oh God, I'm afraid everything will be overturned!
Good morrow, cousin Warwick, good morrow.
Good morning, cousin Warwick, good morning.
We meet like men that had forgot to speak.
We meet like men who've forgotten how to speak.
We do remember; but our argument / Is all too heavy to admit much talk.
We remember how, but our subject is far too heavy to allow much talk.
Well, peace be with him that hath made us heavy!
Well, peace be with him who has made us sad!
Peace be with us, lest we be heavier!
Peace be with us, in case we're made sadder!
O, good my lord, you have lost a friend indeed; / And I dare swear you borrow not that face / Of seeming sorrow, it is sure your own.
Oh, my good lord, you've truly lost a friend, and I'd swear that face of sorrow isn't borrowed; it's surely your own.
Though no man be assured what grace to find, / You stand in coldest expectation: / I am the sorrier; would 'twere otherwise.
Although no one can be sure what favour he'll find, you have the coldest prospects. I'm all the sorrier; I wish it were otherwise.
Well, you must now speak Sir John Falstaff fair; / Which swims against your stream of quality.
Well, you'll have to be polite to Sir John Falstaff now, which goes against the grain of your character.

Sweet Princes, what I did, I did in honour, / Led by the impartial conduct of my soul; / And never shall you see that I will beg / A ragged and forestall'd remission. / If truth and upright innocency fail me, / I'll to the king my master that is dead, / And tell him who hath sent me after him.

Sweet princes, what I did, I did honourably, guided by the impartial direction of my soul, and you will never see me beg for a shabby pardon that's already been refused. If truth and upright innocence fail me, I'll go to my master the King who is dead and tell him who sent me after him.
Good morrow; and God save your majesty!
Good morning, and God save your Majesty!

This new and gorgeous garment, majesty, / Sits not so easy on me as you think. / Brothers, you mix your sadness with some fear: / This is the English, not the Turkish court; / Not Amurath an Amurath succeeds, / But Harry Harry.
