Yet be sad, good brothers, / For, by my faith, it very well becomes you: / Sorrow so royally in you appears / That I will deeply put the fashion on / And wear it in my heart: why then, be sad; / But entertain no more of it, good brothers, / Than a joint burden laid upon us all. / For me, by heaven, I bid you be assured, / I'll be your father and your brother too; / Let me but bear your love, I'll bear your cares: / Yet weep that Harry's dead, and so will I; / But Harry lives, that shall convert those tears / By number into hours of happiness.

This new and gorgeous garment, majesty, doesn't sit as easily on me as you think. Brothers, you mix your sadness with some fear. This is the English court, not the Turkish one, where one Sultan Amurath succeeds another and kills his brothers; it's Harry succeeding Harry. But be sad, good brothers, because honestly it suits you very well. Sorrow looks so royal on you that I will put the fashion on deeply and wear it in my heart. So be sad; but don't take on more of it, good brothers, than a burden we all share. As for me, by heaven, I want you to be sure that I'll be your father and your brother too. Just let me have your love and I'll carry your cares. Weep that Harry's dead, and so will I; but there's a Harry alive who will turn each of those tears into an hour of happiness.
We hope no otherwise from your majesty.
We expect nothing else from your Majesty.
You all look strangely on me: and you most; / You are, I think, assured I love you not.
You all look at me strangely, and you most of all. I think you're sure I don't love you.
I am assured, if I be measured rightly, / Your majesty hath no just cause to hate me.
I'm sure that, if I'm judged fairly, your Majesty has no good reason to hate me.

No! / How might a prince of my great hopes forget / So great indignities you laid upon me? / What! rate, rebuke, and roughly send to prison / The immediate heir of England! Was this easy? / May this be wash'd in Lethe, and forgotten?

No! How could a prince with my great prospects forget the great humiliations you heaped on me? What! Scold, rebuke and roughly send to prison the immediate heir to England! Was that a small thing? Can this be washed in the river of forgetfulness and forgotten?

I then did use the person of your father; / The image of his power lay then in me; / And, in the administration of his law, / Whiles I was busy for the commonwealth, / Your highness pleased to forget my place, / The majesty and power of law and justice, / The image of the king whom I presented, / And struck me in my very seat of judgement; / Whereon, as an offender to your father, / I gave bold way to my authority / And did commit you. If the deed were ill, / Be you contented, wearing now the garland, / To have a son set your decrees at nought, / To pluck down justice from your awful bench, / To trip the course of law and blunt the sword / That guards the peace and safety of your person; / Nay, more, to spurn at your most royal image, / And mock your workings in a second body. / Question your royal thoughts, make the case yours; / Be now the father and propose a son, / Hear your own dignity so much profaned, / See your most dreadful laws so loosely slighted, / Behold yourself so by a son disdain'd; / And then imagine me taking your part / And in your power soft silencing your son: / After this cold considerance, sentence me; / And, as you are a king, speak in your state / What I have done that misbecame my place, / My person, or my liege's sovereignty.

I was then acting as your father's representative; the image of his power was in me. And while I was administering his law, busy for the good of the state, your Highness chose to forget my position, the majesty and power of law and justice, the image of the King whom I represented, and struck me in my very seat of judgement. So, as an offender against your father, I boldly used my authority and sent you to prison. If that was wrong, then be content, now that you wear the crown, to have a son of your own ignore your laws, pull justice down from your awe-inspiring bench, trip up the course of law and blunt the sword that guards the peace and safety of your person — no, more, to kick at your royal image and mock your actions in the person of your deputy. Ask your royal thoughts; make the case your own. Be the father now and imagine a son; hear your own dignity so profaned, see your most dreaded laws so carelessly ignored, see yourself so scorned by a son. And then imagine me taking your side and, using your power, gently silencing your son. After this cool consideration, sentence me, and, as you are a king, say officially what I did that was unfitting for my office, my person or my lord's sovereignty.

You are right, justice, and you weigh this well; / Therefore still bear the balance and the sword: / And I do wish your honours may increase, / Till you do live to see a son of mine / Offend you and obey you, as I did. / So shall I live to speak my father's words: / "Happy am I, that have a man so bold, / That dares do justice on my proper son; / And not less happy, having such a son, / That would deliver up his greatness so / Into the hands of justice." You did commit me: / For which I do commit into your hand / The unstained sword that you have used to bear; / With this remembrance, that you use the same / With the like bold, just and impartial spirit / As you have done 'gainst me. There is my hand. / You shall be as a father to my youth: / My voice shall sound as you do prompt mine ear, / And I will stoop and humble my intents / To your well-practised wise directions. / And, princes all, believe me, I beseech you; / My father is gone wild into his grave, / For in his tomb lie my affections; / And with his spirit sadly I survive, / To mock the expectation of the world, / To frustrate prophecies and to raze out / Rotten opinion, who hath writ me down / After my seeming. The tide of blood in me / Hath proudly flow'd in vanity till now: / Now doth it turn and ebb back to the sea, / Where it shall mingle with the state of floods, / And flow henceforth in formal majesty. / Now call we our high court of parliament: / And let us choose such limbs of noble counsel, / That the great body of our state may go / In equal rank with the best govern'd nation; / That war, or peace, or both at once, may be / As things acquainted and familiar to us; / In which you, father, shall have foremost hand. / Our coronation done, we will accite, / As I before remember'd, all our state: / And, God consigning to my good intents, / No prince nor peer shall have just cause to say, / God shorten Harry's happy life one day!

You're right, Justice, and you weigh this up well. So keep holding the scales and the sword. And I hope your honours will grow until you live to see a son of mine offend you and obey you as I did. Then I'll live to speak my father's words: "I'm lucky to have a man so bold that he dares to do justice on my own son, and no less lucky to have a son who would hand his greatness over to the hands of justice like that." You sent me to prison, and for that I now put into your hand the unstained sword you have carried, with this reminder: that you use it with the same bold, just and impartial spirit as you have against me. There's my hand. You'll be like a father to my youth. My voice will say what you prompt in my ear, and I will bend and humble my intentions to your experienced, wise guidance. And, princes all, believe me, I beg you. My father has gone wild into his grave, because my wild impulses lie buried in his tomb, and I survive with his serious spirit to mock the world's expectations, to defeat the prophecies and to wipe out the rotten opinion that has judged me by how I seemed. The tide of blood in me has flowed proudly in vanity until now; now it turns and ebbs back to the sea, where it will mix with the majesty of the ocean and flow from now on in dignified majesty. Now we'll summon our high court of parliament, and let's choose such limbs of noble counsel that the great body of our state may rank equally with the best-governed nation, so that war, or peace, or both at once, may be familiar things to us. In this you, father, will have the leading hand. Once our coronation is over, we'll summon, as I said before, all our nobles. And, God approving my good intentions, no prince or lord shall have good reason to say, "God shorten Harry's happy life by a single day!"
Nay, you shall see my orchard, where, in an arbour, we will eat / a last year's pippin of mine own graffing, with a dish of caraways, / and so forth: come, cousin Silence: and then to bed.

No, you must see my orchard, where we'll sit in an arbour and eat one of last year's apples from a tree I grafted myself, with a dish of caraway seeds and so on. Come, cousin Silence, and then to bed.
'Fore God, you have here a goodly dwelling and a rich.
By God, you have a fine, rich house here.
Barren, barren, barren; beggars all, beggars all, Sir John: / marry, good air. Spread, Davy; spread, Davy: well said, Davy.
Barren, barren, barren; beggars all, beggars all, Sir John. Mind you, the air's good. Lay the cloth, Davy; lay the cloth, Davy. Well done, Davy.
This Davy serves you for good uses; he is your serving-man / and your husband.
This Davy is useful to you in many ways. He's your servant and your farm manager.
A good varlet, a good varlet, a very good varlet, Sir John: / by the mass, I have drunk too much sack at supper: a good / varlet. Now sit down, now sit down: come, cousin.
A good servant, a good servant, a very good servant, Sir John. By the mass, I drank too much sack at supper. A good servant. Now sit down, now sit down. Come, cousin.
Ah, sirrah! quoth-a, we shall / Do nothing but eat, and make good cheer,
Ah, my friend! As the song says, we'll "do nothing but eat, and make good cheer,"
And praise God for the merry year; / When flesh is cheap and females dear, / And lusty lads roam here and there / So merrily, / And ever among so merrily.
"And praise God for the merry year, when meat is cheap and women dear, and lusty lads roam here and there so merrily, and always so merrily."
There's a merry heart! Good Master Silence, I'll give you / a health for that anon.
There's a merry heart! Good Master Silence, I'll drink your health for that in a moment.
Give Master Bardolph some wine, Davy.
Give Master Bardolph some wine, Davy.
Sweet sir, sit; I'll be with you anon; most sweet sir, sit. / Master page, good master page, sit. Proface! / What you want in meat, we'll have in drink: / but you must bear; the heart's all.

Sweet sir, sit down; I'll be with you shortly. Most sweet sir, sit down. Master page, good master page, sit down. Much good may it do you! What we lack in food we'll make up in drink. But you must put up with it; the welcome is what matters.
Be merry, Master Bardolph; and, my little soldier there, / be merry.
Be merry, Master Bardolph; and you, my little soldier there, be merry.
Be merry, be merry, my wife has all;
"Be merry, be merry, my wife has all,"
For women are shrews, both short and tall; / 'Tis merry in hall when beards wag all; / And welcome merry Shrove-tide. / Be merry, be merry.
"For women are shrews, both short and tall; it's merry in the hall when all the beards wag; and welcome, merry Shrovetide. Be merry, be merry."
I did not think Master Silence had been a man of this mettle.
I didn't think Master Silence was a man of this spirit.
Who, I? I have been merry twice and once ere now.
Who, me? I've been merry once or twice before now.
There's a dish of leather-coats for you. [To Bardolph]
(To Bardolph) Here's a dish of russet apples for you.
Your worship! I'll be with you straight [To Bardolph] / A cup of wine, sir?
Your worship! I'll be with you at once. (To Bardolph) A cup of wine, sir?
A cup of wine that's brisk and fine,
"A cup of wine that's brisk and fine,"
And drink unto the leman mine; / And a merry heart lives long-a.
"And drink to my sweetheart, and a merry heart lives long."
An we shall be merry, now comes in the sweet o' the night.
If we're going to be merry, now comes the sweetest part of the night.
Health and long life to you, Master Silence!
Health and long life to you, Master Silence!
Fill the cup, and let it come,
"Fill the cup and pass it on,"
I'll pledge you a mile to the bottom.
"I'll drink to you though it's a mile to the bottom."

Honest Bardolph, welcome: if thou wantest anything and / wilt not call, beshrew thy heart. Welcome, my little tiny thief [to the Page] / and welcome indeed too. I'll drink to Master Bardolph, and to all / the cavaleros about London.

Honest Bardolph, welcome. If you want anything and don't ask for it, curse you. Welcome, my little tiny thief (to the Page), and welcome indeed too. I'll drink to Master Bardolph and to all the fine gentlemen in London.
I hope to see London once ere I die.
I hope to see London once before I die.
An I might see you there, Davy,—
If I could see you there, Davy —
By the mass, you'll crack a quart together, ha! will you not, / Master Bardolph?
By the mass, you'll down a quart together, ha! Won't you, Master Bardolph?
Yes, sir, from a two-quart pot.
By God's liggens, I thank thee: the knave will stick by thee, I / can assure thee that. A' will not out; he is true bred.
By God's little eyelids, thank you. The rascal will stick by you, I can assure you of that. He won't back out; he's well bred.
And I'll stick by him, sir.
And I'll stick by him, sir.
Why, there spoke a king. Lack nothing: be merry.
Why, that's spoken like a king. Want for nothing; be merry.
Look who's at door there, ho! who knocks?
Look who's at the door there! Who's knocking?
Why, now you have done me right.
(To Silence, seeing him empty a full glass) Why, now you've matched me drink for drink.
And dub me knight: / Samingo. / Is't not so?
"And dub me knight: Samingo." Isn't that right?
Is't so? Why then, say an old man can do somewhat.
Is it? Well then, admit that an old man can still do something.
An't please your worship, there's one Pistol come from the / court with news.
If it please your worship, there's a man called Pistol come from the court with news.
From the court? Let him come in.
From the court? Let him come in.
What wind blew you hither, Pistol?
What wind blew you here, Pistol?
Not the ill wind which blows no man to good. Sweet knight, / thou art now one of the greatest men in this realm.
Not the ill wind that blows nobody any good. Sweet knight, you are now one of the greatest men in this kingdom.
By'r lady, I think a' be, but goodman Puff of Barson.
By our Lady, I think he is, except for goodman Puff of Barson.

Puff! / Puff in thy teeth, most recreant coward base! / Sir John, I am thy Pistol and thy friend, / And helter-skelter have I rode to thee, / And tidings do I bring and lucky joys / And golden times and happy news of price.

Puff! Puff in your teeth, you base, cowardly deserter! Sir John, I'm your Pistol and your friend, and I've ridden helter-skelter to you, and I bring news and lucky joys and golden times and precious happy news.
I pray thee now, deliver them like a man of this world.
Please, now, deliver it like a man of this world.
A foutre for the world and worldlings base! / I speak of Africa and golden joys.
Damn the world and its low worldlings! I speak of Africa and golden joys.
O base Assyrian knight, what is thy news? / Let King Cophetua know the truth thereof.
Oh, low Assyrian knight, what's your news? Let King Cophetua know the truth of it.
And Robin Hood, Scarlet, and John.
Shall dunghill curs confront the Helicons? / And shall good news be baffled? / Then, Pistol, lay thy head in Furies' lap.
Shall dunghill dogs stand up to the Muses? And shall good news be disgraced? Then, Pistol, lay your head in the lap of the Furies.
Honest gentleman, I know not your breeding.
Honest gentleman, I don't know your upbringing.
Give me pardon, sir: if, sir, you come with news from the / court, I take it there's but two ways, either to utter them, or / conceal them. / I am, sir, under the king, in some authority.
Excuse me, sir. If you've come with news from the court, I take it there are only two ways: either to tell it or to keep it quiet. I have some authority, sir, under the King.
Under which king, Besonian? speak, or die.
Under which king, you beggar? Speak, or die.
A foutre for thine office! / Sir John, thy tender lambkin now is king; / Harry the Fifth's the man. I speak the truth. / When Pistol lies, do this; and fig me, like / The bragging Spaniard.

Damn your office! Sir John, your tender little lamb is king now. Harry the Fifth's the man. I'm telling the truth. When Pistol lies, do this (he makes a rude gesture), and give me the fig like the bragging Spaniard.
What, is the old king dead?
What, is the old King dead?
As nail in door: the things I speak are just.
As a doornail. What I say is true.
Away, Bardolph! saddle my horse. Master Robert Shallow, / choose what office thou wilt in the land, 'tis thine. Pistol, I / will double-charge thee with dignities.
Away, Bardolph! Saddle my horse. Master Robert Shallow, choose any office you like in the land; it's yours. Pistol, I'll load you with double honours.
O joyful day! / I would not take a knighthood for my fortune.
Oh, joyful day! I wouldn't swap my fortune for a knighthood.
What! I do bring good news.
What! Didn't I bring good news?
Carry Master Silence to bed. Master Shallow, my Lord Shallow,— / be what thou wilt; I am fortune's steward—get on thy boots: / we'll ride all night. O sweet Pistol! Away, Bardolph!
Carry Master Silence to bed. Master Shallow, my Lord Shallow — be whatever you like; I'm fortune's steward — get your boots on. We'll ride all night. Oh, sweet Pistol! Away, Bardolph!

Come, Pistol, utter more to me; and withal devise something to do / thyself good. Boot, boot, Master Shallow: I know the young king is / sick for me. Let us take any man's horses; the laws of England are at / my commandment. Blessed are they that have been my friends; and woe / to my lord chief-justice!

Come, Pistol, tell me more, and think of something to do yourself some good. Boots, boots, Master Shallow! I know the young King is longing for me. Let's take anyone's horses; the laws of England are at my command. Blessed are those who have been my friends, and woe to my Lord Chief Justice!
Let vultures vile seize on his lungs also! / "Where is the life that late I led?" say they: / Why, here it is; welcome these pleasant days!
Let vile vultures tear at his lungs too! "Where is the life I used to lead?" they say. Why, here it is. Welcome, these pleasant days!
No, thou arrant knave; I would to God that I might die, / that I might have thee hanged: thou hast drawn my shoulder out / of joint.
No, you out-and-out rogue. I wish to God I could die so that I could have you hanged. You've pulled my shoulder out of joint.
The constables have delivered her over to me; and she shall have / whipping-cheer enough, I warrant her: there hath been a man / or two lately killed about her.
The constables have handed her over to me, and she'll get a good feast of whipping, I promise her. A man or two have been killed recently over her.

Nut-hook, nut-hook, you lie. Come on; I'll tell thee what, thou / damned tripe-visaged rascal, an the child I now go with do / miscarry, thou wert better thou hadst struck thy mother, thou / paper-faced villain.

Nutcracker, nutcracker, you're lying. Come on, I'll tell you what, you damned tripe-faced rascal: if the child I'm carrying now miscarries, you'd have done better to hit your own mother, you paper-faced villain.
O the Lord, that Sir John were come! he would make this a / bloody day to somebody. But I pray God the fruit of her womb / miscarry!
Oh Lord, if only Sir John were here! He'd make this a bloody day for somebody. But I pray to God the fruit of her womb miscarries!
If it do, you shall have a dozen of cushions again; you / have but eleven now. Come, I charge you both go with me; for the / man is dead that you and Pistol beat amongst you.
If it does, you'll have your dozen cushions back again; you've only got eleven now. Come on, I order you both to come with me, because the man you and Pistol beat between you is dead.

I'll tell you what, you thin man in a censer, I will have you as / soundly swinged for this,—you blue-bottle rogue, you filthy famished / correctioner, if you be not swinged, I'll forswear half-kirtles.
I'll tell you what, you thin man in an incense-burner, I'll have you soundly beaten for this — you bluebottle rogue, you filthy starving whipper — if you're not beaten, I'll give up wearing skirts.
Come, come, you she knight-errant, come.
Come on, come on, you female knight-errant, come on.
O God, that right should thus overcome might! Well, of / sufferance comes ease.
Oh God, that right should overcome might like this! Well, after suffering comes relief.
Come, you rogue, come; bring me to a justice.
Come on, you rogue, come on. Take me to a magistrate.
Yes, come on, you starved bloodhound.
Come, you thin thing; come, you rascal!
Come on, you thin thing; come on, you rascal!
'Twill be two o'clock ere they come from the / coronation: dispatch, dispatch.
It'll be two o'clock before they come back from the coronation. Hurry, hurry.
Stand here by me, Master Robert Shallow; I will make the / king do you grace: I will leer upon him as a' comes by; and do / but mark the countenance that he will give me.
Stand here beside me, Master Robert Shallow. I'll make the King show you favour. I'll give him a look as he comes by, and just watch the expression he gives me.
God bless thy lungs, good knight!
God bless your lungs, good knight!

Come here, Pistol; stand behind me. O, if I had had to have / made new liveries, I would have bestowed the thousand pound I / borrowed of you. But 'tis no matter; this poor show doth better: / this doth infer the zeal I had to see him.

Come here, Pistol; stand behind me. Oh, if I'd had time to have new uniforms made, I'd have spent the thousand pounds I borrowed from you. But it doesn't matter. This shabby appearance is better; it shows how eager I was to see him.
It shows my earnestness of affection,—
It shows how earnest my affection is —
It doth, it doth, it doth.
It does, it does, it does.
As it were, to ride day and night; and not to deliberate, not to / remember, not to have patience to shift me,—
As it were, to ride day and night, and not to stop to think, not to remember, not to have the patience to change my clothes —
But to stand stained with travel, and sweating with desire to / see him; thinking of nothing else, putting all affairs else in / oblivion, as if there were nothing else to be done but to see him.
But to stand here stained from travelling and sweating with desire to see him, thinking of nothing else, forgetting all other business, as if there were nothing else to do but see him.
'Tis "semper idem," for "obsque hoc nihil est:" 'tis all in / every part.
It's "always the same", for "without this there is nothing". It's all in every part.

My knight, I will inflame thy noble liver, / And make thee rage. / Thy Doll, and Helen of thy noble thoughts, / Is in base durance and contagious prison; / Haled thither / By most mechanical and dirty hand: / Rouse up revenge from ebon den with fell Alecto's snake, / For Doll is in. Pistol speaks nought but truth.

My knight, I'll set your noble liver on fire and make you rage. Your Doll, the Helen of your noble thoughts, is locked up in a low, infectious prison, dragged there by the dirtiest working-class hands. Rouse revenge from her black den with fierce Alecto's snake, because Doll is inside. Pistol speaks nothing but the truth.
There roar'd the sea, and trumpet-clangor sounds.
There roared the sea, and the trumpets blare.
God save thy grace, King Hal; my royal Hal!
God save your grace, King Hal, my royal Hal!
The heavens thee guard and keep, most royal imp of fame!
May the heavens guard and keep you, most royal child of fame!
God save thee, my sweet boy!
God save you, my sweet boy!
My lord chief-justice, speak to that vain man.
My Lord Chief Justice, speak to that foolish man.
Have you your wits? know you what 'tis you speak?
Are you in your right mind? Do you know what you're saying?
My king! my Jove! I speak to thee, my heart!
My king! My Jove! I'm speaking to you, my heart!

I know thee not, old man: fall to thy prayers; / How ill white hairs become a fool and jester! / I have long dream'd of such a kind of man, / So surfeit-swell'd, so old, and so profane; / But, being awaked, I do despise my dream. / Make less thy body hence, and more thy grace; / Leave gormandizing; know the grave doth gape / For thee thrice wider than for other men. / Reply not to me with a fool-born jest: / Presume not that I am the thing I was; / For God doth know, so shall the world perceive, / That I have turn'd away my former self; / So will I those that kept me company. / When thou dost hear I am as I have been, / Approach me, and thou shalt be as thou wast, / The tutor and the feeder of my riots: / Till then, I banish thee, on pain of death, / As I have done the rest of my misleaders, / Not to come near our person by ten mile. / For competence of life I will allow you, / That lack of means enforce you not to evils: / And, as we hear you do reform yourselves, / We will, according to your strengths and qualities, / Give you advancement. Be it your charge, my lord, / To see perform'd the tenour of our word. / Set on.

I don't know you, old man. Say your prayers. How badly white hair suits a fool and a jester! I've long dreamed of a man like this, so swollen with excess, so old and so irreverent, but now that I'm awake I despise my dream. From now on make your body smaller and your virtue greater. Give up gluttony. Know that the grave gapes three times wider for you than for other men. Don't answer me with a jest born of folly. Don't imagine I'm the thing I was, because God knows, and the world will see, that I have turned away my former self, and so I will turn away those who kept me company. When you hear that I'm as I used to be, come to me, and you shall be what you were, the teacher and supplier of my riots. Until then I banish you, on pain of death, as I have the rest of those who led me astray, not to come within ten miles of me. I'll give you enough to live on, so that lack of money doesn't drive you to crime, and when we hear that you've reformed yourselves, we'll promote you according to your abilities and qualities. My lord, it will be your job to see that what we've said is carried out. Move on.
Master Shallow, I owe you a thousand pounds.
Master Shallow, I owe you a thousand pounds.
Yea, marry, Sir John; which I beseech you to let me have / home with me.
Yes, indeed, Sir John, which I beg you to let me take home with me.

That can hardly be, Master Shallow. Do not you grieve at this; / I shall be sent for in private to him: look you, he must seem / thus to the world: fear not your advancements; I will be the man yet / that shall make you great.

That can hardly be, Master Shallow. Don't be upset by this. I'll be sent for in private. You see, he has to look like this to the world. Don't worry about your promotion; I'll still be the man to make you great.
I cannot perceive how, unless you give me your doublet / and stuff me out with straw. I beseech you, good Sir John, let me / have five hundred of my thousand.
I can't see how, unless you give me your jacket and stuff me out with straw. I beg you, good Sir John, let me have five hundred of my thousand.
Sir, I will be as good as my word: this that you heard was / but a colour.
Sir, I'll be as good as my word. What you heard was only a pretence.
A colour that I fear you will die in, Sir John.
A pretence I'm afraid you'll die in, Sir John.
Fear no colours: go with me to dinner: come, Lieutenant / Pistol; come, Bardolph: I shall be sent for soon at night.
Don't fear pretences. Come and have dinner with me. Come, Lieutenant Pistol; come, Bardolph. I'll be sent for early tonight.
Go, carry Sir John Falstaff to the Fleet: / Take all his company along with him.
Go, take Sir John Falstaff to the Fleet prison. Take all his companions with him.
I cannot now speak: I will hear you soon. / Take them away.
I can't speak now. I'll hear you soon. Take them away.
Si fortuna me tormenta, spero me contenta.
If fortune torments me, hope contents me.

I like this fair proceeding of the king's: / He hath intent his wonted followers / Shall all be very well provided for; / But all are banish'd till their conversations / Appear more wise and modest to the world.
I like this fair action of the King's. He intends that his usual followers will all be very well provided for, but they're all banished until their behaviour looks wiser and more decent to the world.
The king hath call'd his parliament, my lord.
The King has summoned his parliament, my lord.

I will lay odds that, ere this year expire, / We bear our civil swords and native fire / As far as France: I heard a bird so sing, / Whose music, to my thinking, pleased the king. / Come, will you hence?
I'll bet that before this year is over we'll carry our swords and our national fire as far as France. I heard a bird singing that song, and its music, I think, pleased the King. Come, will you go?

First my fear; then my courtesy; last my speech. My fear is, your / displeasure; my courtesy, my duty; and my speech, to beg your / pardons. If you look for a good speech now, you undo me: for / what I have to say is of mine own making; and what indeed I / should say will, I doubt, prove mine own marring. But to the / purpose, and so to the venture. Be it known to you, as it is very / well, I was lately here in the end of a displeasing play, to pray / your patience for it and to promise you a better. I meant indeed to / pay you with this; which, if like an ill venture it come unluckily / home, I break, and you, my gentle creditors, lose. Here I promised / you I would be and here I commit my body to your mercies: bate me / some and I will pay you some and, as most debtors do, promise you / infinitely. / If my tongue cannot entreat you to acquit me, will you command me to / use my legs? and yet that were but light payment, to dance out of / your debt. But a good conscience will make any possible satisfaction, / and so would I. All the gentlewomen here have forgiven me: if the / gentlemen will not, then the gentlemen do not agree with the / gentlewomen, which was never seen before in such an assembly. / One word more, I beseech you. If you be not too much cloy'd with fat / meat, our humble author will continue the story, with Sir John in it, / and make you merry with fair Katharine of France: where, for any / thing I know, Falstaff shall die of a sweat, unless already a' be / killed with your hard opinions; for Oldcastle died a martyr, and this / is not the man. / My tongue is weary; when my legs are too, I will bid you good night: / and so kneel down before you; but, indeed, to pray for the queen.

First my fear, then my bow, and last my speech. My fear is your displeasure; my bow, my duty; and my speech, to ask your pardon. If you're expecting a good speech now, you'll ruin me, because what I have to say is my own invention, and what I ought to say will, I'm afraid, be my undoing. But to the point, and so to the risk. Let me tell you, as you know very well, I was here recently at the end of an unpopular play, to ask your patience with it and promise you a better one. I meant to pay you back with this one; and if, like a failed trading voyage, it comes home unluckily, I'm bankrupt and you, my kind creditors, lose. I promised you I'd be here, and here I put myself at your mercy. Let me off some of it and I'll pay you some, and, like most debtors, promise you endlessly. If my tongue can't persuade you to let me off, will you order me to use my legs? And yet that would be light payment, to dance my way out of your debt. But a good conscience will make any repayment it can, and so would I. All the ladies here have forgiven me. If the gentlemen won't, then the gentlemen don't agree with the ladies, which has never been seen before in such a gathering. One word more, please. If you're not too sick of fat meat, our humble author will continue the story, with Sir John in it, and amuse you with fair Katharine of France, where, for all I know, Falstaff will die of a fever, unless he's already been killed by your harsh opinions; for Oldcastle died a martyr, and this is not the man. My tongue is tired; when my legs are too, I'll say good night to you. And so I kneel before you — but in fact to pray for the Queen.
